20250-the-fifth-battalion-highland-light:
The Fifth Battalion, Highland Light Infantry, kept a record of its war from 1914. The battalion moves fast over the span from mobilization to active service. Those early events now seem of small interest, the writers admit. Later readers, they felt, would want the front itself above all.

Glasgow men filled the ranks of this city battalion in wartime. Its path ran through training camps to trenches in France and beyond. Battalion histories name actions and losses that grand histories blur. This record lets families trace one unit's hard road through the war.
22563-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, volume 146, dated January 28, 1914, finds comedy in diplomacy. The American Ambassador, readers were told last week, has a cold. He is confined to his room at the Embassy by it.

Colds, Punch observes, are nasty catching things among people. The staff, it jokes, show cowardice in their chief's confinement. They have apparently locked their chief in his room against infection. Such a squib shows the weekly's habit of deflating dignitaries gently. This issue appeared months before the First World War began. Its lightness reads poignantly against what followed for its laughing readers. Punch kept London smiling on the edge of catastrophe.
22573-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, volume 146, dated February 11, 1914, turns to boxing politics. Kid Lewis's victory last week over Paul Til prompts its joke. Many Germans, Punch claims, hold a strong opinion about that result.

The French Government, they supposedly believe, protected the Entente at all costs. France was determined that the alliance should not be imperilled then. So France sent over a French boxer an Englishman could defeat. The joke ties sport to the alliances arming Europe for war. Within months, those alliances would pull nations into real fighting. Readers today feel the chill under the weekly's light tone. Punch still makes the item funny, which is its own historical interest.
22576-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, volume 146, dated February 18, 1914, invents books for a chancellor. An enterprising publisher has supposedly persuaded Lloyd George to write. Several works of creative fancy are promised at an early date.

Essays on Lamb (shorn) heads the imaginary list of titles. The Fortunes of Montrose follows as another promised fancy work. Punch's joke turns a busy politician into a hack author overnight. Readers were meant to laugh at titles twisted from real books. Such squibs filled the weekly between longer, sharper cartoons and verses. This issue sits in the last calm spring before war. Its trifling gives historians a taste of ordinary Edwardian laughter.
22940-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Darkness falls on Tooting in Punch's issue of April 15, 1914, from volume 146. Punch picks up a Mail report of failed electric lighting across parts of Tooting and Mitcham one evening. One host in Garden Avenue had invited a dozen friends to a card party. He secured candles, and the party played on in their dim light.

That small mishap gets the full Punch treatment, turned into a paragraph of dry delight. The rest of the number mixes cartoons, verses, and jokes from the last spring of peace before the Great War. Nobody in its pages knows what August will bring. Reading it now carries that shadow. As a slice of Edwardian humor, the issue is complete and characteristic.
22989-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Lancastrians dine in London in Punch's issue of April 1, 1914, from volume 146. London's Lancastrians gathered for their yearly dinner the week before, Punch notes in passing. It would have been a kindly act, Punch suggests, to offer a seat to Mr. Masterman, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, now back in town.

That gentle prod at a minister sets the number's peacetime tone. Jokes turn on dinners, clubs, counties, and the small vanities of public men, all before the war rearranged every subject. Cartoons and verse fill out the week's entertainment. Read today, the issue's calm is its most striking feature. It catches London laughing in the last spring when its favorite targets were as mild as a missed invitation.
23032-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
An elephant goes collecting in Punch's issue of April 8, 1914, from volume 146. Kensington's Reservists need a headquarters, so Camp Week hires a full-sized elephant to tour the main streets collecting coins. Punch proposes training the beast to tread, purely by accident, on refusers' toes.

The joke catches the number's world, suburban reservists, charity weeks, and a London still treating soldiering as a part-time hobby. Four months later that world ended. The rest of the issue keeps the same light step, cartoons and paragraphs unaware. Its innocence, preserved whole, is what makes it moving now.
23087-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Hall Caine takes a ribbing in Punch's issue of March 18, 1914, from volume 146. Caine prefaced his serial with a note called Why I Wrote the Story. Punch summarizes the note's purpose as shifting blame, or at least sharing it around. One day, it seems, Mr. Caine heard the story on which the novel rests.

Punch loved puncturing bestsellers, and Caine's solemn self-importance made a broad target. The rest of the number keeps the peacetime mix, cartoons, verse, and theatre jokes for a London amusing itself. Spring 1914 issues like this one read now with an ache their makers never felt. The laughter is genuine, the targets small, and the abyss four months away and wholly invisible.
a-midsummer-night-s-dream-pg1514: Lovers flee to the woods, fairies quarrel over a servant boy, and a troupe of clumsy workmen rehearse a play in this edition of Shakespeare's most enchanted comedy. Puck's love-juice sets every heart astray until dawn puts things right. The most magical night in all the theater, freshly readable here.
abrams-human-energy-1914:
Albert Abrams, a San Francisco doctor, set out his healing theory in Human Energy in 1914. The book is the founding statement of radionics, the fringe practice he built his name on. Abrams claimed the body gives off fine electronic signals that a trained hand can read.

He argues that each disease sends out its own rate of vibration, which can be picked up from a drop of blood. From that rate, he says, a doctor can name the illness and judge its strength. His 'electronic reactions' later filled clinics with his black boxes, and drew sharp fire from medical science.
arxiv-2511-20414:
Cáceres-Burgos and colleagues forecast black hole mergers in the universe's first billion years. Their 2025 paper responds to surprises from the James Webb Space Telescope. Webb found far more active galactic nuclei at early times than expected. Counts at high redshift exceed older predictions by ten to one hundred times. Two seed stories could explain those black holes.

Light seeds near 150 solar masses must gorge beyond normal limits. Heavy seeds start far bigger. The team modeled the heavy-seed route with their Delphi code. Delphi tracks galaxies growing inside dark matter halos over time. Black holes merged either instantly or after a delay. Extreme spin settings bracketed how fast masses could grow. Matching Webb data forced accretion ten to one hundred times stronger than before. The instant model predicts about twenty-eight mergers per year at early epochs. The delayed model predicts about twenty per year instead.
arxiv-2511-20514:
Baker and colleagues track biopsy needles in 3D so clinicians stop guessing tip locations. Their 2025 paper presents an ultrasound system with a photoacoustic beacon. Liver biopsies need exact needle tips to avoid harm and repeats. Ultrasound images often hide tips in tissue or at steep angles. Many services fall back on slow, ionizing CT guidance instead.

A fiber-optic transmitter inside the needle bevel emits ultrasound pulses. Sixteen receivers on a sparse array around the probe listen. Time-of-flight from the beacon fixes the tip's 3D position. That position overlays onto live B-mode images quantitatively. In water the average tracking error measured 1.96 millimeters. In ex vivo tissue it held at 2.05 millimeters average error. Repeatability within the imaging plane stayed below one millimeter. Twelve clinicians tried simulated biopsies with the system. Less experienced users found procedures notably easier. Accuracy sits close to the needle's own diameter.
arxiv-2511-20614:
Ouyang and colleagues build an editor that fixes AI images by checking them against a reference. Their 2025 paper presents ImageCritic for consistent customized generation. Generated images often garble fine details like text and logos. A reference image holds the truth those details should match. Post-editing guided by the reference is their answer.

Training triplets pair a reference, a degraded image, and the target. Vision-language selection plus explicit degradation built that dataset. Studying the model's attention suggested two key components. An attention alignment loss steers focus to mismatched details. A detail encoder supplies the fine features needed for repair. Inside an agent loop, the critic finds and fixes flaws over rounds. Local edits handle complex scenes piece by piece. Experiments spanned open and closed generation models. Detail consistency improved significantly over existing editors. Multilingual text in images was corrected as well.
arxiv-2511-20714:
The Inferix Team, based at Alibaba's DAMO Academy, introduces in 2025 a software engine built for running world models. World models generate long interactive videos that act as simulators for games, robots, and agents. The newest ones use block diffusion, generating video in blocks: diffusion fills each block while earlier blocks condition what comes next. General engines built for chatbots or classic video diffusion fit this pattern poorly.

Inferix organises the work around block-wise KV cache management, borrowing the memory trick that lets language models reuse computations, so videos stay coherent instead of drifting or forgetting. It adds parallel strategies across graphics cards, low-bit quantised computing, streaming, and profiling tools. The need is stark: the team notes that generating a 5-second video with the Wan2.1 14B model takes about 6,800 seconds on a single NVIDIA H20 card. A bundled benchmark, LV-Bench, grades minute-long generation in fine detail.
arxiv-2511-20814:
Md Tanvirul Alam and colleagues release in 2025 Sphinx, a synthetic playground that stress-tests the visual reasoning of AI models. Instead of photographs, Sphinx generates puzzles from motifs, tiles, charts, icons, and geometric shapes, each with a verifiable ground-truth answer. Its 25 task types, in a benchmark of 2,500 questions, cover sequence prediction, chart interpretation, spatial reasoning, geometric transformations, and symmetry detection, the building blocks of visual thought.

The results humble the frontier: GPT-5, the strongest model tested, scored only 51.1 percent accuracy, well below human performance. Because every answer is machine-checkable, the environment doubles as training ground. The authors show that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards sharply raises model accuracy on Sphinx tasks. The gains transferred to external visual reasoning benchmarks too, suggesting that practising on synthetic primitives builds genuine skill rather than test-specific tricks. Code and data are public, inviting others to generate puzzles at scale.
arxiv-2511-20914:
Vivek Pandey and Nader Motee build in 2025 a theory for how failures cascade when autonomous agents meet up under uncertainty. Rendezvous is time-critical, and communication delays plus slightly wrong system parameters can push one agent off course, then its neighbours. The authors model the team as a time-delayed dynamical network. True parameters are assumed to lie in bounded sets around nominal values, and risk is judged against the worst plausible distribution, not just the nominal one.

Their tool is a conditional distributionally robust functional built on a bivariate Gaussian model of pairs of agents. It yields a closed-form risk expression linking delays, network structure, noise levels, and failure modes. The formulas expose which parameters collective safety is most sensitive to, giving designers concrete levers. Extensive simulations confirm the theory. The paper extends the pair's earlier framework from vehicle platoons to the rendezvous problem.
arxiv-2511-21014:
Raymond Matson and Peter Samuelson connect in 2025 two algebraic machines for studying knots: stated skein algebras and double affine Hecke algebras, or DAHAs. Skein modules turn links in a manifold into algebraic objects; for a thickened surface, stacking one tangle atop another gives the skein an algebra structure. Stated skeins add signs, plus or minus, decorating tangle endpoints at the boundary. DAHAs, introduced by Cherednik to settle Macdonald's conjectures, deform group algebras in two parameters.

For sl2, they relate stated Kauffman bracket skein theory to its DAHA. Along the way they find generators for the skein algebra of the punctured torus, a test case with a presentation by Bullock and Przytycki. At the specialisation where DAHA parameters equal 1, the algebra collapses to the group algebra of the root and weight lattices joined with the Weyl group, grounding the comparison. The bridge lets knot and representation tools cross over.
arxiv-2511-21714:
Paweł Batorski and Paul Swoboda write a fresh prompt for every single input instead of one prompt per task, in 2025. Language models are exquisitely sensitive to phrasing, but automatic prompt optimizers need large task datasets, hours of optimization, and still return one static prompt. Their system, GPS, is a general per-sample prompter needing no task-specific tuning at all.

The prompter itself was trained by reinforcement learning on a suite of mathematical, logical, and programming tasks, with a novel regularization suited to per-sample generation. Minimum Bayes Risk decoding stabilizes its outputs. On tasks it never trained on, GPS placed second among baselines at text simplification, third at summarization, and on par at classification, while rivals had trained on those very tasks. For in-domain prompting it reached state of the art on the GSM8K math benchmark. Adaptive, input-specific prompts emerge as a practical paradigm.
arxiv-2511-22314:
Wu, a researcher in decentralized finance, builds the first large dataset mapping how crypto lending protocols owe each other money. When one DeFi protocol fails, losses cascade through its creditors, as the Terra and FTX collapses showed, yet no public data described this web of inter-protocol credit exposure. DeXposure fills the gap with 43.7 million exposure entries covering roughly 4,300 protocols across 602 blockchains from 2020 to 2025, recording who lends to whom, in what asset, and how the links evolve over time.

Graph clustering recovers communities of linked protocols, vector autoregression traces how the Terra and FTX shocks propagated, and temporal graph networks predict future links. Released openly, the dataset lets researchers measure contagion channels instead of treating each protocol's risk in isolation. Systemic-risk dashboards for DeFi can now be built from measured exposures rather than protocol self-reporting.
arxiv-2512-00114:
The neutron skin of a nucleus is the thin layer where neutrons extend beyond the protons. Andreas Vitsos, Leonora Misciattelli Mocenigo Soranzo, and You Zhou study the skin of calcium-48 in a 2025 article. Their evidence comes from collective flow in collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider.

The team uses a method nicknamed imaging by smashing. It links the flow of debris from ultra-relativistic collisions back to the structure of the colliding nuclei. Most earlier work targeted nuclear shape, such as deformation, rather than skin thickness. Measuring the skin helps test nuclear models and connects to the physics of neutron stars. The findings feed into wider efforts to pin down how neutrons arrange themselves in heavy nuclei.
arxiv-2512-00214:
Grammar research increasingly runs on large annotated text collections, yet analyzing them still takes heavy technical effort. A 2025 study examines how agentic large language models could streamline that work across languages. The models reason over annotated corpora instead of single example sentences.

The goal is interpretable, data-grounded answers to linguistic questions, produced with less manual setup. Corpus-grounded agents could help linguists test claims about grammar against real usage at scale. The study speaks to a wider shift in the humanities, where language models are becoming research assistants rather than just text generators. Multilingual coverage matters because grammar traditions and corpora differ sharply across languages. The authors explore the approach rather than claim a finished system.
arxiv-2512-00314:
Counting the traces a formal language can produce is a basic question in theoretical computer science. Alexis de Colnet, Kuldeep Meel, and Umang Mathur study counting and sampling traces in regular languages in 2025. Traces account for which actions can run independently and commute.

The setup fixes an alphabet with an independence relation, a regular language given by a finite automaton, and a length given in unary. Counting and sampling underpin verification of concurrent systems, where independent actions interleave freely. The work clarifies how hard these problems are, guiding tool builders who model real concurrent software. Regular languages are the simplest language class, which makes the hardness results sharper.
arxiv-2512-00614:
Multi-agent systems let language-model agents work as a team with no central controller. Goutham Nalagatla extends AgentNet in 2025 with hierarchical coordination and privacy-preserving knowledge sharing, aiming at scalable autonomous systems. AgentNet showed fully decentralized coordination through dynamic directed acyclic graph topologies.

Limitations remain: scalability with large agent populations, message overhead, missing privacy guarantees, and weak use of shared compute. The extension attacks those gaps with hierarchy and protected sharing. As agent groups grow, coordination that preserves privacy becomes a must for use in business and public systems. Hierarchy gives the coordinator-free system a way to organize very large agent groups. Privacy-preserving sharing lets agents cooperate without exposing their raw knowledge. For firms that plan fleets of such aides, the gain is a way to grow. More aides can join, share what they know, and still keep each firm's facts safe.
arxiv-2512-01014:
Ajneet Dhillon, Nicole Lemire, Jonathan Martin, and Yidi Wang study approximation for classifying stacks in a 2025 math paper. A classifying stack packages all the ways a group can act into a single geometric object. Strong approximation asks whether solutions over local data can be glued into a global one.

The Brauer-Manin obstruction is a known test that can block such gluing. The authors prove that its étale version is the only obstruction to strong approximation for these stacks. The result holds when the group is linear algebraic over a number field. A single complete test simplifies a hard existence question across arithmetic geometry.
arxiv-2512-01114:
Yukinari Sumino proposes a way to measure a bound quark system's wave function in a 2025 physics paper. The wave function of quarkonium, a heavy quark bound to its antiquark, is defined inside potential nonrelativistic QCD, an effective theory for such systems. Until now it had no direct experimental probe.

Sumino uses the three-body decay of the Bc meson, which contains both a bottom and a charm quark. He shows the momentum distribution of the spectator charm quark mirrors the squared wave function of the parent state. If measured, this would be the first experimental handle on a quantity long treated as theory-only.
arxiv-2512-01214:
Hang Wu and five coauthors improve detection of manipulated media in a 2025 paper. Multimodal manipulation, where images, audio, and text are faked together, threatens the reliability of information people receive. Current detection methods often overlook localized information, even though manipulations usually occur in specific areas, especially facial regions.

Their system, M4-BLIP, adds face-enhanced local analysis to a multimodal model. By inspecting faces and other local regions closely, it hunts for the small inconsistencies that global checks miss. Better local detection could help platforms and journalists flag deepfakes that look convincing at a glance.
arxiv-2512-01314:
Pei Yang and co-authors build a tool that strips hidden marks from images. Hidden marks, or watermarks, prove who owns a file. They guard art, photos, and AI-made work from theft. A mark that is easy to strip gives weak proof.

Their tool, TokenPure, tests how strong those marks are. It uses a diffusion model to clean an image while keeping its look. The tool splits the image into parts for form and parts for look. That split helps it erase the mark with less harm. Weak marks found this way push makers to build stronger ones.
arxiv-2512-01614:
Armen Asratian and Carl Johan Casselgren study an edge coloring transform index for graphs. Edge coloring paints edges so touching edges differ. The transform index is the least steps to turn any valid coloring into any other. Steps recolor one edge at a time while staying valid.

That index tells how flexible a coloring system is. Low values mean colorings can be reshaped with ease. The work builds theory for that index across graphs. Flexible recoloring matters for scheduling and network tasks where colors must shift without breaking rules. Recoloring steps mirror live network upkeep, where links change class as loads shift but service rules must hold at every step between.
arxiv-2512-01914:
Rooftop solar panels and electric vehicles are reshaping how buildings draw power, hour by hour, in ways grid operators struggle to predict. Aiko Fias, Md Umar Hashmi, and Geert Deconinck compare methods in 2025 for quantifying that uncertainty in net electricity load profiles.

They study three building types, homes, industrial sites, and offices, under growing adoption of solar generation and vehicle charging. The question is which metrics honestly capture the spread of possible loads at the local distribution level. Choosing the right measure matters, because planners size equipment and set prices around these uncertain forecasts.
arxiv-2512-02014:
Most AI systems either understand images or generate them, and unified models try to do both in one framework. Zhiheng Liu and a large team present Tuna in 2025, a native unified multimodal model built around a single continuous representation of visual content.

Tuna cascades two encoders: a variational autoencoder that compresses images, and a representation encoder that adds meaning. The shared representation space then serves both understanding and generation, for images and video alike, processed end to end. A common visual language inside the model could make its two talents reinforce rather than compete with each other.
arxiv-2512-02214:
Reinforcement learning agents come in many configurations, and picking the wrong one wastes training. Aida Afshar and Aldo Pacchiano study in 2025 online model selection: a selector that watches a class of learning agents during training and adaptively picks the configuration that is performing best.

The aim is to show improved efficiency and performance from weaving selection into the training procedure itself, rather than tuning beforehand by trial and error. Good selection adapts as learning progresses, since the best configuration early may not stay best. Their results matter for practitioners who cannot afford to train every variant of an agent to completion.
arxiv-2512-02314:
The Alexander polynomial of a knot-like link encodes its crossings in a list of coefficients. Fox conjectured in 1962 that for alternating links, those coefficients rise and then fall like a trapezoid. Karola Mészáros, Melissa Sherman-Bennett, and Alexander Vidinas attack the conjecture in 2025 from an unexpected side: dimers.

Dimers are pairings of adjacent points, a statistical mechanics staple, and the authors build a dimer model whose counts mirror the polynomial's coefficients. Special cases of the conjecture have fallen recently, including special alternating links, but the general statement remains open. A dimer viewpoint could supply the combinatorial grip that direct knot theory has lacked.
arxiv-2512-02414:
Satellites and ground stations have been attacked since at least 1977, when a transmission signal was hijacked, yet no single dataset records these incidents properly. Ekzhin Ear and five co-authors build in 2025 a framework for characterizing cyber attacks against space infrastructure when much of the data are missing.

Reports of such attacks are scattered across media stories with many details absent, so the framework is designed for incomplete evidence. Their case study shows how characterization can proceed anyway. As space systems become critical infrastructure, understanding their attack history is a prerequisite for defending them, even when the record is patchy.
arxiv-2512-02714:
Mohsen Fathi, Ariel Guzmán, and J.R. Villanueva compute the fading tones of a black hole in a modified theory of electromagnetism. Quasinormal modes are the characteristic vibrations a disturbed black hole rings with as it settles. Their hole is static, sits in anti-de Sitter space, and is sourced by a Plebański type nonlinear electrodynamics model.

The authors study axial electromagnetic modes, setting waves to fall into the horizon and vanish suitably at the boundary. Mode frequencies test both the hole and the modified theory. Such catalogs guide future comparisons with gravitational wave data. Each tone in the list is a test the next wave of finds can check as new holes are heard to ring.
arxiv-2512-02914:
Zhonghao He and three co-authors grade language models on whether longer reasoning actually tracks truth. Reasoning methods have lifted model performance, raising hopes for accurate, reliable answers. Yet emerging evidence suggests step by step reasoning can entrench early beliefs instead of correcting them.

Their Martingale Score is an unsupervised metric for Bayesian rationality in model reasoning. It checks whether belief updates behave as honest probability updates should. A cheap truth tracking metric could flag models that sound more certain the longer they talk, without becoming more right. A score that needs no gold set can be run each week. That is how drift gets caught while it is still small and cheap to fix.
arxiv-2512-03014:
Matthew Dutson and three co-authors adapt still image models for video without letting outputs flicker. Frame based networks applied one frame at a time often show temporal inconsistency. Time varying corruptions in the input make the flicker worse, as each frame is cleaned differently.

Their Instant Video Models act as universal adapters for image based networks. The adapters stabilize inference and add robustness across the video. One adapter for many models saves retraining each network for video, a gain for restoration, enhancement, and analysis tools that now work frame by frame. One wrap for many tools is a thrift that counts. Each tool would else need weeks of new work to run on film at a fair rate of speed.
arxiv-2512-03414:
Fluid with tiny particles flows differently near a flat plate. Christian Thomas, Sharon Stephen, Jitesh Gajjar, and Paul Griffiths study that flow's stability in this 2025 work. They examine a nanofluid boundary layer, the thin zone where flow meets the surface.

Their two-phase model includes Brownian motion and thermophoresis, two effects that move small particles. It builds on earlier work in the field. Stability analysis shows when smooth flow breaks into disturbances. Such knowledge helps design cooling and coating systems that use nanofluids. Particle motion effects can trigger instability earlier than a simple fluid model predicts.
arxiv-2512-03614:
Yang-yang Tan and co-authors model how matter near the QCD critical endpoint falls behind when conditions change. Heavy-ion physics hunts this point in the map of quark matter, where relaxation should crawl. Their 2025 relaxation model contains no tunable phenomenological knobs, a deliberate discipline.

Simulations extracted how long the critical mode takes to settle across the phase diagram. Only a narrow band radiating from the endpoint along the phase boundary showed dramatically stretched relaxation times. Outside it, times collapsed, confining the dynamic critical region to a small patch. Chemical freeze-out curves, where particle abundances lock in, felt the slowing only mildly.
arxiv-2512-04114: Josiah Foster proves a result in algebraic geometry in a 2025 preprint, one that assumes one key claim. He shows the Lefschetz standard conjectures hold for the Kummer-type varieties he studies, in dimension four times d. The conjectures, part of Grothendieck's programme on cycles, ask whether certain operators on cohomology are given by cycles. The proof assumes a conjecture of Buchweitz and Flenner. The gain is a reduction. For this family of varieties, the Lefschetz package follows once that single input is granted.
arxiv-2512-04214:
Martin Taylor and Renato Velozo Ruiz study how a thin cosmic gas settles as the universe expands, using the Vlasov equation from plasma physics. Their setting is a slowly swelling space shaped like a torus, matched to standard cosmology models. The gas has no collisions, so smoothing must come from phase mixing, where streams moving at distinct speeds blur together. Their 2025 arXiv paper pins down exactly how fast that blur eats density contrasts.

For most expansion rates in their range, the spatial density fades at a set power-law pace. Once the average is stripped away, the rest fades faster thanks to phase mixing. Smooth starting data gain a boost that is fast but not quite exponential. At the borderline rate that fits a radiation-filled universe, the boost turns gentler and takes a logarithmic form. The proof sorts the mixing by frequency bands.
arxiv-2512-04514:
Jin Zhou, Hongliang Yang, Pengfei Xu, and co-authors present SPLICE, a way to edit three-dimensional shapes one part at a time. Neural shape models store forms as smooth fields, which gives fine control of surface detail. Yet older tools edit whole shapes at once, so moving a chair leg can warp the seat. Their 2025 arXiv paper gives each part its own code, restoring part-level control.

SPLICE encodes each part alone and places it with a soft ellipsoid that sets spot, size, and tilt. Dropping global context per part makes parts easy to move, swap, or resize. A global decoder with attention then blends the parts into one coherent shape. A guiding filter stops part features from leaking into the wrong places. The result is structure-aware editing that stays true to the source. Designers could rearrange product or character models with far less cleanup.
arxiv-2512-04614:
Han Dai, Shi Li, and Sijin Peng sharpen approximation algorithms for clustering problems that must run fast when the number of clusters is small. Clustering groups data points around a few centers; the minimum-norm version balances costs in a flexible way. The team studies fixed-parameter tractable time, where runtime may grow fast in the cluster count but stays tame in data size. Their 2025 arXiv paper gives tight results for the capacitated case, where each center can serve only so many points.

They achieve an approximation ratio just above three for general-norm capacitated clustering, and prove it best possible in this setting. Before this work, such a tight bound was known only for the capacitated median problem. As a bonus, the result yields a ratio of three for capacitated center clustering, beating the long-standing ratio of nine. The uncapacitated case gets fresh bounds as well.
arxiv-2512-04814:
Christopher Simic, Korbinian Riedhammer, and Tobias Bocklet describe their winning system for the FAME 2026 challenge, which tests whether a machine can match faces with voices. The challenge adds a hard twist: test voices speak languages the model never trained on. Face-voice association matters for media search and speaker tools. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds separate pipelines for face and voice, then joins them in one shared space.

Each pipeline extracts general features from its input. Extra features for age and gender support the match. Both streams are then projected into a shared embedding space, where matching pairs should land close together. Training uses an adaptive angular margin loss to sharpen the separation. The system took first place in the challenge, with an average equal-error rate near twenty-four percent. Cross-language face-voice matching could help archives tag speakers in footage worldwide.
arxiv-2512-05514:
Jarne Moens and Konstantin Zarembo study Wilson loops on the Coulomb branch of the most symmetric quantum field theory, the maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. A Wilson loop measures the phase a particle gathers around a closed path. On the Coulomb branch, where the theory's scalars take values, the loop's expectation is computed holographically. A surface stretching from the boundary contour to a brane in the bulk space does the computing.

The authors solve for those surfaces for a circular loop. They find it undergoes the Gross-Ooguri transition — a sharp switch between surface configurations — as the loop's radius and angular separation vary. They map the phase diagram of that transition. As a by-product, their results give evidence that the straight loop's expectation value is exact at tree level. The work sharpens the holographic dictionary for an observable in the best-understood example of gauge-gravity duality.
arxiv-2512-05614:
Chunjian Zhang, writing for the STAR Collaboration, reports a new way to learn the shape of an atomic nucleus by smashing nuclei together. The 2025 paper studies collisions of uranium-238, whose nucleus is stretched, with gold-197, whose nucleus is nearly round. When such nuclei collide at high energy, the spray of debris keeps a memory of the shapes that met. The team reads that memory in flow patterns.

By taking ratios between the uranium and gold results, most effects of the messy aftermath cancel out. What remains points to the uranium nucleus's own shape. The sums give shape values that match older, low energy measures. They also give the first hint, from this kind of test, that uranium-238 has a modest pear-like warp, called octupole deformation. The work shows brief, violent collisions can serve as a probe of nuclear shape.
arxiv-2512-05714:
Max Martin Gnewuch, Jan Philip Wahle, Terry Ruas, and Bela Gipp measure how deeply big technology firms have funded their way into artificial intelligence research. Over four decades, AI grew where universities and industry meet. The team gathered about fifty thousand papers from ten top AI conferences, published between 1998 and 2022, and traced millions of citations through the Scopus database.

Industry funding was rare before 2015, under two percent of papers, then jumped past eleven percent by 2020. Funded work also lands harder: in recent years, about twelve percent of industry funded papers reached high citation standing, against four percent for other funded work and two percent for unfunded work. The study finds funded research growing more insular, citing mostly other industry backed papers and fewer outside ones. It also leans toward recent work. The picture is of a field whose agenda is increasingly set by the firms with the deepest pockets.
arxiv-2512-05914:
E Schisano leads the ALMAGAL collaboration's sixth paper, charting how dense cores are arranged inside the massive gas clumps where star clusters are born. ALMA observations covered about a thousand clumps at a resolution of about a thousand astronomical units. This study focuses on the five hundred fourteen clumps rich enough to hold at least four dense cores each. The question is how fragmentation is organized in space as a clump evolves.

Cores usually sit in elliptical groups. In about three quarters of clumps, one characteristic spacing matches the thermal Jeans length. Younger clumps show wider separations, around twenty two thousand astronomical units, shrinking to about seven thousand in older ones. Arrangements stay fractal like, with central concentration appearing late. Mass segregation, heavy cores preferring the center, shows up in one hundred ten systems and grows commoner with age. Fragmentation starts messy and only slowly tidies.
arxiv-2512-06014:
Jiho Shin, Dominic Marshall, and Matthieu Komorowski run a head to head comparison of two chest X-ray foundation models on public data, the kind medical AI needs more of. Both turn X-rays into embeddings for simple classifiers. The contenders are Google's CXR-Foundation and Microsoft's MedImageInsight. The arenas are two open datasets, MIMIC-CXR and NIH ChestX-ray14. One pipeline and fixed classifiers kept the contest honest.

MedImageInsight edged ahead on most tasks. CXR-Foundation held up across the two datasets, a different virtue: performance that travels. Unlabeled clustering recovered disease specific groupings. The main ask is standard tests. Vendors report foundation model results on their own terms, making comparisons mush. Public data and fixed pipelines turn claims into measurements. Clinicians deserve that clarity when choosing systems.
arxiv-2512-06214:
Z Ali and M Abebe present a numerical method for pricing American put options, a common contract in finance. A put gives its holder the right to sell an asset at a set price, and an American put can be used at any time before it ends. That freedom to act early turns pricing into a moving boundary problem, where the best sale point shifts over time.

Their method fixes that moving boundary in place so the math sits on a steady grid, then solves it with a well known time stepping scheme. Tests show the prices come out stable and close to the true values, and the team proves the scheme keeps key signs and order in check under the right step sizes. Traders and risk staff need such fast, trust worthy pricing when early use is part of the deal.
arxiv-2512-06414:
Hossein Teimoori Faal and Hasan Khodakarami study arrays built from Pascal's triangle, the famous table of counting numbers. Their arrays take blocks of that table and record each block's determinant, a single number that sums how the block twists space. The team asks whether each row of such an array is log concave. That means each entry squared beats the product of its neighbors. They also ask whether that trait repeats without end under the same test.

They prove a clean split. The log concavity measure of one array factors into an entrywise product of two neighbors in the family. A second result shows this measure never grows when two such arrays are multiplied entry by entry. Joining the two proves every row of every array in the family is log concave at every depth. The result extends a celebrated theorem once known only for Pascal's triangle itself.
arxiv-2512-06714:
Tony Salloom, Okyay Kaynak, and Wei He forecast water demand in real time with a leaner neural network. Short term forecasts steer how water plants pump and store, so errors at the peaks, exactly when demand surges or crashes, hurt most. Deep models forecast well but carry huge parameter counts, and their worst errors land on those extreme points.

The team's fix starts with the data: they insert virtual points inside the real series, softening the sharp bends around extremes where models stumble. Their network pairs a gated recurrent unit, which tracks the sequence of past demand, with an unsupervised clustering step that builds new features, lifting accuracy while keeping the parameter count low. Trained on real records from two Chinese water plants, the model beat leading rivals and cut model complexity several fold. Better peak forecasts mean steadier supply at lower cost.
arxiv-2512-06814:
Dibyanayan Bandyopadhyay and co-authors want classifiers that read both images and text to explain themselves in plain words. Such models often act as black boxes, and a friendly explanation is worth little if it does not match how the model truly decided. Their framework, called CAuSE, aims to produce reasons that stay faithful to the model's inner steps. Faithfulness, here, means the stated reason reflects the real cause of the output.

CAuSE learns by swapping parts inside the model and watching how its answer changes. In theory, that training makes the explanation a true causal sketch of the classifier at work. The team also built a fresh measure of faithfulness for mixed image and text settings. CAuSE beat rival explainers on that measure across data sets and models, and the authors close by studying where it still fails.
arxiv-2512-07114:
Jue Wang and co-authors teach a soft robot to walk and swim by pretending, in a careful mathematical sense, that it is rigid. Their test animal is an amphibious robotic turtle whose limbs morph in shape. Soft materials make such robots adaptable, but simulators for soft bodies are too slow and shaky for training, while rigid-body simulators run fast yet miss the squish. The team's surrogate approach adds hidden variables inside a rigid simulation to stand for the soft deformation.

Deformation shows up as changes in each limb's effective length and center of mass. Reinforcement learning then trains walking policies while those variables are randomized widely, so the policy expects surprises. The learned gaits moved straight onto the real turtle: crisp performance on hard flat ground, and rougher but robust travel over gravel, grass, and mud.
arxiv-2512-08014:
Chahrazed Ghannoudi, Marie Claude Lavallee, Benjamin Cote, and Luc Beaulieu, medical physicists in Canada, posted a methods study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is high dose rate brachytherapy, where a radioactive source treats cancer from inside the body. Errors can occur, and in vivo dosimetry is the only check that confirms the dose was delivered as planned.

The team details and validates a calibration method for a small plastic scintillation detector. Calibration uses an external six megavolt beam and a hyperspectral technique that removes unwanted stem effects first. They then test the detector against an iridium source in a water tank, comparing measured and standard dose rates. Agreement was close near the source, with larger differences farther away, and a full uncertainty budget explains where the limits come from.
arxiv-2512-08114:
Enrique Garcia Sanchez, David de Hevia, and Mitchell Taylor, mathematicians in functional analysis, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. It tackles an open problem from a 2024 paper by Freeman, Oikhberg, Pineau, and Taylor. Can spaces of continuous functions contain large subspaces that perform stable phase retrieval? That process recovers a signal from magnitudes alone.

The authors prove a clean dividing line. For both real and complex scalars, such a space has an infinite dimensional stable phase retrieval subspace exactly when a certain derived set of the underlying space is nonempty. That derived set comes from repeatedly stripping away isolated points, a Cantor Bendixson construction. They then build large retrieval subspaces whose size is tied, with explicit bounds, to how many such derivatives the space supports, settling the existence question.
arxiv-2512-08214:
Sola S Nova, Noel D Richardson, Jonathan Labadie Bartz, and Samantha Garcia Flores, astronomers, posted an observational study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is lambda Pavonis, a classical Be star: a fast spinning B star that at times builds a disk of gas around itself. How such disks form and fade is still not understood, and this paper catches one being born.

Their data combine hundreds of high resolution spectra with brightness monitoring from TESS during 2023. Near the end of that watch, the star began building a disk from a clean state. The disk appeared within about five days in hydrogen and helium lines, and settled into a circle in about twelve. Decay started in the highest energy helium lines and ended last in hydrogen alpha. The team also tracked star pulsations: two brightness rhythms seen by TESS never showed in the spectra.
arxiv-2512-08314:
M Yashwanth, Gaurav Kumar Nayak, Harsh Rangwani, and colleagues, machine learning researchers in India, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is federated learning, where many clients train one shared model without pooling their private data. Federated models often settle into sharp minima, points where small changes hurt accuracy, and that harms how well they generalize.

The authors trace the problem to the curvature of the loss surface, captured by the largest eigenvalue of its Hessian. Their regularizer, called MAN, shrinks the norm of each layer activations on the client side during training. They prove that doing so lowers the top Hessian eigenvalue layer by layer, steering the joint model toward a flat minimum. Applied on top of existing federated methods, the technique brought clear gains, setting new best results. The work gives federated learning a cheap, client side lever for models that travel better to new data.
arxiv-2512-08714:
Niccolo Cocciaglia and coauthors run long simulations of a stably layered fluid under steady forcing. Such fluids often form a staircase pattern, with well mixed layers split by thin sharp interfaces. Watching that pattern over very long times is hard, because large scale modes evolve slowly and results depend sensitively on physical settings.

Their simulations run for up to ten thousand turnover times, far longer than most past work, at three levels of stratification. A large scale friction term is added to limit shear growth and mimic a finite box. Staircases form in the medium and strong cases, through interfaces either fading or merging. Energy stays fairly steady during fading, but jumps in bursts during merging. Odd bursts in velocity and density cluster near interfaces, linking strong events to the meeting of mixing and layer formation.
arxiv-2512-08914:
David Zenati and Eliya Nachmani introduce SAQ Decoder, a quantum error correction decoder that aims for both high accuracy and fast scaling. Decoding faces a trade off: classic matching methods vary with the noise model and grow costly. Tensor network methods are accurate but very expensive. Recent neural methods are fast but not accurate enough.

Their framework combines a transformer model with constraint aware post processing. A dual stream transformer handles syndrome data and logical information with different attention patterns for each stream. A new differentiable loss directly targets the logical error rate, using smooth approximations over finite fields. On toric codes, the decoder reaches error thresholds very close to the maximum likelihood bounds, under both independent and depolarizing noise. It also beats neural and classic baselines in accuracy, complexity, and parameter efficiency. The result supports learned decoders for practical fault tolerant quantum computing.
arxiv-2512-09314:
Tobi Gaggl and colleagues report a new superconductor in the kagome metal YRu3B2. Kagome materials, whose atoms form a woven pattern of triangles and hexagons, are prized for unusual electronic behavior. A relative of this compound superconducts at a comparatively high temperature, a fact blamed on flat electronic bands working with the lattice's vibrations.

YRu3B2 shares the structure but keeps a cleaner, undistorted kagome lattice. The team measured magnetization, electrical resistance, and heat capacity, and all three showed a true bulk superconducting transition, though at a much lower temperature, below one kelvin. The result adds a pristine member to the kagome superconductor family. Because its lattice is structurally clean, it offers a simpler setting for testing ideas about how flat bands and lattice vibrations conspire to raise or limit superconducting temperatures.
arxiv-2512-09414:
Maciej Frącek and Piotr Kowalski study the model theory of the Heisenberg group, a classic group built from a field, central to quantum mechanics and group theory. Model theory asks which properties of a structure can be expressed and preserved in formal logic. The authors compare the logical complexity of the group with that of its underlying field.

Their main result is an exact match between field and group. A field is model complete, meaning every definable set there has a simple logical form, exactly when its Heisenberg group is model complete in the language of groups. To prove it, they extend a theorem of Levchuk about the group's automorphisms to cover monomorphisms between Heisenberg groups over different fields. They also show the group does not admit quantifier elimination, the strongest such simplification, and examine whether the group and the field can be interpreted inside each other.
arxiv-2512-09514:
Paul Hagemann and colleagues introduce the Transport Novelty Distance, a metric for judging generative models that propose new materials. As machine learning models design candidate materials, researchers need scores that capture both quality and novelty. A model that copies its training data looks good by quality alone, and existing evaluations often miss that failure.

Their metric builds on optimal transport theory. It couples features of the training set and the generated set, then separates the comparison into a quality regime and a memorization regime using a threshold. The features come from a graph neural network trained with contrastive learning to tell materials apart from altered versions of themselves and from differently sized copies. On toy experiments covering memorization, noise, and lattice deformation, and on two real materials datasets, the metric detected both copied and low-quality outputs. The authors also benchmark several popular material generators with it.
arxiv-2512-09614:
Alan Dow determines which uncountable cardinals can arise as the pi-weight of a countable regular Fréchet-Urysohn space, within two models of set theory. Pi-weight is an invariant measuring the smallest size of a family of open sets that can approximate the space's topology from inside. Fréchet-Urysohn spaces are topological spaces where closure can be witnessed by sequences, a convergence property.

The collection of cardinals that occur for such spaces is called the pi-weight spectrum, and it can depend on the set-theoretic assumptions. Dow computes this spectrum in the Miller model, a model built with rational perfect set forcing, and again in the random real model. Short classification papers of this kind map how fragile or robust a topological invariant is. If the spectrum changes between models, the invariant's possible values are not decided by the ordinary axioms of set theory alone.
arxiv-2512-09814:
Zhizhong Wang and colleagues present DynaIP, a plug in adapter for personalized text to image generation. The goal is images of a specific subject, taken from reference photos, that still follow the user's text prompt. Existing adapters struggle on three fronts: keeping the subject faithful without ignoring the prompt, retaining fine details, and handling several subjects at once. DynaIP targets all three for modern multimodal diffusion transformers.

The design starts from an observation about how these models learn: when reference features enter through separate attention branches, concept and prompt information partly decouple. A dynamic decoupling strategy removes concept agnostic interference during generation, improving the balance between fidelity and prompt following, and helping multi subject scenes. A second module mixes features from several levels of a standard image encoder. Across single and multi subject tests, DynaIP beat existing approaches using only single subject training data.
arxiv-2512-10014:
Yusuke Inoue, Keiichi Maeda, Takashi Nagao, and Tatsuya Matsumoto simulate the material shed around two white dwarfs before they merge and explode. Many Type Ia supernovae show an early excess of light within about a day of explosion. That flash is a clue to the progenitor system. The authors model the binary's orbital evolution and the phase where one star spills matter faster than the other can accept it, ejecting circumstellar material. 

Their violent merger scenario produces a circumstellar density profile falling steeply with radius. The simulated light curves reproduce the early excesses seen from optical to ultraviolet light, including how the color evolves, in the unusual supernovae thought to be merger candidates. That match supports the idea that those objects really are violent white dwarf mergers. A helium ignited variant should also shed material before ignition.
arxiv-2512-10514:
Lorenzo Versini and a large team describe a small, light-heated atom source for loading ions into traps, the devices that hold single charged atoms for precision experiments and quantum work. Their source releases a beam of neutral calcium when warmed by light alone, with no bulky oven hardware. And the atoms are then ionised inside a room-temperature trap.

The team measured loading rates that reached well above twenty ions per second at modest heating power. And reliable single-ion loading in under half a minute at even lower power. They calibrated a thermal model by imaging the glow of the calcium beam, and found the oven's performance is limited mainly by heat lost as radiation. They also mapped how the ionising laser's power affects loading, and predict the source suits many metals used in ion trapping.
arxiv-2512-10914:
Jucheng Lin and co-authors tune chaos in a flake of bilayer graphene. Confine electrons inside a finite graphene cavity. Their motion can be orderly or chaotic. It depends on the cavity's shape and on the warped Fermi surface of bilayer graphene. That material's tunable energy gap also suits future nanoelectronics. The authors show the dial is simply rotation: turn the cavity boundary relative to the atomic lattice underneath.

That rotation drives a quantum transition from nearly integrable dynamics to a chaotic regime, visible at once in the statistics of the energy eigenvalues and in the shapes of the eigenstates themselves. A semiclassical ray treatment, following electron trajectories as bouncing rays, exposes the classical backbone beneath the quantum crossover. Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the work presents bilayer graphene cavities as a laboratory for engineering quantum chaos on purpose, not just observing it.
arxiv-2512-11014:
Hikaru Wakaura proposes a generative adversarial network whose generator is built from a quantum form of Kolmogorov Arnold Networks. Those networks can learn more accurately than standard neural networks while using fewer parameters, but they train slowly, which has limited their use as generators. A variational quantum version may avoid that weakness.

The new model uses quantum circuits and their output patterns to learn efficiently with far fewer parameters. Training and generation were tested on two standard image datasets, handwritten digits and small colour images. The method reached higher accuracy than neural network generators and an earlier quantum adversarial model while using less data. The work points to compact quantum assisted generators as a practical direction.
arxiv-2512-11114:
Xinyu Zhang and colleagues present TAMO, a transformer trained to solve multi objective optimisation problems in a single forward pass. Balancing rival goals, such as cost against performance, appears in drug design and autonomous systems. The standard Bayesian approach fits a fresh surrogate model for each new problem, which is slow and rarely transfers.

TAMO instead learns a universal policy from many problems at once. It handles varying numbers of inputs and objectives, reads the whole history of past trials, and proposes the next design directly. Reinforcement learning trained it to maximise long term improvement of the trade off frontier. On synthetic and real tasks it matched or beat rival methods' solution quality while proposing designs hundreds of times faster. The authors see a path toward plug and play optimisers for scientific discovery.
arxiv-2512-11214:
Hemant Kumar Sharma studies what happens when a famous quasiperiodic lattice is laid out along a spiral instead of a straight line. In the Aubry André model, an irregular but patterned potential can trap particles that would otherwise spread. Bending the chain into a spiral stretches and squeezes the spacing between neighbouring sites, which changes how easily particles hop along it.

The on site pattern stays the same, yet the geometry driven hop changes reshape the energy spectrum and trapping behaviour. Using measures of how concentrated each state is, plus a full multifractal analysis, Sharma finds that curvature makes states localise much more readily, even under weak quasiperiodic patterns. Clear windows appear where states are strongly multifractal, in between spread out and fully trapped behaviour. The results suggest tunable localisation for platforms such as light waveguides, cold atoms, and mechanical metamaterials.
arxiv-2601-07014: Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar, Girish, and Muskaan Singh present DIVINE in a 2026 arXiv paper. DIVINE is a tool that reads both the voice and the face to spot signs of nerve and face disorders. The team holds that shared cues and cues found in just one stream should be kept apart. Each stream comes from a large pre-trained model. Kept apart, the cues may help the tool work well on new cases. They may also help doctors see why the tool flags a case.
arxiv-2601-07314: Research by Sebastian Nehrdich and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with mitrasaṃgraha. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. While machine translation is regarded as a "solved problem" for many high-resource languages. Close analysis quickly reveals that this is not the case for content that shows challenges such as poetical language. Philosophical concepts, multi-layered metaphorical expressions, and more. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07414:
E. Poultourtzidis and a large team wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on three new planets. Each planet crosses the face of its star, a pass called a transit. Two of the planets are sub-Neptunes, worlds a bit smaller than Neptune. The third is a rocky world like Earth in kind. All three stars are M dwarfs, small cool stars.

The planets first showed up in data from TESS, a space telescope that hunts for transits. The team then checked each world from the ground. They took light reads to firm up the transits. They took radial velocity reads with CARMENES, a tool that tracks how a star wobbles as a planet tugs it. The three hosts are called TOI-1243, TOI-4529, and TOI-5388. Each planet has a short year. The years run 4.65 days, 5.88 days, and 2.59 days. The checks let the team confirm all three worlds as real.
arxiv-2601-07514:
Matteo Garbelli links machine learning forecasts to routing decisions for utility repair crews. His 2026 preprint studies a stochastic vehicle routing problem with time windows and capacity limits. The setting is gas meter maintenance, where each job's duration is uncertain. Better duration forecasts should lead to better routes and schedules.

He trains XGBoost, a tree-based gradient boosting method, on eight years of maintenance data. It produces both point predictions and uncertainty estimates for job durations. Those outputs then drive a search routine with more than one goal, bred and tested over many rounds. The study shows how forecasting and optimization can feed each other, rather than sit in separate boxes. Utility workforce managers are the natural readers. The crews fix and check gas lines and meters at homes and firms each day.
arxiv-2601-07714:
Igor Uljarević writes a short note on loops in contact geometry with a positivity twist. Contactomorphisms are the symmetry maps of contact manifolds, spaces that model odd-dimensional geometry. He considers contractible loops of such maps that are positive over some nonempty closed subset. Such subsets are called immaterial. His 2026 note argues a geometric point about their complements.

Specifically, the complement of a Reeb-invariant immaterial subset can be seen as big in contact geometric terms. Big here means large in the sense that matters to contact rigidity results. Short notes like this often supply one clean idea that later work builds on. The paper is aimed at symplectic and contact geometers. It sharpens how positive loops constrain the space around them.
arxiv-2601-08314:
Tian-Liang Feng and four co-authors study CP violation in rare baryon decays. Their 2026 arXiv paper follows a recent LHCb report of the first CP violation seen in baryon decays. That observation carried significance above five sigma, a strong discovery threshold.

The result motivates checks in more baryon decay processes. The authors examine decays of Lambda-b and Xi-b baryons into a Lambda(1520) plus a meson. CP violation measures how matter and antimatter behave differently. Finding it in baryons, not just mesons, tests the Standard Model account of the matter-filled universe. Each new channel adds a place where that account could fail.
arxiv-2601-08814:
Gianluigi Del Magno, Joao Lopes Dias, and Jose Pedro Gaivao study chance driven maps that keep area fixed. Think of a ball that jumps by a rule picked at random at each step. Such maps model gas flow and other spread out motion. A key ask is when the motion stays tame, with no fast split of near paths.

The team proves a firm rule for this class. If all growth rates of path splits are zero, then a fixed spread law must live on a linked bundle of lines. That law is a sign of tame, near clock like motion. A reader in dynamics gets a test that ties flat growth to deep order. It helps split tame random motion from wild random motion.
arxiv-2601-09014:
Agata Barsotti and three co-authors study how noise in a drive tone can harm a qubit. A qubit is the base unit of quantum work. It is steered by tones with a set phase, like a clock hand. If that phase jitters, each steer step errs a bit. As lab qubits live long and read tools get sharp, tone noise grows as a cap on score.

The team sums how phase noise builds through long chains of steer steps. Small phase slips can add, not cancel, in a chain. Their sums tell lab staff how pure a tone must be for a set task. A reader who builds quantum gear gets a firm noise cap to design to.
arxiv-2601-09114:
Yufan Xia and three co-authors use learn tools to set thread counts for a core math task. The task is matrix times matrix, the work horse of science code. On one thread, the best tune is well known. On many threads that share RAM, the best count of threads is hard to call. Too few wastes cores. Too many clogs the RAM path.

The team trains a model to call the best thread count for each new task shape. It learns from past runs on like tasks. At run time it sets the count in a flash, with no trial runs. A reader who runs science code gets a way to cut wait time on a task that eats much of world compute.
arxiv-2601-09214:
Jiri Cerny and Flavio Dalessi study the far edge of a branching walk in a chance land. Walkers branch and step on a line of whole points. The land shifts at random from site to site, yet stays fixed once set. The far edge is the most far point a walker has reached. Past work found how that edge tends to sit in a plain land.

In a chance land, they prove the edge law stays tight round its mid point. Tight here means the edge does not spread out with out bound as time grows. That holds for near all lands, not just on mean. A reader in chance work gets a firm tale for a walk where the land itself is a throw of dice.
arxiv-2601-09314:
Gerold Alsmeyer and Anita Behme study the tail of a class of chance flows that pull back to a mean. Such flows model rates, winds, and counts that jump, then drift back. Here the drift rules are set by a hid chain that flips state. Each state has its own pull and jump form. The tail asks how oft a vast value can still show.

They read the tail through a chain of random affine maps. Each map scales and shifts the last value. Tails of such chains have known power forms, with rates set by the maps. A reader in chance work gets a tail law for a flow that can flip its own rules as it runs.
arxiv-2601-09514:
Sagardeep Talukdar, R. Ramakrishnan, Sudipta Nandy, and M. Lakshmanan follow bright pulses as they travel down a flawed fiber. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies soliton dynamics through the variable-coefficient Fokas-Lenells equation. The fiber is inhomogeneous: its dispersion, nonlinearity, and gain or loss change with time.

The authors set up the model for ultrashort pulses in such fibers. They then examine how bright solitons interact, along with conservation laws, modulation instability, and soliton tunneling. Solitons that survive a changing fiber are prized for fast optical links. Knowing when they pass through barriers, or break up, guides fiber design.
arxiv-2601-09614:
Xiang-Xiang Sun and six co-authors compute the electric shape of two light nuclei from first principles. Their 2026 arXiv paper predicts charge form factors and radii for lithium-6 and beryllium-8. The method is the Jacobi-coordinate no-core shell model.

The forces come from chiral two- and three-nucleon interactions, with matching one- and two-nucleon charge operators. Two-body charge terms are the paper's focus: do they matter at this precision? Form factors tell how charge is spread inside a nucleus, and radii give its size. Clean predictions give experiments a theory benchmark with no fitted knobs at all.
arxiv-2601-09914:
Nathaniel Grimes, Christopher Costello, and Andrew Plantinga study fishers and a new form of cover. Fish stocks face shocks from storms and shifts in the sea. These shocks hit both the stock and the pay of those who fish. Index cover pays out when a set index drops, not when one boat has a bad trip.

Such cover could shield fishers from risk. But it may also change how they fish. If cover makes risk feel low, effort may rise. That could add strain to stocks that are prone to over use. The paper weighs this trade off. It urges care in how such plans are set up and rolled out.
arxiv-2601-10314:
Eske Pedersen and co authors pull a faint bias from galaxy shapes in survey data. Galaxies tend to point in ways set by their birth place. That lean can fake the weak lens signal that maps dark mass. The lean is named intrinsic alignment.

The team add a self tune step to a known lens pipe. The pipe is the LSST DESC 3x2pt chain. They run it on year one data from the Dark Energy Survey. The step uses the data itself to split lean from lens. It shows the pipe can do both jobs at once. That bodes well for the vast LSST runs to come.
arxiv-2601-10514:
Madeline Lucey and co authors report the first five carbon rich metal poor stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Such stars hold far more carbon than iron for their age. In our own galaxy, they are a large share of old halo stars. They code facts about the first stars and their bursts.

No such stars were known in that dwarf galaxy till now. The team found five. Each is a clue to how the first bursts seeded that galaxy. The mix in a dwarf may part from our own in key ways. The finds give a first base for that match.
arxiv-2601-10614:
Yair Hayut and Alejandro Poveda study the Rudin-Keisler order, a way of ranking ultrafilters on measurable cardinals. Set theorists use such rankings to compare very large infinite sets. The paper asks how directed this order is: can two ultrafilters always be bounded by a third? Their main theorem gives a precise answer in terms of consistency.

For regular cardinals in the stated range, two theories turn out to be equiconsistent with ZFC, the standard axioms of set theory. That means each can be true if the other can. Results like this map the possible shapes of the ultrafilter order. They guide set theorists who probe what large cardinals force and what they leave free.
arxiv-2601-10914:
Francis N. Nji and Jianwu Wang present a factorized-attention ConvLSTM for climate data. Learning useful patterns from high-resolution Earth data is hard. Local weather shifts fast, distant regions sway each other, and the whole system drifts over time. ConvLSTM2D is a common baseline, but its dense gating costs much compute. Its local view also misses long-range structure.

The authors add factorized attention to widen the model's reach while cutting cost. The design aims at physically meaningful space-time patterns across many variables. Climate data are a natural test: teleconnections link oceans and continents. A leaner, wider model could sharpen forecasts and help scientists pull apart tangled climate dynamics.
arxiv-2601-11214:
Hanchen Xia, Baoyou Chen, Yutang Ge, Guojiang Zhao, and Siyu Zhu train diffusion language models. Their 2026 preprint names its method T-star, built on TraceRL. Masked diffusion models write text by filling blanks in blocks. Block size sets a trade-off between speed and quality of the text.

The team's plan grows the block size in steps during training. It starts from a small-block model first trained in the standard way. Then it moves to larger blocks in a smooth path. Larger blocks let the model decode more text in parallel. Tests on math reasoning tasks show small loss of quality. The gain is faster decoding with far more done at once.
arxiv-2601-11314:
Jiatong Yi and Yanyang Li test membership attacks on language models in the wild. Their 2026 preprint deals with large language models as found in use. A membership attack asks if one text trained the model. That test audits what opaque training sets truly held.

Most past tests lean on things users cannot see. Logits and other internals are hid by real services. In a strict black-box case, only the output text shows. Tests also tend to fail when the domain shifts. The team's work targets that real-world black-box case. It aims at an audit tool that needs no inside access. Such a tool helps check privacy and copyright claims.
arxiv-2601-11514:
Yawar Siddiqui and seven coauthors rebuild 3D shapes from casual captures. Their 2026 preprint presents ShapeR, a conditional generation method. Recent 3D generation methods post strong results on clean inputs. Clean means unoccluded and well segmented from the start.

Real captures rarely meet those tidy conditions at all. Phones grab cluttered scenes with parts hidden from view. ShapeR takes casually captured sequences as its input. It generates the object's full 3D shape from them. The conditioning comes from the messy footage itself. Robust shape tools serve scanning, retail, and robot work. The method aims to close the lab-to-life gap.
arxiv-2601-12014:
Elio Masciari, Vincenzo Moscato, Enea Vincenzo Napolitano, and their co-authors test language models on a new structured output format called TOON. Models in pipelines must now give outputs that code can read at once. Good prose is not enough if the form is wrong.

Their test weighs two goals: strict form skill and lasting cost. A format may be cheap yet hard for models to keep valid. Or it may be safe yet waste tokens. The trade map helps teams pick formats for machine-to-machine work with eyes open.  The test also tracks cost per task for each format.
arxiv-2601-12114:
Yikang Lu, Ying Wang, Alfonso de Miguel-Arribas, Lei Shi, and Yamir Moreno model vaccine choice under peer pressure in groups of three. Vaccine games in higher-order settings are still little studied. Yet group pressure shapes views and joint choices in real life.

Their model has two layers. One layer spreads disease by the SIR process on a grid. The other is a hypergraph of triad links where views are pressed. The pair shows how group pressure can lift or sink uptake. Such models can guide fair, peer-led health drives.  Group size in the model is fixed at three peers.
arxiv-2601-12214:
Ahhyun Jeong, Aditya N. Singh, Josh Portner, and a large team align atoms in superlattices of lead sulfide nanocrystals. Nanocrystals are building blocks for new materials, and their self-assembly can yield traits no bulk solid has. The team use compact inorganic ligands on the crystal surfaces.

They reach atomic alignment via reversible oriented attachment, where crystals join and can still adjust. Aligned lattices can carry charge and light in new ways. The work shows a route to ordered films with atomic registry. Such films suit sensors and solar tools.  Atomic registry is the main gain over past films.
arxiv-2601-12314:
Yiwen Zhang, Hui Zhang, and Fanqin Meng link musical structure to military strategy via a similarity network. Music perception is a multi-sense act tied to synesthesia, and it is a core part of music aesthetic education. Grasping music structure aids both perception and teaching.

In music, many strands of information join to form a melody. In strategy, many acts join to form a plan. Their network maps likeness between the two kinds of structure. That odd link may give new tools for music teaching.  The link is drawn for use in aesthetic education.
arxiv-2601-12414:
Nawaf Mohammed compares two classic ways to measure spread in a set of risks. One is the standard deviation, taught in every basic stats course. The other is the Gini mean difference, less known but widely used in economics. A natural question is which of the two tends to be larger, and when.

Mohammed drives the whole analysis with one structural object. That object is the mean excess function of the gap between two draws of the same risk. The tail of that gap turns out to govern the order of the two measures. Work of this kind helps users know what each spread measure is really picking up. It also warns when the two can rank the same risks in opposite ways.
arxiv-2601-12514:
Graph total colorings get extended to cell complexes in work that links coloring with domination. A total coloring paints both the vertices and the edges of a graph. It is called efficient when each color class forms an efficient dominating set on the vertices. Efficient domination is a strict form of coverage with no overlap or waste.

The focus falls on two cell complexes whose one dimensional skeletons are toroidal graphs. Toroidal graphs live on a doughnut shaped surface, which gives them a rich, regular structure. Extending coloring ideas from graphs to complexes tests how far the concepts stretch. Results here sit in combinatorics and topology at once. The author line in the record is blank, so no creator is named here.
arxiv-2601-12614:
Neural surrogates for global space plasma simulations are built in work with no author named in the record. The target simulations use a hybrid Vlasov method that resolves ion kinetic effects. They model how the solar wind interacts with the magnetosphere of Earth. Even reduced five dimensional runs of this kind are very expensive to compute.

The team train graph based machine learning emulators on four such runs. All four runs use identical steady solar wind conditions. The emulators learn how fields and ion moments evolve in near Earth space. Both deterministic and probabilistic surrogates are built and compared. A fast surrogate could let researchers scan many scenarios that full runs cannot afford.
arxiv-2601-13114:
Abdelrahman Soliman, Ahmed Refaey, Aiman Erbad, and Amr Mohamed build a smart agent for next gen mobile nets. Such nets aim to run by intent. An operator states what the net should do, in plain high level terms, and tools make it so.

Their agent is called IntAgent. It is built on a large language model. It draws on NWDAF, the net data analytics role in 5G cores, plus a set of tools. With that mix it can read net state and act to meet an intent. For net teams, the work shows how language agents may cut hand work in day to day net care.
arxiv-2601-13514:
Ronan Perry, Snigdha Panigrahi, and Daniela Witten do post pick inference for penalized M estimators by score thinning. An M estimator fits a model by a loss sum. A sparsity penalty picks which parts stay. Inference past that pick is hard, since the pick used the same data.

Old routes need a bespoke proof for each penalty. Their route is more plain. They add and take a crafted noise from a Gaussian count. That split yields two free Gaussian counts. One can drive the pick. The next can drive a plain trust span past the pick. A shared trick for many penalties beats a new proof per task.
arxiv-2601-13614:
Bo Peng, Sirui Chen, Lei Xu, and Chaochao Lu study how machines can find cause and effect in data in 2026. Pure data methods can stall, since two causes may look the same in the numbers. Newer methods ask large language models for help with cause hunts. But some ignore the data proof, and others trust model guesses that no one has checked.

Their system, CauScientist, aims to make models respect the data first. Model ideas must face the stats proof found in the data itself. The goal is cause claims that stay tied to what was seen. Sound cause work backs both science and hard choices in real life.
arxiv-2601-13914:
Lars Georg, Robert Harlander, and Robert Mason compute a coupling in quantum electrodynamics with a new scheme in 2026. The gradient-flow scheme defines the QED coupling in a smooth, flow-based way. They evaluate it in three and four space-time dimensions. Their general result applies to any theory with a U(1) gauge field.

Other fields and arbitrary interactions are allowed in the result. As an example, they treat QED with a set number of flavors. They evaluate the beta functions, which show how the coupling runs with energy. Such results test field theory methods across dimensions.
arxiv-2601-14114:
Liam Chung and Tobias Kappé extend a logic for reasoning about programs in 2026. Kleene algebra is a tool for proving general program equivalences. Its equational theory is decidable and complete. Yet it cannot always prove equivalences between specific programs.

For those cases, users add hypotheses that encode program-specific knowledge. Linear hypotheses are the focus of this work. The team studies partial reductions for Kleene algebra with such hypotheses. Better tools here help verify compilers and program transformations with proof. The cuts keep proofs short while the added facts stay in view. Tool builders can add these cuts to their own provers.
arxiv-2601-14214:
Julia Venturini and co-authors build a global formation model for planets in binaries in 2026. Binary stars are as common as single stars in the galaxy. The number of detected planets orbiting binaries is rapidly increasing. Transit surveys, Gaia, and high-resolution direct imaging campaigns drive that synergy.

Global planet formation models around binary stars are still underdeveloped. That gap limits theoretical understanding of planets in binary systems. Their PAIRS project aims to close the gap with a global model. Observers need such models to interpret the growing census of two-sun worlds.
arxiv-2601-14614:
