Víctor Mayoral-Vilches leads a large team on AI in cybersecurity in this 2026 paper. They define cybersecurity superintelligence as artificial intelligence exceeding the best human capability in both speed and strategic reasoning. They call it the next frontier in security. The paper documents the emergence of such capability through three major contributions that pioneered AI Security.

The first contribution they name is PentestGPT from 2023. It established LLM-guided penetration testing. The paper's title traces a shift: from AI-guided humans to human-guided AI. The tone is bold. The team claims a new age is here, and they lay out the proof step by step. Readers get a field history and a claim about where the balance of initiative between analyst and machine now sits.
arxiv-2601-15014:
Michelle Ching, Ioana Popescu, and co-authors study how transformers learn a task from the prompt itself. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with in-context learning for nonparametric regression. The unknown curve is only assumed to be smooth, in the Hölder sense, with no fixed formula.

In-context learning means the model adapts from examples shown to it, with no new training. The authors ask how well a transformer can fit such curves this way. Their results are of the efficient and minimax-optimal kind. That means no method can do much better in the worst case.
arxiv-2601-15114:
Valerio La Gatta, Gian Marco Orlando, and co-authors give simulated social media users more lifelike habits. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with generative agent-based models. Large language models drive agents that mimic people on social platforms.

Such models can show how posts spread and how influence flows. But most agents are defined by demographics, personality traits, and interests alone. They lack behavioral traits, the leanings that shape how a person acts on a platform. So all agents engage in much the same way. The authors add those missing behavior traits to the agents.
arxiv-2601-15214:
Yoshiki Nakamura completes a logic for a common tool in computing. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with regular expressions with lookahead, a pattern language used to match text. Reasoning about when two such patterns match the same text needs firm rules.

Nakamura gives an axiomatic account of that reasoning. He covers both plain language equivalence and the largest substitution-closed equivalence that stays sound. His route uses a variant of propositional dynamic logic on finite linear orders. Two extra operators restrict a stated relation to the identity or else to its complement.
arxiv-2601-15514:
Shome Chakraborty asks whether broad economic signals can help forecast public health capacity in a 2026 arXiv paper. Economic conditions shape the setting in which health systems work. Yet no one had checked in a systematic way whether they act as leading signals. That gap is what the study takes up. The question is practical: can today's economic data hint at tomorrow's strain?

Chakraborty tests a set of macroeconomic indicators for useful signal. The targets are all tied to capacity. They include jobs in the health and social assistance workforce. They include new business applications in that sector. They also include spending on health care construction. If such links hold, planners gain an early-warning tool. Forecasts could draw on data that already arrives fast and often.
arxiv-2601-15714:
Ryoma Sato proposes a strict yardstick for language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. He calls it the Zero-Error Horizon. It is the maximum range over which a model solves tasks with no errors at all. Averages can hide rare slips. The horizon exposes them: one slip ends the run. Sato argues that this simple measure yields rich insight. He tests it on state-of-the-art models.

His example is pointed. Even GPT-5.2, he reports, fails at counting to five under his test. The title uses that failure as a warning. Trustworthy use needs error-free stretches, not just high average scores. A surgeon-grade tool must be right every time in its working range. The horizon frames exactly how far that range extends for each model.
arxiv-2601-15814:
Ryosuke Yamano and Tetsuo Shibuya improve an algorithm for genome-style string problems in a 2026 arXiv paper. The shortest common superstring problem asks for one short string. It must contain each given string as a substring. A variant adds reverse complements. For each input, either the string or its reverse complement must appear. That variant arises naturally in bioinformatics, where DNA strands come in both orientations.

The authors improve approximation ratios for this variant. An approximation ratio bounds how far a fast method can stray from optimal. Better ratios mean shorter superstrings, found with guarantees. Genome assembly leans on such problems. Reads must be merged into longer sequences with little waste. Sharper guarantees help assemblers promise more about their output.
arxiv-2601-16014:
Eder Baron-Prada, Adolfo Anta and Florian Dörfler study how to test if a power grid stays stable. Their 2026 preprint looks at grids where much of the power now comes through grid tied converters. Old checks can be slow and hard to use. The team uses Scaled Relative Graphs, a graph tool, to split the grid part and the converter part apart.

By split, the authors mean each part can be checked on its own. The checks then join to show if the whole loop stays stable. The method works for both linear loads and loads that do not act in a straight line way. That breadth helps grid teams who must plan for real loads. It gives them a fast and clear way to judge new converter setups.
arxiv-2601-16114:
Alex Plyukhin asks if a known noise form is in fact not needed. His 2026 preprint deals with the broad Langevin maths for systems with drag. Tests of that maths oft use a set noise form. They check if long time ends match true rest states. The noise in his study is heat noise from in the system. Its form is not the bell curve form.

Plyukhin shows the maths can hold true with this noise form. Yet he argues the extra form adds no new use. The same ends can be reached with the plain form. That claim trims need less parts from the theory. The work is a close read of what the maths needs.
arxiv-2601-16414:
John Wu and coauthors set out PyHealth 2.0, a tool kit for ward deep learning. Their 2026 preprint deals with blocks that slow ward AI work. Blocks span hard base lines, high compute cost and need for deep ward facts. The kit aims to cut all three blocks at once. It claims a full model can be built in just a few lines.

Few line builds let more teams test ward task ideas fast. Shared base lines make scores fair to weigh side by side. Low cost paths open ward AI to small teams and schools. The kit is free and open for all to use. It builds on the first PyHealth set of tools.
arxiv-2601-17114:
Heng-Yu Chen, Nick Dorey, Sanefumi Moriyama, Rishi Mouland, and Canberk Şanlı tie two brane tales in one claim. M2 and M5 branes are vast sheets in M-theory. Each hosts its own field tale on its face. Their 2026 preprint claims a tight link twixt two such tales. One tale is the ABJM tale in three dims. It rules stacks of M2 branes in flat space-time.

Count marks, called indices, are the link's test. A giant graviton growth gives one side of the tie. If the tie holds, counts in one tale fix the next. Such dual ties are gold in string work.
arxiv-2601-17514:
Nitin Jha and Abhishek Parakh survey if quantum voting can work in practice. Quantum voting aims for ballot secrecy with public proof of the tally. Its shield rests on physics, not just hard math. Superposition, no-cloning, and entanglement are the core tools. The authors weigh those promises against real-world needs.

Elections demand scale, ease of use, and trust by non-experts. A scheme can be sound in theory and fail at the polls. The survey maps that gap in plain terms. It helps officials judge claims from quantum vendors. It also shows researchers which flaws to fix first. Ballot trust is too key to rest on lab demos.
arxiv-2601-17614:
Yimeng Liu, Misha Sra, and Chang Xiao present AlignUI for interface design with language models. Good interfaces match user taste, but finding that match takes long cycles. Teams prototype, test, and refine again and again. LLM-based UI generation speeds the build phase. AlignUI aims to steer that speed toward user preference.

A fast tool that misses taste saves little time. Alignment methods close the gap between first draft and fit. Designers can explore more options in the same span. Users gain screens shaped to their habits. The work joins generation with feedback in one loop. It serves product teams under real deadlines.
arxiv-2601-17914:
Casper Vedder, Thomas Bakx, Nora Elisa Chisari, Henk Hoekstra, and Matthieu Schaller measure a subtle effect in how galaxies line up. Their 2026 preprint uses the FLAMINGO simulations, a large set of virtual universes. Galaxies and their dark matter halos tend to align with the web around them. These intrinsic alignments can mimic the lensing signal that cosmologists use to weigh the universe, so they must be modeled with care.

The team goes past pairs and measures three-point statistics. They compute a three-point correlation and a third-order aperture-mass measure. The sample covers galaxies and halos above a set mass in a huge simulated volume. Three-point data add checks that pair data cannot give. The results help lensing surveys clean their signals.
arxiv-2601-18014:
Adeeba Tarannum and co-authors build a system that turns messy name and address text into clean fields. Their 2026 preprint targets a basic pain in large information systems. Free text must be split into parts like first name, street, and city before it can be used. Rule-based and statistical tools do well on clean input but fail on noisy or multilingual text. Neural models and language models, in turn, can lack steady control and repeatability.

The team's system uses large language models with those flaws in mind. Steady output matters when records feed billing, shipping, and identity checks. Better parsing cuts errors across huge record sets. The work serves any group that cleans contact data at scale.
arxiv-2601-18314:
Lina Felsner and co-authors report a student hackathon built around reproducing MRI results. Their 2026 preprint describes the design, protocol, and outcomes of the event. Students set out to replicate three influential MRI reconstruction papers. One is MoDL, an unrolled model-based network with learned denoising. The second is HUMUS-Net, a hybrid unrolled design that mixes CNN and transformer parts. The third is an untrained, physics-regularized method for dynamic MRI that uses a quantitative prior.

Reproduction is a hard test of whether a paper gives enough detail to rebuild its claims. A hackathon format turns that test into training. The outcomes show where advanced methods stand up to fresh hands. Such exercises strengthen the field's habits of care.
arxiv-2601-18714:
Judith Vilella-Cantos and four colleagues teach farm robots to know where they are in a field of vines. A vine field is a hard place to get one's place. Rows look the same, there are few firm marks, and leaves shift with the wind and the year. Tools that work in towns, with their signs and walls, fail in such sameness. Place tools for farms have lagged those for roads.

The team use a beam tool that reads range by light. They teach it codes for each place that nest like dolls, from broad to fine. A nest of codes can be both small to store and sharp to match. A cheap, firm place read could let farm robots run rows on their own. That would cut hand work in a trade short of hands.
arxiv-2601-19714:
G. Lacopo and four colleagues speed up the imaging software behind radio astronomy. Modern radio interferometers pour out enormous data volumes. Turning those measurements into sky images is a heavy computation. The coming SKA telescopes will dwarf today's instruments, so the pipelines must scale.

The team presents RICK 2.0, a new version of their radio imaging code. It uses a library for distributed Fourier transforms, the mathematical heart of the imaging step. The design aims at high performance that still ports across different supercomputers. Tests use data from precursors of the SKA telescopes. Faster, portable imaging is a precondition for the science those telescopes promise.
arxiv-2601-19814:
Marco Antonio Rosas Pulido and colleagues propose a new way to describe a city's economy. A city's firms, institutions, and spatial layout interact in intricate ways. Standard measures of economic complexity lean on what a city exports. The authors instead build a framework from three structural dimensions of economic units: abundance, diversity, and longevity.

Abundance counts how many units exist, diversity how varied they are, and longevity how long they last. Together these serve as proxies for complexity and resilience. A city strong on all three should weather shocks better. The framework gives planners a fresh lens on urban economies. It can be computed from firm-level records many cities already keep.
arxiv-2601-19914:
Maxwell Crouse and four colleagues build training data for AI agents that call tools. Synthetic data can teach smaller, cheaper models to handle multi-turn tool conversations. Many frameworks for making such data assume the tools run in a stateful environment. That environment remembers earlier calls and their effects.

Real deployments often run tools statelessly, with no memory between calls. The authors simulate complex multi-turn interactions inside such stateless execution environments. Their simulations must carry the needed context in the conversation itself. Training on data that matches the deployment setting should transfer better. The work closes a quiet mismatch between how agent data is made and how agents actually run.
arxiv-2601-20114:
J. N. Bai and four colleagues propose a way to build an exotic quantum model inside an array of Rydberg atoms. The target is the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, a chain model known for skin effects, where states pile up at one edge. Their setup uses a chain of atoms with three atoms in each unit cell.

A synthetic gauge field is made by shining multi-color laser fields on the atoms. Each atom can be addressed on its own, which gives fine control over the chain. The scheme offers a clean lab test bed for non-Hermitian physics, where loss and gain are part of the model rather than a flaw.
arxiv-2601-20714:
Raul de la Rosa, Ivana Dusparic, and Nicolas Cardozo study learning agents that must cope with change. Their 2026 paper is about reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by trial and reward. In the real world, the rules of the game can shift mid-task. Rewards may change, or new actions may open up. Most agents handle such shifts poorly.

The team presents morphin, a self-adaptive form of Q-learning. Q-learning is a classic method where an agent learns the value of each action. Morphin adjusts on the fly when the action set or rewards change. It does so without full retraining from scratch. The paper speaks to anyone who needs agents that keep working when their world will not sit still.
arxiv-2601-20914:
Nicolás Cardiel and six co-authors built a Python package to teach a core astronomy skill. Their 2026 paper presents teareduce. The package supports teaching the reduction of astronomical data. Reduction is the step that turns raw telescope output into clean, usable images. The package serves students in practical classes. Their courses process images from various instruments and telescopes.

Good teaching tools must be simple but honest. Teareduce gives students utilities that mirror real workflows. They can learn calibration and cleaning steps on actual data. The authors are astronomers and educators sharing their classroom material. Open teaching code helps other schools run the same practicals. The paper is a resource note for anyone who trains new observers.
arxiv-2601-21014:
Haixiang Sun and five co-authors make causal discovery cheaper by thinking locally. Their 2026 paper presents VISTA, a framework for learning causal structures from observational data. The task is fundamental but computationally intensive. In high dimensions, the search space grows super-exponentially. Existing methods strain under the load. VISTA answers with modular subgraph integration, as its full name spells out.

The framework splits the global problem into local subgraphs. Each subgraph is built from Markov blankets, the small sets that screen off each variable. Local structures are learned separately, then merged. A voting step integrates the pieces into one acyclic graph. Modularity keeps the cost in check as data grow. The method serves scientists who need causal maps from big, passive datasets.
arxiv-2601-21414:
Chenxu Yang and eight co-authors blend fast gut-level replies with slow careful reasoning in one language model. Human thought is often split into a quick intuitive mode and a slow deliberate one. Training a single model to switch between the two modes runs into clashes between them.

Earlier fixes mostly capped what the slow mode could output. The authors instead blend the two modes by mixing the models themselves, with the mix shifting as needed. Dynamic blending lets the system stay quick on easy items and slow down when a task demands care. That balance is key for cheap, reliable AI help.
arxiv-2601-21714:
A memory system for language model agents rebuilds past episodes in full context instead of compressing them. Long, careful problem solving needs memory that stays faithful over long spans. Most current memory tools squeeze past events into embeddings or graphs before storing them.

That squeezing cuts the context that gives each event its meaning. The authors' multi-agent design reconstructs episodes with their sequential links intact. Keeping context whole should support deeper reasoning across long tasks. The work targets agents that must stay coherent over hours of work, where a mangled memory can quietly wreck the whole chain.
arxiv-2601-21814:
Eduard Paul Enoiu, Jean Malm, and Gregory Gay argue that software teams run partly on folklore. They mean the stories, myths, rituals, jokes, and informal know-how that circulate inside development communities and shape how people actually work. Their 2026 paper sets out to define this idea properly for software engineering.

Drawing on folklore studies, the authors use a literature review and thematic analysis to characterize the concept. They gather example items. These include beliefs about where defects tend to occur. They also include the legend of the developer who is ten times better than peers. Naming this folklore matters because unwritten beliefs guide real choices about process, hiring, and quality, whether teams admit it or not.
arxiv-2601-21914:
Zhouyou Gu, Jihong Park, and Jinho Choi plan links inside vast constellations of low Earth orbit satellites. Laser links between satellites offer high-capacity, long-range connections that can make these networks resilient. Planning them well is harder than it first looks.

Existing schemes often ignore the mechanical limits of laser terminals, which must physically aim, and the uneven traffic demands around the globe. The team's 2026 preprint jointly handles link matching and traffic routing, using Lagrangian decomposition to split the big problem into solvable parts. Better link planning means more usable bandwidth from the same satellites, which affects the cost and quality of global satellite internet.
arxiv-2601-22014:
B. D. Lailey and T. A. A. Sigut check whether the standard ways of finding Be stars are biased by viewing angle. Be stars are fast-spinning stars with disks of gas around them. Whether we look at such a system nearly edge-on or nearly pole-on is its inclination, and it changes what we see.

The authors review several identification methods for bias with respect to inclination. They focus on two photometric methods that use narrow-band filters centered on the hydrogen alpha line. And one spectroscopic method that hunts for peaks in that line. Their 2026 preprint matters because biased catalogs distort everything built on them, from how common Be stars are to how their disks evolve.
arxiv-2601-22314:
Gyu Whan Chang and Giulio Peruginelli give a full account of a family of rings that sit between two classic polynomial rings. Their 2026 preprint studies domains — number systems with no zero divisors — that are integrally closed and Noetherian. The family lies between integer and rational polynomial rings in one variable.

The team sort the family by sorting the Krull domains inside it. A complete map of this kind closes a gap in ring theory. It gives algebra scholars a firm base for nearby questions. The work is pure math, with no device in view. Its value is the finished map itself.
arxiv-2601-22614:
Shyam Venkatasubramanian and a team steady transformer training with a consensus rule. Standard attention models can go unstable when the learning rate is set too high. Their 2026 preprint notes that most fixes tweak the optimizer, while the architecture itself stays untouched.

Their consensus step acts inside the model to curb that instability. Stable training at bold rates would cut tuning time and failed runs. It matters most for huge models, where one bad run costs a fortune. The work is an architectural answer to a training pain. It aims for calm by design.
arxiv-2601-22714:
Alexander Nikulin and four co-authors use vision-language models to teach latent action models what counts as a real action. Latent action models learn action codes from video, and feed the training of robot-ready systems. Their 2026 preprint notes that they fail when the scene holds distractors that move with the action.

People split true motion from noise at a glance; the team give models that task sense. Cleaner action codes should yield robots that learn faster from video. The work links language-guided vision to robot skill. It fixes a subtle, common flaw.
arxiv-2601-22914:
Fabrizio Canfora and three co-authors find exact black hole solutions with uneven, bumpy horizons. The solutions come from Einstein's equations joined with a model of superfluid pions, a kind of matter field. Their setup uses spinning pion patterns arranged as many vortices.

With that pattern, the matter equations shrink to a simpler first-order system. The gravity side becomes a known equation whose source shapes the horizon's bumps. Exact solutions are rare in gravity, and they give clean tests for theories of black holes and dense matter. Bumpy horizons stretch the usual picture of black holes as smooth spheres, showing how matter fields can deform them.
arxiv-2601-23014:
Yanwei Yue and co-authors train memory agents that manage their own memories. Unlike fixed pipelines, these agents decide how to process, store, and fetch what they learn. Training them is hard because rewards arrive sparsely, only after long chains of memory operations.

Their method, Mem-T, densifies those rewards so learning signals come more often. Denser feedback makes end-to-end training of memory policy practical. Agents with well-managed memory could handle long projects without forgetting key facts. Densifying rewards means the agent no longer waits through long memory-operation chains for a single delayed training signal. Earlier paradigms left agents wandering such chains with almost no feedback, which stalled end-to-end learning of memory policy.
arxiv-2603-01714:
Jinluan Yang, Yuxin Liu, Zhengyu Chen, and colleagues pick better training data for agents that use tools. Their 2026 work faults the usual filter, which keeps only winning runs and tasks with middling pass rates. A winning run may still waste steps or never show recovery from an error, so outcome alone misleads.

Their frame, TopoCurate, merges many trial runs of one task into a single map of shared states. On that map, good runs stand out by recovery skill, lean steps, and varied strategy. For practice tasks, the frame favors tasks rich in error branches and mixed plans. Tests on two agent benchmarks show steady gains for both fine-tuning and reward-based training. The map makes interaction structure, not just wins, drive what agents learn from.
arxiv-2603-01914:
Shixiang Song, He Li, Zitong Wang, and colleagues let each token in a language model choose how much compute it needs. Their 2026 work builds on recurrent models that loop a fixed number of times per token. Fixed loops waste effort on easy tokens and starve hard ones of extra passes.

Their model, AdaPonderLM, learns token-wise early exit during pre-training with no hand-set pruning ratios. Gates that grow stricter by iteration decide when each token stops looping, under a monotonic halting mask. Cached key and value states for halted tokens are reused, which keeps training and testing consistent. Across several backbone sizes, inference compute drops by about a tenth at equal quality. Gate analysis shows hard tokens, with high loss, indeed earn more passes than easy ones.
arxiv-2603-02214:
Jungwon Seo, Ferhat Ozgur Catak, Chunming Rong, and Jaeyeon Jang map a new way for models to team up in this 2026 paper. In federated inference, private models owned by different parties answer queries together. They share neither their training data nor their inner weights. No shared framework yet explains how such teamwork should work.

The authors name two must-haves: privacy at query time and real gains from teamwork. They formalize the setup as shielded joint computation. Then they trace the trade-offs when privacy, uneven data, and limited oversight collide. A working example shows friction in privacy, teamwork, and fair rewards. Their claim is that query-time teamwork behaves in ways training-time teamwork does not predict.
arxiv-2603-02314:
Stefan Arseneau, J Hermes, Maria Camisassa, and colleagues weigh the outer layers of white dwarfs in this 2026 paper. A white dwarf's hydrogen skin forms its whole visible surface. Yet theorists model its mass poorly, and observers have few direct checks. That gap clouds white dwarf masses and cooling ages.

The team fits a mixture model to gravity shifts in light from almost five hundred white dwarfs. Radius data come from the Gaia space mission's spectra. The joint fit traces how mass grows with radius across the sample. Results match leading evolution models closely. Models with thick, mass-dependent hydrogen skins beat a fixed-skin model. Careful progenitor modeling thus matters, and gravity shifts offer a promising probe of these thin skins.
arxiv-2603-02514:
Tram Thi Minh Tran, Adrian Wong, Callum Parker, and colleagues examine non-human voices in crisis planning in this 2026 paper. Resilience planning usually centers human participants and interests. Species and ecosystems affected by crises rarely get a seat at the table. A workshop with HCI researchers probed how technology might represent them.
