austen-mansfield-park-1814:
Jane Austen published Mansfield Park in 1814, her most grave and moral novel. Fanny Price, poor and shy, is raised at her rich uncle's great house. The book asks what good breeding and good conduct truly mean in practice.

Fanny watches her cousins flirt, act plays, and chase thrills she finds wrong. Henry Crawford woos her, but she holds out for worth she can trust. Edmund, the younger son she loves, learns slowly where true merit lies in life. Scandal in London proves Fanny's quiet judgment right in the end at last. Austen's irony cuts deep here, and the stakes feel high throughout.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-14:
The second part of Tract Baba Bathra fills volume fourteen of Michael L. Rodkinson's English Babylonian Talmud. Part one laid down courtyards, boundaries, and the start of sales law. The Last Gate now swings to documents, wills, and the division of estates.

The rabbis weigh bonds and deeds: how they are signed, witnessed, and proved in court. Inheritance rules follow, sorting sons, daughters, and widows, and the gifts a dying man may make by word of mouth. Guarantees on sold land close the tractate's plan. With this volume, the Talmud's three Gates of civil law stand complete in English.
boutroux-natural-law-1914:
What do we mean when we call something a law of nature? Emile Boutroux posed that question in De l'idee de loi naturelle in 1895. Fred Rothwell translated the French work into English in 1914. The book moves between two fields that both rely on the idea, science and philosophy.

Boutroux traces how the notion of natural law formed and what work it does in each field. He shows that a law states how things behave, yet leaves deeper questions open. His treatment links the habits of science with the aims of thought. It pairs well with his earlier book on contingency.
bradley-essays-truth-reality-1914:
Essays on Truth and Reality, published in 1914, gathers Bradley's late papers in defense of absolute idealism. By then pragmatism and the new realism were in full attack, and Bradley, aging and ill, answered them in his most polished prose.

The essays treat truth, error, and the coherence by which thought judges itself, always pointing beyond thought to the Absolute where contradictions rest. His style here is famous: sentences like honed blades, irony worn smooth. Bradley lost the argument of his century, but few think he lost on points of craft. These essays are his fighting testament.
broad-perception-physics-reality-1914:
Perception, Physics, and Reality, published in 1914, is C. D. Broad's first book, a critical examination of scientific realism. The young Cambridge philosopher asks how the world physics describes can be squared with the world we actually perceive.

Broad works through the theory of sense-data, the patches of color and sound from which we infer tables, atoms, and forces. He tests realism against idealism and phenomenalism with exemplary fairness, a trait that became his signature. The book is technical but never murky. It announced a philosopher of rare patience, soon to become a central figure at Cambridge.
bukhari-traditions-islamiques-houdas-mar:
Tome IV, printed in 1914, closes Les Traditions Islamiques, the complete French version of al-Bukhari's Sahih by Houdas and Marçais. Eleven years of work at the Imprimerie nationale end with the collection's last books. Reports on the Prophet's life, the end times, and the unity of God round out the vast whole.

Al-Bukhari died in 870, and Sunni Islam has ranked his gathering first among hadith books ever since. The French set gave European readers the full text, chains and all, in their own tongue. Tome IV completes a translation that remains a working tool for scholars of Islam.
burr-narratives-witchcraft-cases-1914:
George Lincoln Burr, a professor of medieval history at Cornell, edited Narratives of the Witchcraft Cases for a series on early American history. The book came out in New York in 1914. It gathers first-hand accounts of witch trials in New England between 1648 and 1706.

Fourteen narratives let judges, ministers, and accused people speak in their own words. The cases span the decades before and after the famous Salem trials of 1692. Burr's notes and framing help readers place each account in its town and court. The volume still serves as the standard one-book source for these trials.
burroughs-at-earths-core-1914:
Edgar Rice Burroughs opened his Pellucidar tales with At the Earth's Core in 1914. A rich young man, David Innes, tests a new burrow craft with its maker. The craft bores down through the crust of the Earth. It breaks out in a world lit by a small sun at Earth's core.

Pellucidar holds beasts of the old world and men of the stone age. Vast ape men and the winged Mahars rule the folk by fear and mind speech. Innes fights to free the tribes and wins a bride in the fray. The book is the pulp root of the whole inner world line.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-th: A 1913 entry on the Jesuits' suppression — the dark forty years. John Hungerford Pollen unfolds the tragic tale. Clement crushed the holy order. The exiles kept the faithful vow. The night of the Society's eclipse. Its 1814 restoration is famed.
chretien-cliges-comfort-1914:
Chretien de Troyes wrote Cliges as his second Arthurian romance in the twelfth century. W. W. Comfort translated it into English in 1914. Byzantine intrigue and an answer to the Tristan legend drive its plot.

Young Cliges travels from Constantinople to Arthur's court in Britain. He loves Fenice, who is married to the emperor, his uncle. A feigned death and a hidden tower let the lovers escape scandal briefly. Chretien argues that love should join body and heart in one person. The romance feels more artful and self-aware than his first. Comfort's version keeps the intricate plotting readable for English audiences.
chretien-erec-et-enide-comfort-1914:
W. W. Comfort translated Chretien de Troyes's Erec et Enide into English in 1914. Chretien composed the romance around 1170 in northern France. It is the first Arthurian romance, the work that founded a tradition.

Knight Erec wins the lady Enide and marries her in joy. Then whispers that marriage has softened him drive the couple back to adventure. Enide rides with him, forbidden to speak, yet warns him of dangers. Their trials test love, obedience, and knightly honor together. Comfort's translation opened Chretien to English readers in modern prose. European letters learned the chivalric love story from this book. Camelot's long literary life begins here.
chretien-lancelot-comfort-1914:
Chretien de Troyes wrote Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart, in the twelfth century. W. W. Comfort translated the romance into English in 1914. The poem defines courtly love for the whole Arthurian tradition after it.

Queen Guinevere is abducted, and Lancelot pursues her without hesitation. He climbs into a criminal's cart, the deepest shame a knight could accept. Love outranks honor at every turn of his quest. A sword bridge and a reluctant host's son test him further. Chretien left the poem unfinished, and another hand completed it. The forbidden love at Camelot's heart begins in these pages. No Arthurian theme proved more influential afterward.
chretien-yvain-comfort-1914:
Chretien de Troyes composed Yvain, the Knight of the Lion, in the twelfth century. W. W. Comfort's 1914 translation carries the beloved romance into English. A magic fountain in the forest starts the knight's troubles.

Yvain defeats the fountain's guardian and marries the dead man's lady, Laudine. Granted a year for tournaments, he overstays and loses her love entirely. Madness drives him naked into the wilderness to live like a beast. A lion he rescues from a serpent becomes his faithful companion. Together they perform rescues that slowly rebuild his honor. Chivalry, wilderness, and second chances fill Chretien's most humane romance here.
chronicle-novgorod-michell-forbes-1914:
Monks of Novgorod wrote their city's chronicle year by year from 1016 to 1471, and Michell and Forbes Englished it in 1914. Wars, princes, famines, and fires fill its terse entries. Novgorod, a proud republic of merchants, stood apart from princely Russia.

The chronicle lets medieval Russia speak in its own spare voice. A fire, a flood, a battle, a new church: each gets its brief line. Editors prize it as a base source for all Russian history of the age. This first full English version opened the record to a wide new readership, plain and precious at once.
cia-0000012414:
September 25, 1961: meeting number thirty-three carries the Paris sessions through the autumn. The colonel's Paris autumn was running at full pace by then. Handlers worked him in a borrowed city, under fresh cover. Each sitting added answers on Soviet forces to the growing file. Each also spent a little more of the luck that had held since April.

The thirty-third session's record keeps the harvest in order. Autumn in Paris, and the revelations continued without pause or drama. For readers, the page shows the operation's middle age: proven, productive, and quietly counting its remaining time.
cia-0000013214:
Where exactly was the American prisoner compound in Hanoi? A CIA item from January 1969 opens with that question of location. The item's title pairs the compound's place with a second North Vietnamese topic, cut short in the file. Pinpointing the prisons mattered beyond curiosity: every rescue plan ever drawn, and every bombing map ever marked, began from the camps' coordinates.

The item fixes the prison on the map as sources then reported it. Geographic precision was a form of care in this accounting. For readers, the page shows the search for the missing conducted at the level of streets and walls.
cia-0000013614:
Chile's situation and prospects fill a CIA paper from September 1963, as the long, narrow republic neared an election. Salvador Allende, the Marxist senator, was climbing toward the presidency he would contest the next year. Washington watched his rise with growing alarm. The paper tracks the parties, the copper wealth, and the voters who might carry a socialist to power by ballot for the first time anywhere.

The study weighs the Marxist's path year by year. It shows the agency's Chilean watch at an early, formative stage. For readers, it opens the long file that ended, a decade later, in a coup.
cia-0000013914: A captured American airman in Bo Trach District is the subject of a CIA note dated November 5, 1967. Bo Trach sits in Quang Binh Province, in North Vietnam. District level detail was rare and useful, since it narrowed where a man was held. The note pins one airman's capture to a single small district.
cia-0000014714: Communist exploitation of the Rosenbergs is the subject of a CIA paper dated January 5, 1953. The paper tracked how Communist parties used the case in their campaigns. A death sentence in New York gave them a theme heard around the world. Tracking its use told Washington where the case hurt its image most.
cia-0000015314: A letter to Luis Alvarez from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated April 4, 1958. It concerns Leon Davidson's possible step, the title says in clipped form. Alvarez was a top physicist with a Nobel Prize ahead of him. His name joins the ring of big science men copied on the Davidson question.
cia-0000015414: Word reached the CIA in September 1958 of a Washington man photographing odd shapes through a backyard telescope. He claimed his film caught shaped objects passing between the telescope and the moon, again and again over three months. The writer of the note had not seen the pictures himself. Still, the claim was logged, like many photo claims that reached the agency in those years.
cia-0000021514: Two American pilots were held prisoner in a cave and executed in retaliation, an untitled CIA record dated in 1965 reports. The title states the grim end plainly, with no names given. Cave prisons in Laos were a known horror of that secret war. A report this stark shows the worst kind of news the prisoner watchers had to pass on.
cia-0000022314: Under the heading Gary Powers, an address memo is kept in a CIA record dated October 5, 1962. The title does not say whose address or what kind of memo it is. Powers had come home that year in the spy swap for Rudolf Abel. A bare label like this leaves the reader a folder tab, not a story, and the description claims no more.
cia-0000025014: Cooperation among Latin American terrorist and insurgent groups is mapped in a CIA paper dated in 1970. The title's spelling, amoung, is the catalog's own. Rebel groups traded training, money, and safe houses across borders in that era. A paper on their teamwork treated the region's violence as one web, not a set of separate national troubles.
cia-0000044414:
El Salvador's foreign minister accused the FMLN of killing the priests, in a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. A foreign minister speaks to other governments, not only to home. His charge carried the government's case into foreign capitals.

Inside, the minister's accusation against the rebels is set down. Blaming the FMLN was the government's first line of defense abroad. It asked friendly states to doubt the charge against the army. The file preserves that diplomatic effort at its start, when the case was young and each side was racing to fix the story in foreign minds.
cia-0000049014: Pressure built again among El Salvador's middle-level officers in 1981 to remove those above them, and a CIA item from that year measures the strain. Middle ranks pushing upward was the classic first sign of a coup in the making. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, a gauge of the officer corps mid-war.
cia-0000049114: The Salvadoran military worried in 1985 about Christian Democratic publicity linking the armed forces to a bogus confession. A CIA item from that year records the concern. Image was a battlefield too: the brass fought stories as hard as charges. The item survives among the Truth Commission records of the war.
cia-0000049414: Rebel fronts disagreeing over suspension of peace talks in El Salvador are recorded in declassified CIA document 0000049414, dated October 3, 1987. The heading is cut short in the catalog but names the dispute clearly. The brief item centers on disagreement among the rebel fronts themselves, a dated sign of division preserved in the declassified record.
cia-0000098314: Memorandum for the Holders of SNIE 80-61 on security conditions in Caracas and beyond, in cut-short heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000098314, dated November 4, 1961. The audience is holders of a numbered estimate. The brief file is a follow-on memorandum record, its subject security conditions in a named capital city.
cia-0000098714: Somaliland President Egal speaks on a mysterious bomb blast, according to declassified CIA document 0000098714, dated January 4, 1996. The heading names the speaker and calls the blast mysterious. The brief file records a president's remarks on an unexplained explosion, the latest-dated item in this catalog run and a change of region and decade.
cia-0000119214:
Dated January 1, 1968, this CIA document gives the location of work camps for Vietnamese prisoners near Nam Dinh. Nam Dinh sits in North Vietnam, and the camps held prisoners put to labor during the war. The entry is the first item in its file, which suggests a short field report rather than a long study.

Forced labor camps were part of how North Vietnam used its prisoners, and knowing where they stood mattered to American planners. A map of camp locations could guide rescue thinking, bombing choices, and talks about prisoner treatment. The document preserves the agency's picture of the camps as its sources reported them in early 1968.
cia-0000124314: Dated July 1951, this CIA document covers American prisoners of war in Shanghai. Captured Americans passed through China's great port city on their way inland during the Korean War. The paper records what the agency knew of men held so far from the fighting. Shanghai held foreign residents, journalists, and consulates longer than most Chinese cities, which made prisoner sightings there more likely to reach the agency in detail.
cia-0000132414: New plans by the Castro government are the subject of item 13 in the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated November 2, 1959. Its headline breaks off just after the words set up new, leaving the object unnamed. New bodies, new militias, or new offices could each fit the gap. The short item reports what the government was preparing, whatever the missing word was.
cia-0000132514: Cuba seeking support from Ecuador fills a CIA item dated April 1, 1961. A second Cuban topic follows in the headline but is cut short in the record title. The invasion at the Bay of Pigs was only days away at that point. Havana needed every friend it could still find. The short item tracks the courtship of Quito as analysts recorded it.
cia-0000132614: Argentina worrying over Cuban links with the Peronistas fills item 10 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 1, 1960. Its headline misspells the country as Agentina, a slip kept from the original. Buenos Aires feared Havana's influence over the exiled Peronist movement. The short item reports that concern and its sources.
cia-0000135714: The catalog dates this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document to 6 March 1961 and marks the date as estimated. March 1961 was the brigade's final month of preparation before the Bay of Pigs landing. An estimated date means the agency's reviewers placed the item in time rather than reading a date off it. No subject is recorded. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, its timing approximate and its contents unstated in the record.
cia-0000135814: A second meeting under the K-Program fills a CIA paper dated April 5, 1954. The paper is marked operational, and its specific subject was deleted before release. An attachment rides with the meeting record. Code names like K-Program hid the moving parts of the Guatemala campaign from plain view. The short paper keeps the meeting record in its filed form.
cia-0000136214: 1 May 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA cable about Instructions 1 on currency reform, guidance for LANGEVIN on the money of a future government. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136314: Fighter aircraft parts top LINCOLN's list of most urgent needs in this June 1954 PBSUCCESS cable. The station asks for ten F-47 tires and tubes plus main gear tires, noting aircraft grounded at two locations for lack of them, and requests air delivery capacity from Washington. It also wants maintenance personnel sent at once to work on CALLIGERIS's aircraft, suggesting specially selected men sworn to secrecy. Logistics, here, is the operation's weak point.
cia-0000136614: Dated 4 January 1961, this document in Spanish is one of several 2506 Brigade records bearing that date. Brigade 2506 was made up of Cuban exiles trained and armed by the CIA for the Bay of Pigs landing. The catalog record states no subject for the item. It survives in the original Spanish in the declassified release, identified by date and collection, with its contents left to the text itself.
cia-0000136714: This Spanish-language document from the 2506 Brigade files carries an estimated date of 5 January 1960, earlier than the brigade's formation period and flagged as an estimate in the catalog. An earlier summary spoke of stakes, teamwork, and a watched enemy; none of that is in the record, and it is dropped. What stands is a Spanish brigade document with an estimated, unusually early date, released in the CIA's declassified files.
cia-0000137014: Requests for aid should go to Washington, not through Bannister to the group, headquarters urges the Guatemala City station in this July 1954 cable. It knows the station will follow up on attacks; the station should also advise whether press reports that communists escaped from embassies are true, and report on other embassies. Bannister, CALLIGERIS, and the ambassador should all receive details and guidance, since at this stage any matter CALLIGERIS raises involves policy directly or indirectly. The new regime's needs were already Washington's business.
cia-0000137314: Cuba dominates the briefing for the 427th National Security Council meeting. The meeting sat on 16 December 1959. Che Guevara returned in September from a long trip. He visited nine Afro-Asian countries and Yugoslavia. Foreign Minister Raul Roa spoke at the UN that month. Cuba sees the American and Soviet systems as twin evils, he said. It would ally with underdeveloped nations. Roa plans a January trip to Cairo. A high-level economic mission may follow. Egypt's ambassador backed inviting Raul Castro.
cia-06859714: LIBERIA: UPDATE ON PEACE PROCESS, a CIA document. The peace update. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:
Cicero wrote De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum, On Ends, in 45 BCE. In it he tests the rival Greek schools on one question: what is the highest good a life can aim at? H. Rackham translated it for the Loeb series in 1914, with the Latin on facing pages. The work runs to five books of staged debate.

Speakers make the case for Epicurus, then for the Stoics, then for the school of Plato's heirs, while Cicero presses each side in turn. No other Roman book gives so full a map of these schools' ethics. Cicero's dialogue kept Greek moral thought alive for Latin readers and for every age after them.
constitution-dominica-2014: Dominica's 1978 Constitution, amended through 2014, frames its island republic. It guards rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It freed a green isle. Crown left. Votes ruled. Nature kept. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-namibia-2014: Namibia's 1990 Constitution, amended through 2014, frames its republic. It guards rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It freed the desert. Apartheid fell. Voters came. Dunes held. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-nicaragua-2014: Nicaragua's 1987 Constitution, amended through 2014, frames its republic. It lifted term limits. The Tower library holds the full text. It kept long rule. Votes amended. Terms lifted. Power stayed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-russia-2014: Russia's 1993 Constitution, amended through 2014, frames its federation. It centers the Kremlin. The Tower library holds the full text. It ordered vast lands. Soviets fell. President rose. Power centered. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-switzerland-2014: Switzerland's 1999 Constitution, amended through 2014, frames its confederation. Citizens vote often. The Tower library holds the full text. It perfected direct rule. Cantons voted. Alps stood. People decided. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
croce-historical-materialism-marx-1914:
Historical Materialism and the Economics of Karl Marx, published in English in 1914, gathers Croce's early critical essays on Marx. Written in the 1890s, they made his name in Italy before the Philosophy of Spirit appeared.

Croce's aim is rescue by division: to save Marx's economics as a useful method while rejecting the materialist metaphysics built on it. Historical materialism, he argues, is a canon for reading history, not a philosophy of the universe. The essays are sharp, respectful, and firm. They began Italy's long, serious argument with Marx, and they show Croce's mind before the system.
czaplicka-aboriginal-siberia-1914:
Maria Czaplicka wrote this study of the native peoples of Siberia, and Oxford brought it out in 1914. She drew on field trips and on reports in many tongues. Her aim was to give English readers one clear map of a vast, cold land.

Much of the book deals with shamans, the healers and guides who speak with spirits for their groups. She shows how the word shaman came to name a whole class of such roles. Scholars still cite her work as the first strong English account of the theme.
dante-divine-comedy-cary-1814:
Dante Alighieri wrote the Divine Comedy in Italy in the early 1300s, and Henry Francis Cary made the first full English version in 1814. Cary's verse, with notes, at last let English readers take the whole trip. Blake drew pictures for this famed text.

Dante, lost in midlife, tours Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise with guides. He meets sinners, saints, old foes, and his lost love Beatrice. Each realm has strict ranks, strange pains, and bright rewards. The poem mixes faith, politics, and love into one vast plan of the soul. Cary's notes made the hard parts clear to new readers.
dawson-woodward-piltdown-supplementary-1:
Dawson and Woodward returned to the Geological Society in 1914 with more Piltdown material. New fragments from the same Sussex gravels seemed to confirm their dawn man. A canine tooth held the spotlight in the supplementary note.

The tooth appeared to settle arguments about how the jaw and skull fitted. In fact it deepened a forgery that fooled experts for decades. Read today, the note shows how planted evidence can confirm itself. Each new piece made doubters look stubborn and believers feel certain. The fraud's grip tightened precisely because the additions seemed so responsive.
dhalla-zoroastrian-theology-1914:
Maneckji Nusservanji Dhalla was high priest of the Parsis of Karachi and a scholar trained at Columbia. His Zoroastrian Theology, published in 1914, sets out the doctrine of his ancient faith in systematic form. It was the first modern Parsi theology written in English.

Dhalla traces belief from the prophet Zoroaster through centuries of rule, invasion, and life as a small minority in India. He explains the war of good and evil, the duties of prayer and purity, and the hope of a final renewal. Parsi readers gained a clear account of their own tradition in a modern voice.
dickinson-single-hound-1914:
The Single Hound appeared in 1914, the first new book of Emily Dickinson's poems in nearly twenty years. Martha Dickinson Bianchi, the poet's niece, selected these poems from manuscripts kept in the family. The title comes from a line Dickinson had sent her as a girl.

Bianchi chose poems that showed her aunt's playful, nature-loving side alongside the famous meditations on death. The selection helped restart Dickinson's reputation in the modernist era, when new poets recognized a kindred spirit. Editorial habits of the time still regularized some punctuation. Even so, the freshness of the voice is unmistakable. The Single Hound marks the moment Dickinson's revival truly began.
doe-osti-3367800-close-out-report-for-de: DE-SC0020414 got close-out-reported, and this DOE report covers the close-out. The pages detail the findings. The researchers get their closeout. The report was close-out. The closeout was researcher. The DE-SC0020414 were out. The close-out were report.
dostoevsky-crime-and-punishment-garnett-:
Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote Crime and Punishment in Russian, and Constance Garnett made it English in 1914. Garnett's version brought Dostoevsky to the English-speaking world in force. The novel tracks a murder and the long torment that follows it in Petersburg.

Raskolnikov, a poor ex-student, kills a pawnbroker to prove he stands above morals. Guilt and fever wreck his health, and a shrewd detective toys with his mind. Sonya, a meek girl forced to the streets, shows him a path of confession. He gives himself up and faces Siberia, with Sonya at his side in exile. Few novels dig so deep into crime, pride, and the hope of grace.
dreiser-titan-1914:
Theodore Dreiser published The Titan in 1914, the middle volume of his Trilogy of Desire. Frank Cowperwood, ruined and jailed in Philadelphia in The Financier, moves west to rebuild. Dreiser follows the career of the real traction king Charles Yerkes in Chicago, much as he had in Philadelphia.

Cowperwood buys streetcar lines, bribes aldermen, and fights for a fifty-year franchise against the city's whole political order. His marriage to Aileen curdles as mistresses succeed one another, each drawn in full Dreiser detail. Chicago itself, raw, rich, and corruptible, is the true titan of the title. The novel is huge, clumsy, and compulsively readable. It completes Cowperwood's rise to his greatest height before the final volume's English fall.
driesch-vitalism-ogden-1914:
Hans Driesch was a German biologist whose sea urchin trials convinced him that life cannot be reduced to a machine. His History and Theory of Vitalism, in Ogden's 1914 translation, traces the idea of a life force from Aristotle onward. It is both a history and a defense.

Driesch argues that a cut embryo, which still grows into a whole animal, defies any purely mechanical account. He names the guiding factor entelechy, a goal-bearing force inside living things. Most later biologists rejected his answer, but his questions about form and growth still reward reading. He writes as a working scientist, not only as a thinker about science.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-14: Volume fourteen of the Essays continues the self-portrait. Montaigne examines his body, his moods, and his aging mind without flinching. Nothing human is foreign to his curiosity. The most personal of all philosophers, and the most honest.
europmc-pmc10028514:
Eysenbach reflects on the role of ChatGPT and similar AI tools in medical education in a 2023 paper. ChatGPT launched in late 2022 and reached a huge user base within two months. Teachers faced a tool that could write fluent medical text on demand, for good and for ill.

The paper takes the form of a conversation with ChatGPT itself about its classroom role. It weighs uses in learning and writing against risks to honesty and skill. It ends with a call for papers on the theme. The piece captures an early moment of change in medical training.
europmc-pmc10369014:
Chen and colleagues modelled the world cost of a chronic lung disease from 2020 to 2050. The disease is COPD, in which air flow out of the lungs slowly worsens. It is the third top cause of death in the world. The team built an economic model for 204 nations and areas.

Their model counts lost work from illness and death, plus care costs that drain savings. Chen puts the total loss at 4.326 trillion dollars over the 30 years. That is like a yearly tax of 0.111% on world output. China bears the largest share, at 1.363 trillion, with the USA next at 1.037 trillion. The team urges states to invest now to curb the disease.
europmc-pmc10583314:
Zhang and co-authors tested a blood index in 2023 as a death risk mark for heart patients with diabetes. The index, called TyG, joins blood fats and blood sugar in one number. The team drew 1,072 US adults with heart disease and diabetes or pre-diabetes from a national survey. Death records were tracked through 2019.

Over 7,541 person-years, 461 people died, 154 of them from heart causes. Zhang found a U-shaped link between the index and death risk. Risk bottomed near a TyG of 9.05 for all deaths and 8.84 for heart deaths. Below those points, higher values meant lower risk. Above them, higher values meant higher risk. The mark may help flag patients who need closer care.
europmc-pmc10719114:
Yao led a large team in 2023 to chart cell types across the whole mouse brain with place and gene data. The team read genes in about 7 million single cells. Near 4.3 million cells also got a place on a spatial map. The two views merged into one atlas of the adult brain.

The atlas stacks 5,322 clusters into 1,201 supertypes, then 338 subclasses, and at last 34 classes. Yao found that gene identity matched place closely for most types. The top half of the brain held fewer but more distinct nerve cell types. The lower half held more types, each closer kin to the next. A code of gene switches defined types across all regions.
europmc-pmc10730214:
Gavzy and co-authors reviewed Bifidobacterium in 2023, a gut bacterium genus with calming effects on the immune system. These friendly microbes live in the guts of many mammals. When they thin out or vanish, immune balance can slip toward self-attack. Their surface parts and waste products carry much of their signal.

The cells boost Treg cells, the immune arm that damps attack, Gavzy reports. They also firm the gut wall seal and tune other immune cells nearby. Two swelling programs in the gut, Th2 and Th17, get dialled down. The review sorts the paths by which molecule does the work. It ties those paths to the wider gut microbe mix as well.
europmc-pmc1215514:
Agarwal, Gupta, and Sharma reviewed oxidative stress in female fertility in 2005. Reactive oxygen species are active molecules cells make each day. Antioxidants keep them in balance in a healthy body. When that balance tips, stress harms tissues.

These molecules play two roles in the female tract. At low levels they signal normal steps like egg release. At high levels they damage eggs, embryos, and DNA. Stress also links to early labor and fertility decline with age. Agarwal shows antioxidants may guard eggs during ovulation. It appeared in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology.
europmc-pmc1241714:
Schecter and co-authors reported flame retardant levels in United States breast milk in 2003. No prior study had measured PBDEs in milk from single American mothers. PBDEs come from foam, resin, and plastic products in homes. Use was allowed in the United States but banned in parts of Europe.

European milk levels looked low but rising, possibly peaking in late-1990s Sweden. American data were nearly absent before this work. The team extended its earlier milk studies on dioxins and PCBs. Schecter fills a national gap on infant exposure to persistent chemicals.
europmc-pmc1312014:
Rhodius and co-authors compared a bacterial stress response across related genomes in 2006. Bacteria meet stress by switching on alternative sigma factors. These factors steer gene-copying machinery to stress gene sets. Predicting their target sites is hard because patterns vary.

A validated model predicted 89 sigma E controlled units in E. coli. Predictions extended to eight related genomes. The shared core ensures building blocks of the outer membrane. It covers lipopolysaccharide and porin proteins, the membrane essentials. The variable portion points to disease-related jobs instead. Rhodius separates universal stress duties from species-specific ones.
europmc-pmc1481614:
How staff feel about safety in a ward may shape patient harm. Sexton and co-authors tested a survey for those attitudes in 2006, the Safety Attitudes Questionnaire. They gave it to 10,843 health workers in 203 clinical areas across three countries.

Six attitude themes fit the answers well: teamwork climate, job satisfaction, stress recognition, working conditions, safety climate, and views of management. The scales scored high on reliability, at 0.9. Attitudes varied widely within and between hospitals. Sexton offers the survey as a benchmark tool. Hospitals can compare scores, target weak spots, and check whether fixes shift attitudes over time.
europmc-pmc1665414:
Poor diet may decide whether air pollution harms a pregnancy. Kannan and co-authors built a framework for that question in 2006. Particles in air are linked to low birth weight, stunted growth in the womb, and early delivery.

They outline five plausible pathways, running through oxidative stress, inflammation, clotting, vessel function, and blood flow control. Nutrition touches each of those pathways. So the same pollution dose may harm a poorly nourished mother more. Kannan proposes studies that measure diet and pollution together, rather than treating either in isolation.  The framework also gives clear strategies for testing the model in future studies.
europmc-pmc1854914:
Gross, Ploner and co-authors showed in 2007 that fast brain waves in the touch cortex mirror how much pain a person feels. Gamma oscillations, rhythms between about 30 and 100 cycles per second, mark sensory input the brain selects for priority processing. Pain always demands priority, so the team tested painful stimuli directly.

Using magnetoencephalography, which records the brain's magnetic fields, they applied selective pain stimuli to volunteers. The stimuli drove gamma rhythms between 60 and 95 hertz in primary somatosensory cortex, the first touch area. Rhythm strength rose with both the physical stimulus level and the reported pain. Near the pain threshold, stimuli that were felt produced stronger gamma than equal stimuli that went unnoticed. The signal thus tracks perceived pain rather than the stimulus alone.
europmc-pmc1868914:
Schmitt reviewed in 2007 how ice-age cycles sculpted the genetic map of European animals. Repeated glaciations pushed species into warm refuges, then let them spread again as ice retreated. Genetic tools had lately made those hidden histories readable, and this review gathers the patterns.

Three broad groups emerge. Mediterranean species often split into three lineages, isolated on the Iberian, Italian, and Balkan peninsulas during glaciations. Their return trips north were channeled by the Pyrenees and Alps, giving four main expansion patterns. Continental species trace to refuges east or north of the Mediterranean instead. Alpine and arctic species show younger patterns tied to present cold habitats. Some cases break the scheme, with extra splits inside single peninsulas or across North Africa and Asia Minor.
europmc-pmc1906714:
Diamond and co-authors built in 2007 a model of how strong emotion changes memory over time. Their temporal dynamics model draws on work about stress and LTP, how brain links grow stronger and last, a process thought to underlie learning. It covers the hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex, three regions central to memory and emotion.

In the model, a strong emotional event briefly switches plasticity on in the hippocampus and amygdala, then blocks new plasticity for a while. That quiet window protects the fresh memory while it sets. The hippocampus also flips from a map-building mode to a flashbulb mode, which fits why traumatic memories feel vivid yet broken up. The model ties flashbulb memories, traumatic memory, and stress-induced amnesia to the Yerkes-Dodson law on arousal and performance.
europmc-pmc1950214:
Chen, Alman and co-authors probed in 2007 when a bone growth signal helps or hurts fracture repair. Slow-healing fractures disable many patients and often need extra surgery. The beta-catenin pathway, a WNT-driven signal that builds bone in embryos, had an unknown role in adult repair.

Protein tests showed beta-catenin rising during healing of mouse shinbone fractures. A reporter mouse confirmed the pathway's gene-switching activity in both new bone and cartilage zones, and several WNT signal molecules appeared during repair. Blocking the pathway with the antagonist DKK1 disturbed healing. The detailed results show the pathway's role flips between phases of repair: needed at one stage, harmful if forced at another. That timing split is the paper's warning for any drug meant to speed bone healing.
europmc-pmc2125014: A medical paper on the cause of excessive calcium excretion in infantilism. The stunted children. This article preserves that pediatric research. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2125114: A medical paper on hematogenous and obstructive icterus, experimental studies. The jaundice types. This article preserves that hepatology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2126314: A medical paper on blood volume in wounded soldiers, the use of forced fluids. The battlefield fluids. This article preserves that military medicine. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2128214: A medical paper with studies on measles, acquired immunity after experimental measles. The measles defense. This article preserves that immunology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128314: A medical paper on the growth-promoting function of leucocytes. The helpful white cells. This article preserves that cell biology. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2131014: A medical paper on immunological relationships of pneumococcus cell constituents, second paper. The germ's parts again. This article preserves that immunology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2131214: A medical paper with comparative pathology of South African jagziekte and Montana progressive pneumonia. The sheep lung diseases. This article preserves that veterinary pathology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2131514: A medical paper with studies on fowl paralysis, clinical features. The paralyzed chickens. This article preserves that veterinary neurology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2265414:
Sommereyns, Paul, Staeheli and Michiels compared two interferon systems in mice in 2008. Interferons are antiviral defence signals. Type I interferons and the newer type III, called IFN-lambda, use different receptors yet regulate similar genes. The team measured where each is produced after virus infection. They then expressed individual interferon genes in living mice. They mapped which tissues and cells responded, using the lambda receptor's distribution as a guide.

In brain, type I interferons were readily produced after RNA virus infection, while lambda production stayed low. In liver, both systems switched on. Responses to lambda were prominent in stomach, intestine and lungs, yet very low in brain and spleen. In kidney and brain, lambda responses were restricted to epithelial cells, the surface lining cells. Type I responses spanned many cell types, strongest in blood vessel cells.
europmc-pmc2267814:
Lewis, Hughes, Rambaut, Pozniak and Leigh Brown reconstructed HIV transmission patterns in 2008 among men who have sex with men in London. Interview-based contact networks often clash with the transmission network hidden in viral genetics. HIV evolves fast, so dense sequence sampling can reveal real links. The team compared viral protease and reverse transcriptase sequences from 2,126 patients, mostly from that population.

Of these, 402 patients had a close genetic match to at least one other sequence. Nine large clusters were confirmed by Bayesian phylogenetic analysis. A quarter of matched individuals linked to ten or more others. Dated family trees suggested 65 percent of within-cluster transmissions happened between 1995 and 2000. About 25 percent occurred within six months of infection. The epidemic was thus episodic, with bursts of rapid spread in the late 1990s.
europmc-pmc2329914:
Jahreiss, Menzies, and Rubinsztein filmed the life of autophagosomes in living cells in 2008. An autophagosome is a bubble that wraps worn-out cell parts and carries them off for breakdown. This cleanup process is called autophagy, and it also helps cells survive starvation.

Using a live-cell test, they watched the bubbles form at random spots near the cell edge. The bubbles then rode along tracks called microtubules toward the cell centre, pulled by a motor protein named dynein. There they met lysosomes, the cell's digestion sacs. Meetings took two forms. Some bubbles merged fully, while most used kiss-and-run fusion, passing some contents across and parting again. The merged compartment lasted longer than expected.
europmc-pmc2394514:
Lattin and a large team catalogued sense receptors on mouse macrophages in 2008. Macrophages are immune cells that eat germs and steer inflammation. Their surface carries many G protein-coupled receptors, a large family of sensors that detect chemicals and are common drug targets.

Using gene chips, the team compared resting macrophages with other cell types and with macrophages stirred by a bacterial product called LPS. One sensor, P2ry6, appeared almost only in macrophages, and a sister sensor, Gpr84, was also macrophage-restricted. Two others appeared in macrophages and nerve tissue alike. LPS treatment strongly cut two family members, P2ry1 and P2ry5. Two lab-grown macrophage types shared much of the list but each kept some private sensors. The authors said these unstudied receptors may open new routes to anti-inflammatory drugs.
europmc-pmc2563014:
Meyer and colleagues launched a public web server in 2008 for analysing metagenomes, the DNA collected wholesale from an environment's microbes. Sequencing had grown cheap, so the bottleneck moved to interpreting millions of fragments from organisms never grown in a laboratory. Their system, the metagenomics RAST server, handles that interpretation using high-performance computing.

Users upload a metagenome and the pipeline compares its sequences against protein and DNA databases to assign likely functions and tell which organisms the fragments came from. It produces summary charts of the community. It also gives tools for comparing several metagenomes side by side. Accounts keep each user's data private. Users can still share with collaborators. All results can be downloaded. The authors offer it free, as an open-source backbone for the field.
europmc-pmc2570914:
Keawcharoen and colleagues infected six wild duck species in 2008 with the highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu virus to learn which could carry it over long distances. Migrating waterbirds were suspected in the virus's westward spread, yet critics argued infected birds sicken too badly to travel. The team used a 2005 European isolate and tracked illness and virus shedding in 46 captive-bred ducks.

Species split sharply. Mallards shed abundant virus from the throat while staying healthy, making them the prime long-distance vector candidate. Tufted ducks and pochards shed heavily too, but their heaviest shedders developed severe brain inflammation and neurologic disease, so they would die rather than migrate, acting as sentinels instead. Teal, wigeon, and gadwall shed little virus. Shedding was mainly from the throat, not the gut.
europmc-pmc2588614:
Swick, Ashley, and Turken tested in 2008 whether the brain's left inferior frontal gyrus is needed to stop an action already in motion. Brain imaging had tied response inhibition to the matching region on the right side, and right-side dominance had become the accepted view. Data on the left region were conspicuously missing, so the team tested twelve patients with left-sided damage on a Go/NoGo task.

Patients pressed for frequent Go signals and had to withhold presses for rare NoGo signals. They made more false alarm errors than healthy controls in both easy and hard blocks. Their deficit grew in the hard block. There, NoGo trials fell to 10 percent and inhibition demands rose. A comparison group with orbitofrontal damage performed normally. The authors conclude the left region is also critical for inhibitory control.
europmc-pmc2627714:
Mead and colleagues produced in 1999 the landmark estimate of foodborne illness in the United States, combining data from multiple surveillance systems. Policy needed firmer numbers on how much sickness, hospital care, and death contaminated food causes each year. Their synthesis separated illnesses from known pathogens from those due to unknown agents.

They estimate foodborne diseases cause about 76 million illnesses, 325,000 hospitalisations, and 5,000 deaths annually in the United States. Known pathogens account for roughly 14 million illnesses, 60,000 hospitalisations, and 1,800 deaths. Just three pathogens, Salmonella, Listeria, and Toxoplasma, cause 1,500 of those deaths, over 75 percent of the known-pathogen total. The remaining 62 million illnesses were chalked up to unknown agents. Overall, illness counts ran higher, but deaths lower, than earlier estimates suggested.
europmc-pmc2667514:
Xie and Tammi presented in 2009 a method called CNV-seq for spotting copy number changes in DNA using fast modern sequencing. Such changes, where stretches of DNA are gained or lost, are a major source of human variation. The standard tool, a chip-based comparison method, has built-in limits on sharpness and cost.

Their approach counts how many short reads land in each stretch of the genome. A statistical model then calls gains and losses, with confidence values attached. Tests showed that the sheer number of reads matters, not their length, which suits the new machines that pour out millions of short reads. In simulations the method proved highly accurate across a wide range of coverage, and it worked on real data comparing two people's genomes.
europmc-pmc2672614:
Hu and a large team built in 2009 a functional atlas of the gut bacterium E. coli, aiming at its many mystery proteins. A third of the bacterium's 4,225 genes had no known job. Some are shared with distant microbes, hinting at basic roles; others appear only in E. coli, including disease strains.

The team fished out tagged proteins to see which partners each one holds, and layered in clues from gene neighborhoods. The haul: nearly 6,000 likely physical contacts and about 74,800 looser functional links, most of them new. Grouping the network placed mystery proteins inside known teams and processes. Follow-up tests confirmed roles for some in protein building, food chemistry, surface film growth, swimming, and assembling the cell's outer envelope. The atlas gives the best-studied microbe on Earth a far more complete job chart.
europmc-pmc2686714:
Jain and colleagues described in 2009 the rebuilt website of UniProt, the world's main protein database. UniProt collects protein sequences and what is known about them, and most life scientists pass through it. For years its three partner institutes ran separate sites with different search pages, a confusing split for users and costly to maintain.

The new single site, launched in July 2008 after a year of public testing, gives one front door to the data. It offers plain and field-based text search, similarity search, sequence alignment, bulk download, and translation between the many naming systems proteins collect. The design serves beginners and experts, and machines as well as people, since software can query it directly. It was built with open-source tools and is free for academic and commercial use alike.
europmc-pmc2701414:
Makarova, Wolf, and Koonin conducted in 2009 a genome-wide census of type 2 toxin-antitoxin systems, the paired poison-and-antidote modules scattered through bacterial and archaeal genomes. These two-gene modules make a cell dependent on keeping them, yet also serve in stress defense. Many families were suspected to remain undiscovered.

Using distant-similarity searches and gene-neighborhood analysis across 750 complete genomes, the team found many unnoticed relatives of known toxins and antidotes. They predict twelve new toxin families and thirteen new antidote families, and flag several unsuspected modules as likely systems. One extremely common pair, a minimal transferase with a HEPN partner, may be a novel system abundant in heat-loving microbes. The survey shows these modules move between genomes at exceptional rates, blurring the line between selfish hitchhiker and useful stress tool.
europmc-pmc2718614:
Christensen and co-authors mapped in 2009 how DNA methylation, a chemical tag that can silence genes, varies in normal human tissues with age and exposures. Such tags guide development and cell identity, and their faults link to cancer. Yet normal variation across people and body sites was poorly charted.

They profiled two hundred seventeen tissues from ten body sites at over fourteen hundred tag sites near hundreds of genes. Patterns predicted both tissue origin and age with strong accuracy. In solid tissues, sites inside CpG islands, dense tag-prone stretches, gained methylation with age, while sites outside islands lost it. The split held across tissues and in blood, which warns disease studies to expect age drift.
europmc-pmc2726614:
Qin and co-authors profiled in 2009 how growing through a pistil, the female part of a flower, changes gene activity in pollen tubes of Arabidopsis. Pollen tubes carry sperm to ovules, but in lab medium they grow slowly and wander at random. Contact with stigma and style tissues makes them faster and able to follow guidance cues.

Tubes that grew through pistil tissue switched on a far larger share of the genome than pollen grains or lab-grown tubes. Genes for signaling, gene control, and tube growth were enriched in that set. Testing induced genes found seven new growth genes: two needed for navigation through the pistil, and five for best growth in the lab.
europmc-pmc2808214:
Fowkes, Richards, Simpson, and Beeson pooled the evidence in 2010 on whether antibodies against malaria's merozoite stage protect people from illness. Merozoites are the form of the Plasmodium falciparum parasite that invades red blood cells. Which of their surface proteins truly mark protection decides which ones belong in a vaccine.

The review gathered cohort studies from regions where malaria is common and merged their results. Antibodies to several parasite proteins, including MSP-3, AMA-1, EBA-175, and GLURP, tracked with lower rates of later malaria in many study groups. Effects differed by protein version and by how strongly a place was exposed, so the authors urge standard methods in future work.
europmc-pmc2824714:
Dyer, Goldsmith, Sharples, and Buxton reviewed in 2010 how the EQ-5D health questionnaire performs in heart and vessel disease studies. The EQ-5D turns a patient's answers about mobility, self-care, activity, pain, and mood into a single utility score, a number used to weigh treatments in cost studies. Their search pulled one hundred forty-seven papers, of which sixty-six fit the rules.

Evidence generally backed the tool as valid and reliable in this field. Scores fell steadily as disease grew worse: heart failure patients slid from mild to severe groups, and the same staircase appeared in angina. The authors supply pooled scores across heart conditions and treatments, meant to feed future cost-effectiveness models that count quality-adjusted life years.
europmc-pmc2841614:
Nadell, Foster, and Xavier used computer models in 2010 to ask how cooperation can survive among single cells that grow in clumps. A cooperative cell pays a cost to make goods its neighbors can use, which invites cheats that take the goods for free. If goods stay local, though, kin may reap them instead.

Their simulations grew virtual cell groups under varied growth rates, food levels, and food spread. Lineages sorted themselves in space in ways set by those few settings, with no planning needed. Under a wide range of realistic conditions, cooperators clustered with their own kind and beat the exploiters locally and overall. Adjusting food supply flipped which side won, showing how physics shapes social evolution in microbes.
europmc-pmc2844414:
Jakobsson and colleagues tracked throat and gut bacteria in 2010 before and after a standard antibiotic course against Helicobacter pylori, the stomach germ behind ulcers. Volunteers took clarithromycin and metronidazole for a short course, and their bacterial communities were read by DNA sequencing at points stretching four years.

One week after treatment, diversity crashed and community makeup swung sharply in every treated person, while untreated controls stayed stable. Actinobacteria fell hard in both throat and gut. Most communities drifted back toward their old shape, yet some stayed altered the full four years. A resistance gene against the drug family also stayed high four years on, showing that one short course can leave a long shadow.
europmc-pmc2847914:
Uppuluri and colleagues investigated in 2010 the least-studied stage of Candida albicans biofilms: dispersion, when cells break away to seed new infections. This yeast forms tough biofilms on catheters and implants, and escaped cells drive bloodstream infections that kill many patients. Growing biofilms in a flow model, the team captured the released cells and compared them with free-floating yeast.

How many cells dispersed depended on the food source and acidity during growth. Dispersed cells were mostly round yeast, yet they stuck better, sprouted filaments faster, and formed new biofilms more eagerly than ordinary planktonic cells. In mice they caused worse disseminated disease. Tuning two shape-control genes, UME6 and PES1, dialed dispersion up or down, tying release to the fungus's shape-shifting program.
europmc-pmc2855614:
Chacko, Thambi, Kuttan, and Nishigaki reviewed the health effects of green tea in 2010, drawing on one hundred five studies across cell, animal, and human work. Most benefits trace to catechins, a family of plant compounds making up nearly a third of the dry leaf, and above all to one member called EGCG. The review also weighs absorption, interactions with metal ions and drug-handling enzymes, and side effects.

Long-term tea drinking was linked in the evidence to protection against high-fat diet obesity and type two diabetes, plus lower coronary risk. Reported actions span antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, antiviral, and cholesterol-lowering effects. The authors call for trials meeting international standards to pin down doses, mechanisms, and safety.
europmc-pmc2885414:
Sabetta and colleagues followed in 2010 whether blood vitamin D levels predict who catches viral respiratory infections. Vitamin D drops in fall and winter at northern latitudes, matching the cold and flu season, which hints at a link. They measured levels monthly in one hundred ninety-eight healthy adults through the 2009 to 2010 season, with assessors kept blind to the values.

Nearly everyone finished the study. Light skin, lean body mass, and taking supplements each tracked higher vitamin D levels. Adults who maintained levels at or above a fairly high threshold caught about half as many acute respiratory infections as those below it, and they lost fewer days to illness. The difference was stark and statistically strong, though the design cannot prove the vitamin itself deserves the credit.
europmc-pmc3089914:
Kitagawa and colleagues explained in 2011 why centrioles, the tiny barrels that seed hair like cilia and organize cell division, always show nine fold symmetry. Centrioles look like a cartwheel, with nine spokes radiating from a central hub, in nearly all species. The team studied the protein that builds the hub, called SAS-6, and its relative in algae.

The protein forms long paired rods that link head to head into oligomers, and that linking proved essential for building centrioles in both worms and human cells. In the algae protein, nine such rods assemble into a ring with the rods radiating outward, exactly the hub's geometry. Lab made protein built hub like structures on its own. The authors conclude the nine fold pattern is written into this one protein's shape. A universal feature of cells thus traces to a single molecular ruler.
europmc-pmc3123714:
Rozalia Dimitriou and colleagues reviewed how bone regrows and how doctors help it in a 2011 paper in BMC Medicine. Bone rebuilds itself during normal fracture healing and throughout adult life. Some injuries, though, leave gaps too large to bridge, or healing stalls because of infection, poor blood supply, or bone disease.

Current help ranges from grafting the patient's own bone, still the benchmark, to donor bone, growth factors, scaffolds, and stem-like cells. Stretching bone gradually to grow new length is another proven route. Newer work in tissue engineering and gene therapy tries to make substitutes matching real bone, speed healing, or lift repair across the whole skeleton. The review weighs each option's strengths and limits for hard clinical cases.
europmc-pmc3145614:
Rozenn Lemaitre and colleagues searched the genome for controls on healthy fish-type fats in blood in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. These long fats come from food or are built in the body from a shorter plant fat. The consortium pooled genome scans from five population studies of nearly nine thousand people of European ancestry.

Variants near two fat-processing genes shifted levels in a see-saw pattern: carriers held more of the starting plant fat and less of two built fats. A lengthening gene variant raised some products while lowering the longest fat. A sugar-control gene region also turned up unexpectedly. Similar patterns appeared in African, Chinese, and Hispanic samples for the main gene. The work shows blood fat levels are partly written in the genes.
europmc-pmc3203114:
Bryna Erblich and colleagues asked what the colony stimulating factor-1 receptor does in the brain, in this 2011 study in PLoS ONE. The receptor sits on microglia, the brain's resident immune cells. Using a reporter mouse line, the team first checked which brain cells actually carry the receptor.

They found it only on microglia, not on neurons or other support cells. Mice lacking the receptor lost nearly all their microglia. Embryonic brain development looked normal, but after birth the brain's structure went awry. Ventricles enlarged, tissue was squeezed, and neuron and astrocyte numbers rose while oligodendrocytes fell short. The olfactory bulb and cortex were hit hardest. Mutant mice lacking the receptor's signal also performed poorly on food-finding tests of smell.
europmc-pmc3248214:
Michael Haffner and colleagues mapped a DNA mark called 5-hydroxymethylcytosine across mouse and human tissues, in this 2011 paper in Oncotarget. The mark forms when enzymes of the TET family convert the standard methylation mark, and it was known to be plentiful in embryonic stem cells and brain. Its distribution in most other tissues had not been rigorously explored.

Using antibody staining, the team found the mark abundant in most embryonic and adult tissues, with levels tracking how specialized the cells were. Fully mature cells carried the most; the stem and progenitor compartments of tissues carried very little. In cancers of the prostate, breast, and colon, levels were profoundly lower than in healthy tissue. The authors suggest the mark plays a distinct part in cell specialization and is lost on a large scale in cancer.
europmc-pmc3266614:
María López-Barragán and colleagues sequenced directional gene transcripts across the life stages of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum, in this 2011 paper in BMC Genomics. Roughly a quarter of the parasite's predicted genes were known to contain errors, and genes used in the sexual and mosquito stages were the least verified. The team built libraries that preserve which DNA strand a transcript came from.

Comparing eleven libraries from blood stages, sexual stages, and the mosquito-stage ookinete against the reference genome revealed stage-specific antisense transcripts, messages read from the opposite strand, and new splice junctions. More genes appeared one-directional in sexual stages than in blood stages, and alternative splicing proved widespread. Antisense messages in sexual and mosquito stages may help regulate gene activity, and the authors urge future studies to use directional libraries.
europmc-pmc3317714:
Ghanbari, Anwar, Alkharfy, Gilani, and Saari cataloged the useful compounds found across the olive tree, in a 2012 review. Olives first came from lands around the Mediterranean and western Asia, and the tree is now grown worldwide for oil and table fruit. Its fruit carries a rich mix of protective plant chemicals alongside oils, pigments, and natural acids.

Compounds in olives have shown antioxidant, anti inflammatory, germ fighting, and blood pressure lowering effects in studies, among many others. Virgin olive oil is prized for its heart friendly fats plus minor components such as plant sterols and vitamin E relatives. The review also covers leaves and other byproducts, and explains how variety, growing region, harvest timing, and processing change what ends up in the final product.
europmc-pmc3342314:
O'Reilly and colleagues introduced a method that analyzes several traits at once to find gene variants, in a 2012 paper. Genome wide association studies have found hundreds of variants tied to diseases and measurements, yet they almost always test one trait at a time. That habit wastes information when traits overlap or move together, as blood fats do.

Their tool, MultiPhen, flips the usual regression around and asks which blend of traits best matches a given variant. In simulations, the joint approach found far more true signals, including variants affecting several traits or only one. Unlike some rival joint methods, it did not invent false positives on the uneven data of case control studies. On real Finnish birth cohort data, it found about a fifth more known variant links than the standard approach. Its trait blends echoed the formula doctors use to compute cholesterol.
europmc-pmc3373114:
Parashar and co-authors updated the global toll of rotavirus in 2006, the leading cause of severe diarrhea in young children. Their earlier review of studies through 1999 credited the virus with about a fifth of diarrhea hospital stays. Newer hospital studies were finding the virus far more often.

Pooling studies from 2000 to 2004, the share of diarrhea hospitalizations blamed on rotavirus rose to nearly two fifths. Applied to world diarrhea deaths, that share implied roughly six hundred thousand rotavirus deaths a year in young children. Asian surveillance found the virus in close to half of hospitalized cases. The numbers strengthened the case for rotavirus vaccines then nearing use.
europmc-pmc3374614:
Huse and colleagues asked in 2012 what a core human microbiome looks like when bacteria are sorted into fine clusters. They used gene sequences from eighteen body sites in more than two hundred people, gathered for the Human Microbiome Project. A core type was one shared by nearly every person at a site.

Oral sites held the most core types, while vaginal sites held the fewest. The same broad genus could appear at many mouth sites, yet its fine clusters differed sharply by site. Stool samples carried the richest communities, roughly ten times richer than skin or vaginal samples. Even types found in almost everyone swung widely in abundance between people.
europmc-pmc3413714:
Brady and a large mapping team built a consensus map in 2012 of where dengue virus actually spreads, country by country. Dengue is growing in reach and force, yet health agencies disagreed on which nations have it, thanks to patchy diagnosis and reporting. The team scored every available kind of evidence for each country.

Their method weighed evidence quality and agreement, flagging countries whose status stays uncertain. The map counts well over a hundred countries with solid evidence of dengue, including dozens that major agencies had classed as dengue-free. An early upper estimate puts several billion people at risk. The work opens a five-year program to chart dengue risk properly and lists where surveillance must improve.
europmc-pmc3446314:
Segata and colleagues mapped the bacteria of the human digestive tract in 2012 across ten sites, from seven mouth surfaces to tonsils, throat, and stool. Defining health requires knowing the normal community first, and the gut holds the body's densest bacterial population. Samples came from over two hundred healthy adults in the Human Microbiome Project.

The sites sorted into four community types, with tooth plaque standing apart from other mouth surfaces. Three bacterial families appeared everywhere, though their member genera shifted by site. Most metabolic jobs were spread along the whole tract, with local accents such as different sugar transporters in plaque versus stool. The data set a baseline for disease studies.
europmc-pmc3486814: Body awareness got MAIA. This 2012 paper introduces MAIA, a body-awareness questionnaire. The authors reveal the scale. Their work guides research. Mehling's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped mind-body research. The scale is widely used.
europmc-pmc3491314: Opportunistic germs got a virulence review. This 2012 paper reviews how opportunistic germs turn virulent. The authors map the plasticity. Their overview guides medicine. Brown's review is a classic. The paper is widely cited. It shaped infection control. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3627314: Plants got TRY. This 2011 paper introduces TRY, a global plant-trait database. The authors reveal the database. Their work guides ecology. Kattge's team led the work. It is open source. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Ecologists rely on it.
europmc-pmc3646214: Mothers got a care-gap study. This 2013 paper studies gaps in mom-and-child health coverage. The authors reveal the gaps. Their work guides policy. Barros's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped global health.
europmc-pmc3693914: Dopamine got a metabolism maze. This 2013 paper maps the maze of dopamine metabolism. The authors chart the maze. Their review guides neuroscience. Meiser's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped Parkinson's research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3702514: Feet got a magnesium-screw trial. This 2013 trial compares magnesium and titanium foot screws. The authors reveal the tie. Their work guides surgeons. Windhagen's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped foot surgery.
europmc-pmc3712914: Sickle cell got a global-burden model. This 2013 paper models sickle-cell burden in kids. The authors reveal the model. Their work guides policy. Piel's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped newborn screening.
europmc-pmc3816614: Arthritis got a gut-bug bloom study. This 2013 paper links a gut-bug bloom to arthritis. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides rheumatology. Scher's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped arthritis research.
europmc-pmc3834214: Cisplatin got a power-plant-attack study. This 2013 paper finds cisplatin hits cell power plants. The authors reveal the hit. Their work guides oncology. Marullo's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped chemo research.
europmc-pmc3844414: Genomes got Assemblathon 2. This 2013 contest grades genome assembly methods. The authors reveal the winners. Their work guides bioinformatics. Bradnam's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped assembly science. Labs rely on it.
europmc-pmc3853314: Farms got a drug-limits survey. This 2013 paper surveys drug limits on food farms. The authors map the limits. Their review guides policy. Maron's survey is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped food policy. The survey is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3855514: PFOA got a cancer-neighbors study. This 2013 paper studies cancers near a chemical plant. The authors reveal the rates. Their work guides epidemiology. Barry's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped chemical rules.
europmc-pmc3898614: Monocytes got a vessel-cleanup-crew study. This 2013 paper finds monocytes clean vessel walls. The authors reveal the cleanup. Their work guides immunology. Carlin's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped immune science.

europmc-pmc8775814: A fresh look at polycystic ovary syndrome: a thorough review of pathogenesis (how the disease develops), care, and drug repurposing arrived with this 2022 review paper. europmc-pmc8967714: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at GD2-CAR t cell therapy for H3K27M-mutated diffuse midline gliomas. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9068614: Doctors and scientists took on e(3)-equivariant graph neural networks (brain-inspired computer models) for data-efficient and accurate interatomic potentials in this 2022 research paper. europmc-pmc9457814: This 2022 review paper covers prostate cancer review: genetics, diagnosis, treatment options, and alternative ways. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc9794814: A fresh look at active hydrogen boosts electric nitrate reduction to ammonia arrived with this 2022 research paper. Electric nitrate reduction to ammonia is a promising alternative strategy to the traditional haber-bosch process but suffers from a low. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9805914: Pang and co-authors published this research paper in 2023 on aimed at integrin pathways: mechanisms (the inner workings) and advances (new steps forward) in therapy. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc9825514: A 2023 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at uniprot: the universal protein knowledgebase in 2023. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
flinders-voyage-terra-australis-vol1-181:
Matthew Flinders circled Australia in the small sloop Investigator in 1801 to 1803, charting its coasts for the first time. Volume One of A Voyage to Terra Australis appeared in 1814. Flinders proposed the name Australia for the continent, and the name stuck.

He surveys the south coast, the Gulf of Carpentaria, and the reefs of the north, naming capes and bays as he goes. His cat Trim, famous in his own right, sails through the story. The charts were so good that sailors used them for a century. Flinders wrote the account while his health failed from years of captivity.
flinders-voyage-terra-australis-vol2-181:
Volume Two of Flinders's Voyage to Terra Australis completes his Australian survey and tells what hardship followed. On the sail home in 1803 his rotten ship Porpoise wrecked on a reef. Flinders rowed hundreds of miles to fetch rescue for his crew.

Seeking aid, he called at Mauritius, where the French governor held him prisoner for six and a half years. The volume mingles chart work, shipwreck, and captivity, all told plainly. Flinders died the day after his book appeared in 1814. His name now marks bays, islands, and a university across the continent he named. The atlas of charts that completes the set is still praised by sailors.
freud-psychopathology-brill-1914:
Sigmund Freud published The Psychopathology of Everyday Life in German in 1901. The English text here is A. A. Brill's translation of 1914. Freud studies small failures of daily life: forgetting names, misreading, slips of the tongue, and lost objects. Such slips, he argues, are not chance but signs of hidden wishes.

The unconscious, in his account, betrays itself in these small errors. Examples fill the book, many from Freud's own life and patients. The term Freudian slip entered common speech from this work. It is Freud's most readable book for many readers. Its method launched a habit of reading slips as clues.
frost-north-of-boston-1914:
Robert Frost published North of Boston in 1914, a book of dramatic poems set in rural New England. Sixteen pieces tell stories of farm life in the voices of the people themselves. Mending Wall and The Death of the Hired Man are the most famous. Neighbors, hired hands, and couples speak in blank verse close to real talk.

The scenes show loneliness, pride, kindness, and quiet grief. An old hired man comes home to die, and two neighbors rebuild a wall while doubting why. Frost lets each voice make its own case. The book made his name in America. It remains a core work of American poetry.
frus-1861-d114:
Chevalier Hülsemann, the Austrian envoy in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 August 1861. The letter is document 114 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Hülsemann was a veteran of a famous clash with Washington a decade earlier. Austria watched the American war from a cool distance. His August letter brings the voice of the Vienna court into the record, through its careful envoy at the capital. Hülsemann's earlier clash with Washington, in 1850, had made his name known across America. A known name in Washington cut both ways, and Hülsemann wore his with care.
frus-1861-d14:
Norman Judd wrote from Berlin to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 July 1861. The dispatch is document 14 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Three days earlier, Union troops had been beaten at Bull Run in Virginia. News of that scale crossed the ocean slowly, and posts abroad braced for its effect. Judd's late July letter belongs to the uneasy weeks when Europe asked whether the Union could last. Judd's standing with Lincoln gave his reports a weight beyond his post's small size. News from home reached him by the same slow mails he used to answer it.
frus-1861-d214:
In a report dated 10 June 1861, Mr. Dillon wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 214 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The letter comes from the opening months of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d114:
One more voice from abroad reached Washington on 31 July 1862: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London writing to Seward. It was printed as Document 114 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d14:
