In a letter dated 5 February 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 14 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d214: Dated 30 May 1862 and addressed to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, a letter from a Mr. Edwards survives as Document 214 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, filed among the British papers. The record gives no first name or post for Edwards. So the entry rests on its date, its reader, and its place in the legation file.
frus-1862-d314:
Four Seward dispatches to Paris bear the date 24 September 1862, and the first is Document 314 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All four went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

The cluster went out two days after the Emancipation Proclamation was announced, the busiest diplomatic moment of the fall. Washington had much to send: the proclamation itself, the war news, and fresh guidance. This first letter of the set opens a batch that shows the Department working at its highest tempo of the year. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d414:
Horace J. Perry, secretary of the American legation in Madrid, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 December 1861. It is Document 414 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Perry closed the year 1861 in Madrid as the legation's working hand, reporting between ministers. Spain had troops landing in Mexico that month, and Cuba lay close to the seat of war. His year-end report gave Washington a view of Spanish plans and temper at a moment when the Trent affair had just strained ties with Britain. Such reports let Seward judge which European courts might still be kept friendly or at least quiet.
frus-1862-d514:
James Shepherd Pike wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from The Hague on 13 August 1862. His report is Document 514 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress. Its heading keeps the punctuation as it stands in the volume.

Mid-August 1862 found the Union calling for more men and Europe debating whether the war could ever end. Pike's reading of Dutch opinion in that debate was useful precisely because the Netherlands had little at stake but trade. His reports also handled the post's steady small business. The letter is one of the densest month's entries in the Hague file. It shows how much wartime work had accumulated at even the quieter posts. That work had piled up by the war's second summer.
frus-1862-d614:
On 10 February 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Bradford R. Wood, the American minister in Denmark. The instruction is Document 614 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

February's Union victories gave Seward material to send his ministers, and the Danish order carried it to Copenhagen. Denmark watched the war from a trading nation's distance, with its own German question absorbing its court. Wood's task was to keep the American cause correctly understood there and to handle the maritime business that arose between the two states. The dispatch is one of the early-year orders by which Seward set all his northern posts to the same work in the same weeks.
frus-1862-d714:
Five days after Molina's letter reached him, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote back, on 24 September 1862. Molina was Costa Rica's envoy in Washington. The reply is document 714 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Quick answers kept foreign envoys in good humor and their business moving. Seward's reply to Molina is one turn in a brisk exchange that ran through the fall of 1862. The two men's letters dealt with the ties between the United States and Costa Rica. Washington had little thought to spare for small lands, yet it gave some. That courtesy, on paper, is part of the record.
frus-1863p1-d114:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 11 March 1863 to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 114 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The middle sheet of a three-letter day took its own head of the brief, as was Seward's habit all through this file. Adams dealt with the British foreign office week by week, and each sheet armed him for a point. This letter is the second of the 11 March set. With its mates, it shows Washington feeding its envoy in the tight loop the sea mail allowed.
frus-1863p1-d14:
William H. Seward addressed this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 15 December 1862. Adams held the London legation, the post Washington watched most closely. The letter is document 14 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mid-December letters from Washington carried the government's line after a hard autumn of war. Seward had to tell Adams how to meet British feelers about peace talks without giving ground on the Union's cause. This letter is part of that guidance. It shows the secretary at his desk work: short sheets, sent by each steamer, that kept one envoy aimed at one great aim.
frus-1863p1-d214:
One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 17 June 1863. It appears as document 214 of the 1863 papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The CSS Alabama, built near Liverpool, had slipped away in 1862 and was raiding Union trade. Washington pressed London to stop such ships and answer for the losses. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d314:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Gideon Welles, the Secretary of the Navy, on 31 October 1862. The letter is document 314 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Foreign complaints about the Union navy landed on Seward's desk, while the ships themselves answered to Welles. Letters between the two secretaries sorted out which captures to defend, which to explain, and which to regret. Blockade seizures of British vessels were the sorest point between Washington and London. This internal note shows the machinery behind the polished answers sent to the British legation.
frus-1863p1-d414:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 9 March 1863. It stands as document 414 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Read together, these letters trace a slow cooling of the crisis mood of 1861 and 1862. Recognition of the South grew less likely with each month the channel stayed open. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d514:
15 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d614:
William Stuart took up his pen on 17 August 1863 and wrote to William H. Seward. Stuart was Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d114: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on November 10, 1943, and the message is Document 114 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It reached Washington as the president prepared to sail, and it belongs to the last exchange of letters before the leaders met in person. The record names the date and the two men only. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series, closing the long written courtship of Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d14: Crossing with Roosevelt's own note of the same date, Churchill's message to the president of June 28, 1943 is Document 14 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two letters passing each other in a single day was normal for these two leaders in wartime. The catalog record gives no topic for this one. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the papers that carried the alliance from summer argument to autumn agreement.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d214:
Prime Minister Churchill sent President Roosevelt telegram number 503 from London on 12 November 1943. Marked personal and most secret, it answers Roosevelt's message 417 of 10 November. That message had asked for Indian help in building four air bases for long-range bombers bound for the war against Japan.

Churchill's whole reply is one sentence of action. He says he has immediately telegraphed General Auchinleck, the commander in India, to render every possible assistance in the construction of the four bases. The short cable shows the Chengtu bomber plan moving from proposal to orders within two days.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d314:
Admiral William Leahy, the President's chief of staff, sent Roosevelt a memorandum at Cairo on 25 November 1943 on the effect of north Burma operations on cargo delivery to China. It feeds the running dispute between Lord Mountbatten and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek over airlift tonnage.

Stilwell's figures set the minimum monthly tonnage over the Hump. The tonnage must keep the Yunnan Force, the Fourteenth Air Force, and the Chinese-American Composite Wing supplied. It runs from about 8,050 tons in January to 10,000 by June. Mountbatten treats those numbers as targets, not guarantees, since he must use some transport planes for Operation Tarzan in Burma. Chiang demands the full 10,000 tons a month regardless. An optimistic forecast of what the Air Transport Command could actually carry runs alongside.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d414:
Steve Early, the President's secretary, telegraphed Harry Hopkins from Washington on 4 December 1943 about the Moscow radio leak of the Tehran Conference. Sent for Hopkins with the traveling party, the message urges the fastest possible answer in print.

All press and radio here, Early writes, headline reports received through London. The reports say Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin met at Tehran a few days ago. They discussed the war against Germany and political questions. Their conferences have now concluded, and a detailed statement is expected at any moment. The reports come from government-controlled Moscow radio, and they further complicate the mess left by Reuters' premature disclosures about the Cairo Conference. If it can mechanically be done, Early urges the quickest possible release and publication of the Tehran communiqué.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d514:
Howard Bucknell, counselor at the American embassy in London, sent this message to Secretary of State Hull on December 9, 1943. The counselor is an embassy's second officer, handling much of its daily reporting. The State Department printed Bucknell's message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Embassy reports from London in December 1943 brought home British reactions as the Tehran and Cairo decisions became known. Bucknell's channel ran from the heart of the allied capital straight to Hull's desk. For readers, the message shows the routine reporting that kept Washington informed between summits, written by a professional diplomat watching Britain absorb the results of the conferences.
frus-1944-quebec-d114:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued this top-secret memorandum on August 22, 1944, numbered C.C.S. 618/1. Its subject was machinery for coordinating the military efforts of the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union. By late summer 1944, the three armies were closing in on Germany from the west and the east.

The chiefs proposed attaching a Soviet liaison group to Eisenhower's headquarters, and possibly a second one in the Mediterranean. The military missions in Moscow would first sound out the Soviet General Staff. Overall strategy would stay with the national chiefs of staff. The paper, with its draft message, shows the allies building practical links before their forces met on German soil.
frus-1944-quebec-d14:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on July 16, 1944. American and British forces were then breaking out of Normandy while the Red Army destroyed German armies in the east. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Churchill's mid-summer letters carried both triumph and anxiety: the war was being won, and the shape of the peace was being set by armies' positions. He wrote to Roosevelt to keep British views inside every decision. For readers, this message is part of the bridge between the Normandy summer and the Quebec autumn, when the two leaders would meet to divide the work of finishing the war.
frus-1944-quebec-d214:
Hull answered Roosevelt's letter on German cartels on September 11, 1944, and the exchange was released to the press at Quebec two days later. The president had urged steps to eliminate the political activities of German cartels and curb practices restricting trade. Hull agreed the aim followed naturally from America's liberal trade program and its long campaign against monopoly at home.

For more than a year, he reported, an interdepartmental committee had been studying cartel questions at his suggestion. He would now press the Executive Committee on Economic Foreign Policy to expedite its work and be ready with definitive proposals on short notice. Plans for discussions with other United Nations on commercial policy as a whole would follow.
frus-1945-50-intel-d114:
A memorandum by Wright, the director of central intelligence's executive officer, is dated 11 July 1946. Executive officers turn a director's wishes into the staff's orders. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Wright's paper belongs to the CIG's build-out under Vandenberg, when the group was hiring, drafting charters, and claiming missions at speed. An executive's memorandum shows the director's office thinking on paper: priorities listed, tasks assigned, arguments framed. Readers interested in how a small coordinating staff became an agency will find these staff papers essential. The famous letters between chiefs decided the questions; papers like this one made the decisions run.
frus-1945-50-intel-d14:
Executive Order 9621, signed by President Truman on 20 September 1945, is one of the landmark papers in the volume. By it, the Office of Strategic Services ceased to exist. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The order split the OSS in two. Its research and analysis branch went to the State Department. The rest went to the War Department as a leftover unit. With one signature, the wartime spy service Donovan had built was gone, and the fight over its heirs began in earnest. Readers will find nearly every later paper in the volume living in this order's shadow. It is the hinge on which the whole collection turns.
frus-1945-50-intel-d214:
Dated 14 May 1947, this memorandum runs from the National Intelligence Authority to the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter). It is document 214 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d314:
A memorandum dated 13 October 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner). The reader was Joseph A. Frank of the Office of Policy Coordination. The State Department prints it as document 314 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d414:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote to the Army's director of intelligence, Irwin, on 15 February 1950. The memo is document 414 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Army intelligence was older, larger, and proud of its own record. The CIA director had to coordinate it without owning it, a hard task set by law. A direct memo between the two chiefs shows that uneasy partnership at work in the third year of the agency's life. The Army guarded its own secrets hard, so each such memo was a small act of trust.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d114:
A directive from Washington troubled Ambassador Winant so much that he held it back. He wrote to the Secretary of State on 28 January 1945 to explain why. An Economic Directive for Germany sat unpresented in London. Excerpts of his letter are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The directive was sent to him for the European Advisory Commission. Yet it clashes with the State Department's own latest statement on Germany, a statement close to the informal Russian and British positions. Winant is postponing the paper until he can talk with the President. If he tabled it now, he fears Moscow might refuse to confirm either the control machinery agreement or the zones protocol.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d14: Another Churchill message followed on 23 October 1944, one day after his previous letter to Roosevelt. It is document 14 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. Back-to-back letters were normal for Churchill, who ran much of his alliance diplomacy personally, in writing, and expected the president to answer in kind.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d214:
“France” is the plain heading of a briefing book paper prepared for the President's trip and printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary starts from American interest, not French pride. France is to be helped back to strength and sway, in body and in standing alike.

Treat France, the paper argues, by what she can become, not by what she is today. The President has already backed, in principle, the five French claims to equality in German affairs. On the zone, Paris keeps its eyes on the Rhineland. There is every likelihood, the paper warns, that the French will cherish an occupation there so long that it may easily harden into permanence. A French share in the control machinery is part of the same design.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d314:
Montgomery House in Floriana, Malta, hosted a session of the Combined Chiefs of Staff at noon on February 2, 1945. The page preserved here lists who filled the room. General Marshall, Admiral King, and General Kuter led the American side. Field Marshal Brooke, Admiral Cunningham, and Air Marshal Portal headed the British group.

Field Marshal Alexander and Field Marshal Wilson, both fresh from the Mediterranean war, sat in for part of the session. The roster alone tells a story: nearly every senior Allied commander in Europe was in Malta that week. Together they were settling the last joint plans before the party flew on to Yalta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d414:
British drafting offers Persia an early start home for foreign troops in this proposal of February 9, 1945. The draft conclusion cites Article 5 of the Tripartite Treaty of Alliance with Persia, covering withdrawal of Allied forces. Progress against Germany, it says, now lets the three powers act on that promise.

Withdrawal need not await the end of hostilities. It should begin in stages, side by side, as military needs and the Persian supply route allow. The first stage would be the evacuation of Tehran. Military authorities of the three countries would agree the stages in Moscow, and Persia would be kept fully informed. The paper turns occupation into a timetable.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d114:
President Truman authorized the reparations team to attend the Berlin meeting in a telegram to Ambassador Harriman on July 3, 1945. The brief message is document 114 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Edwin Pauley had asked from Moscow that he, Dr. Isador Lubin, and four assistants be allowed to come and report to the President.

Truman's answer is two short lines. Pauley, Lubin, and the four assistants are authorized to report to him on the proposed reparations plan during the coming meeting, and the Army has been notified. The approval put the American reparations experts on the Potsdam roster, where the size of Germany's bill would be one of the hardest questions the three leaders had to settle.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d14:
Truman welcomed Bidault to the White House on May 18, 1945, in Grew's memorandum of the meeting. Grew met the French Foreign Minister and the French Ambassador at 12:15 and presented Bidault to the President; Admiral Leahy was also present. Truman said he desired to strengthen the friendship between the United States and France, which had commenced with the founding of the American nation.

He thanked Bidault for his cooperation and helpfulness at San Francisco, and for the French delegation's contribution to the conference's work. Bidault expressed pleasure at the President's remarks. The extract preserves the courtesy — the plea for de Gaulle, which fills the next document in the file, came after.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d214:
Truman's action brief for the conference was put together on July 12, 1945. The five-part paper is document 214 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. An editor's note explains that Truman, Byrnes, and Leahy shaped it up aboard ship, and that Truman used it as his action paper at the first plenary meeting on July 17.

The brief opens with the six topics of the President's agenda letter, starting with machinery for the peace settlements. Its second part drafts the proposed Council of Foreign Ministers. The third sets out policy toward Germany and proposes that the Control Council start work at once, under an attached draft of political and economic principles for Germany's first control period. The papers printed in full later in the volume show the exact proposals Truman laid before Stalin and Churchill.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d314:
Washington answered Schoenfeld on July 13, 1945, with the American position on Hungary's coming elections. The Department agreed that the three allied governments should act together under the Crimea Declaration. Their shared aim was to secure for Hungarians the right to build democratic institutions of their own choice.

Joint action might be needed around the elections, Grew wrote. But Washington would not press for allied supervision of the vote unless Hungarian authorities plainly meant to deny voters a free choice. The question, he added, stood on the American agenda for the Potsdam meeting of heads of government.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d414: An editor's note stands in place of a document at No. 414 of this volume. It records what the President's briefing book held on the European Advisory Commission. The book included the Commission's report, agreed upon but not signed on July 4, 1945. With it came a draft agreement on added requirements to be imposed on Germany. The note points readers to the signed texts, printed in the volume's second part. Those texts, signed on July 25, vary from the drafts in minor ways only.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d514:
Poland's western boundary is weighed in an extract from the Joint Strategic Survey Committee's memorandum on dismemberment of Germany. Since Poland's political orientation, toward the eastern or the western European powers, cannot be foreseen, the committee is reluctant to recommend extending Poland's western boundary to the Oder River. That reluctance, it admits, has limits.

From the military point of view, it would appear impracticable to offer serious objections to the transfer, if the Soviet Union insists upon it. The bargaining possibilities of the issue, the committee adds, should be recognized. The memorandum was prepared, at Admiral Leahy's request, to help the President prepare for the Berlin conference, though the Joint Chiefs had not approved its views.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d614:
Britain's chiefs of staff pushed back on the U.S. line about sharing war facts with Russia on July 15, 1945. Their top secret memo, written at Babelsberg, is document 614 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It answers the U.S. memo printed as document 611.

The British say they cannot agree that the matter is unfit for joint agreement. All through the war against Germany, they note, the two staffs made a habit of consulting on dealings with the Russians. That habit, they argue, has been wise and profitable, and Moscow never resented it. If the two staffs now split, each telling Moscow its own tale, the Russians may play one off against the other. The memo is a plea to keep the wartime partnership tight in the war's last weeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1014:
Britain's delegation submitted this secret memorandum on disposal of the German fleet and merchant ships at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. It builds on the plenary talks of July 19, which had taken up the Soviet memorandum. Surface ships, London recalls, were to be shared equally among the three powers.

The British now suggest weighing a share for France, a full member of the Control Council. An expert commission should list every surface ship and propose the split. Most U-boats would be destroyed, with a token number kept for research. London accepts the Soviet claim to a share of naval stores in principle, but wants an inventory first, since the Germans scattered them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1114:
Samuel Reber, special aide to the Director of European Affairs, wrote this internal note to his chief, H. Freeman Matthews, on 20 July 1945. The European Affairs office owned the Germany problem day to day in the State Department. Reber's note is staff work from inside that office.

Notes at this level carried facts, judgment, and advice up the chain. They were the layer where expert knowledge first took shape as policy. Potsdam is remembered for three famous men at one table. Papers like this one show the trained staff beneath them, doing the reading and the drafting that made the leaders' choices possible.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1214:
Hurley in China addressed this message to the President and the Secretary of State on 20 July 1945. A dispatch aimed at the very top marks the weight its writer gave it. Hurley's post stood at the center of the China tangle, where war with Japan mixed with a looming civil clash.

American policy sought to hold China together as an ally and a future great power. Hurley reported on that effort to the two men who owned the policy. This message carried his word to the summit level. It shows how far the Potsdam web reached: a cable from China landing on the president's desk in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1314:
Prime Minister Attlee wrote to President Truman on 1 August 1945, the summit's last full day. Attlee had led the British team for less than a week. His note to the president belongs to the closing business of the conference.

By then Britain's new government had taken the talks' reins in full. The final protocol was being readied for signing, and the leaders' own channels carried the last courtesies and confirmations. This message is Attlee's word in that closing set. It shows the new prime minister ending the summit as a partner in his own right, no longer in Churchill's shadow.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1414:
A memorandum of conversation dated 23 August 1945 records a talk held after the Potsdam Conference and after the war's end. Such memoranda were written by an officer who sat in, to fix what was said. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Memoranda of conversation are the nearest thing to transcripts that diplomacy keeps. They note who met, what each side said, and what was left open. Readers prize them because spoken words, unlike cables, can be denied later unless a paper like this one pins them down. Placed near the volume's end, this record shows the conference's business still being talked through weeks after the leaders went home.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-114:
On July 25, 1945, Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote again to Ambassador John Winant in London. The letter is the second from Byrnes to Winant in this run of Potsdam papers. Winant, though absent from the conference, held a post central to Anglo-American work. The exchange was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Repeated letters show a working channel, not a one-off courtesy. Byrnes kept London informed as the talks shifted day by day. Readers see the conference's outer circle: men who had to act on its results without sitting at its table. The letter widens the story beyond the three leaders.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-14:
No official record survives of a private lunch between Truman and Churchill on July 18, 1945. The pair lunched at Churchill's quarters, 23 Ringstrasse in Babelsberg, then walked to Eden's quarters. An editorial note in volume two marks the gap.

In place of minutes, the editors quote Churchill's own account from his war memoirs. Churchill says he spoke of Britain's melancholy position that day. Britain had spent more than half her foreign investments for the common cause while fighting alone. She now faced an external debt of three thousand million pounds, run up buying supplies abroad. Truman, Churchill writes, followed with sympathy and attention. The United States, Truman declared, owed Britain an immense debt for having held the fort at the beginning.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d714:
On July 22, 1945, the foreign ministers of the three powers approved the text kept as document 714. Ministers did the daily grinding at Potsdam. They cleared what they could and sent the rest to the leaders. The approved text joined the agreed papers in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Minister-level approval shows the conference's middle gear at work. Byrnes, Molotov, and Eden could settle much without the heads of government. Readers see the range of business closed at that level. The document also reveals pace: by July 22 the machine was producing results. Those results fed the protocol adopted at the close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d814:
Melbourne reported from Rumania on July 24, 1945, in document 814. The acting representative wrote to the Acting Secretary of State at Potsdam's midpoint. His letters give the volume a steady Rumanian pulse. This one joined the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

A midpoint report from Bucharest shows a mission holding its course. Melbourne reported through frustration without losing clarity. Readers can measure the gap between the summit's hopes and the commission's reality. The document shows why the Balkan files resisted settlement. On the ground, the facts were already moving against the West's designs.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d914: Edwin Pauley cabled Charles Kindleberger in Washington on July 23, 1945, asking for figures on East Prussia. Kindleberger was the liaison officer for the reparations delegation. Pauley wants estimates for East Prussia as a whole, and for the part north of a line through Goldap and Braunsberg, near Königsberg. For each area he asks the value of factory and farm resources. He also asks the yearly value of industrial output and of farm output, so far as the data can be found.
frus-1952-54v10-d114: A 1952-1954 FRUS editorial note on the Anglo-Iranian oil dispute. Britain and America maneuvered over Iran's oil. This note provides that context. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
frus-1961-63v10-12msupp-d714: A 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the microfiche supplement. The extra records. This document holds that memo. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
frus-1961-63v10-d114: A 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the President's special assistant on Cuba. The White House watched Havana. This entry preserves that memo. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
galileo-two-new-sciences-crew-1914:
Galileo Galilei's Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences appeared in English in 1914, translated by Henry Crew and Alfonso de Salvio. Galileo wrote the Two New Sciences at the end of his life, under house arrest after his trial. It was his final masterpiece, printed in Holland in 1638.

Two sciences anchor the book: the strength of materials and the motion of bodies. Galileo set out the laws of falling bodies and of projectiles, the base of modern mechanics. The form is a dialogue among three speakers across four days. This translation made the founding text of modern physics widely readable in English, notes and all, for students of science.
gao-gaoreports-b-296741-14: Olympus Building Services took its April 2007 contract fight to GAO — the fourteenth and fifteenth rounds of a long docket — and the combined ruling settles both claims. The firm challenged the awards; the call weighs each claim with care. Marathon dockets still get careful answers.
gao-gaoreports-b-299014: L-3 Communications doubled its January 2007 protest — two case numbers, one defense fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-310814: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Accumark, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-514: New York's 9/11 crisis counseling grants got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines FEMA grants after the attacks. The findings take the measure. The report shows the grieving city's aid was studied. The grants had to be understood. The grieving city's aid was studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-614: Base closures past and present got a GAO once-over in 2005, and the report observes on prior and current BRAC rounds. The review reads the closures' report card. The towns and the troops both felt the verdicts. The rounds were studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-114: Federal STEM programs got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines science, technology, engineering, and math programs and trends. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the future scientists deserved strong programs. The programs had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-14: D.C.'s tuition grant program needed better management in 2005, and GAO's report says financial and program improvements were required. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the students' grants deserved sound handling. The improvements had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-214: Federal workplace fairness needed better teamwork in 2006, and GAO's report says improved coordination was required between the EEOC and OPM. The findings demand the partnership. The report warns that the discrimination fighters should fight together. The coordination had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-314: Indian irrigation projects needed fixing in 2006, and GAO's report says numerous issues had to be addressed for better management. The findings target the problems. The report warns that the tribal water projects deserved sound handling. The issues had to be addressed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-414: Welfare block grant spending needed better tracking in 2006, and GAO's report says better information was required to understand states' TANF uses. The findings demand the data. The report warns that the safety-net dollars deserved daylight. The information had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-514: Consumer-directed health plans were small but growing in 2006, and GAO's report says enrollment was fueled by rising coverage costs. The findings track the trend. The report warns that the do-it-yourself health funds needed watching. The growth had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-914: Privatizing base utilities needed watching in 2006, and GAO's report says actions had improved management, though concerns remained. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the sold-off pipes and wires needed oversight. The privatization had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1014: The tax gap had a freelance problem in 2007 — GAO's report says any plan to close it had to tackle sole proprietors skipping out. The findings put the self-employed at the center of the missing billions. The report's logic is simple: chase the biggest leak first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-114: The SBA's disaster readiness was lacking in 2007, and GAO's report says more steps were needed to prepare for future catastrophes. The findings press for action. The report warns that the small-business lifeline should not snap in the next storm.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-14: UN reform was crawling in 2007, and GAO's report says management changes were progressing slowly, with many awaiting assembly review. The findings document the drift. The report warns that the world body could not reform at a diplomat's pace. The changes had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-214: The Medicaid money-watch was sound but soft in 2007 — GAO's report says the federal oversight push fit the payment principles yet needed more teeth. The findings bless the direction taken. The report's nudge: good principles need sharp enforcement behind them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-314: Law school accreditation got a GAO look in 2007, and the report examines the issues around who blessed the nation's lawyers-in-training. The findings probe the process. The report asks whether the gatekeepers of the bar were guarding quality or turf.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-614: The VA's benefits computer was finally being replaced in 2007 — GAO's report says the long payment-system overhaul had progressed, with challenges left. The findings credit the momentum. The report's caution: the finish line for giant IT projects is always farther than it looks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-714: Small firms were missing the tech boat in 2007 — GAO's report maps the federal programs meant to float them on science funding. The findings inventory the interagency effort. The report asks whether the innovation ladder had rungs for the little guy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-814: War-worn trucks and guns needed fixing in 2007, but GAO doubted the Army and Marines' repair math. Their reset plans, the report says, could not promise gear would be ready while the fighting went on. The findings dig into the unglamorous logistics of keeping two wars supplied with working hardware.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-914: The government's books were a mess in 2007 — GAO's report says ancient, creaky money systems posed a first-class challenge. The findings describe financial plumbing held together with habit and hope. For the world's biggest enterprise, the report argues, the ledger should not be the weakest link.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-14: The Government Accountability Office dug into energy Markets: Increasing Globalization of Petroleum Products Markets, Tightening Refining Demand and Supply Balance, and Other Trends Have Implications for U in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-314: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at supplemental Appropriations: Opportunities Exist to Increase Transparency and Provide Additional Controls. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-414: GAO published its findings on 2010 Census: Bureau Needs to Specify How It Will Assess Coverage Follow-up Techniques and When It Will Produce Coverage Measurement Results in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-614: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at medicaid: CMS Needs More Information on the Billions of Dollars Spent on Supplemental Payments. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-814: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at elections: Federal Program for Certifying Voting Systems Needs to Be Further Defined, Fully Implemented, and Expanded. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-05-1914:
Volume 5 of Frazer's Golden Bough, third edition, appeared in 1914, as Adonis, Attis, Osiris, Part 1. James George Frazer turned to the great dying gods of the eastern Mediterranean. Adonis, Attis, and Osiris were mourned and celebrated in rites tied to the seasons.

Frazer described the festivals of Adonis in Syria and Greece, where women mourned the young god each year. He linked the rites to the death and return of plant life in a hot, dry land. Gardens of Adonis, grown fast and left to wither, pictured that cycle in miniature. Part 1 opens a long comparison that Part 2 completes, and it shows Frazer's rite-and-season theory at its clearest.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-06-1914:
Volume 6 of the third edition of The Golden Bough appeared in 1914, completing Adonis, Attis, Osiris. James George Frazer had begun the pair of volumes with the rites of Adonis. Part 2 moves to Attis in Phrygia and Osiris in Egypt, the most famous dying god of all.

Frazer told the Osiris story in full: murder, search, and revival, with the Nile flood and grain harvest woven through it. He argued that Egypt's rites acted out the yearly death and return of crops. The detail on Egyptian sources is among the richest in the whole work. Readers get the ancient evidence and Frazer's bold pattern laid over it.
goldman-social-significance-drama-1914:
Emma Goldman lectured on modern plays in The Social Significance of the Modern Drama, printed in 1914. Ibsen, Shaw, and Strindberg stand among her main subjects. Goldman, the famed anarchist speaker, treated drama as a vehicle for radical ideas. A play, in her hands, becomes an argument about society.

She reads each dramatist for the social charge inside the art. Marriage, property, church, and state all face the stage's criticism. Her talks turn art criticism into social theory without losing the plays themselves. The book preserves her platform voice, direct and urgent. It shows how anarchists of her day used culture. Modern readers gain a period lens on famous plays.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Fourteen volumes in, Carlyle's Frederick the Great rolls on: Voltaire at Sans Souci, the famous friendship and the famous quarrel. Philosophy, flattery, and fireworks between the two great egos. The most entertaining section of the whole vast work, sparkling with anecdote.
hobson-work-wealth-1914:
Work and Wealth, from 1914, carries Hobson's economics into a human valuation of wealth. The subtitle states his standard: wealth should be judged by human well being. Standard measures count output and profit, whatever they cost in health or joy. Hobson demands a better accounting.

He weighs the human costs of industry against its goods, item by item. Drudgery, strain, and stunted lives enter the ledger beside wages and products. His underconsumptionist view supports the reform side of the argument. The book is a work of welfare economics before the field had that name. It asks what an economy is for. That question gives the book its lasting pull.
hodgson-men-of-the-deep-waters-1914:
Short sea tales fill Men of the Deep Waters, William Hope Hodgson's set from 1914. Sailors meet ghost ships, sea beasts, and storms that test nerve and skill. Some tales scare. Some praise grit and plain hard work at sea.

The set stands as a mate to his long sea novels. Hodgson drew on his own years as a sailor for each scene. Salt, wind, and fear of deep water run through all the tales. Fans of sea horror will find rich stores here. Storm, wreck, and shark tales sit by the ghost tales here. The mix shows Hodgson could thrill with plain fact as well as with dread lore.
hunter-civic-biology-1914: A Civic Biology, Hunter's 1914 textbook. The Scopes trial text. This book preserves that book. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
ignatius-spiritual-exercises-1914: The Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius, adapted for an eight-day retreat in this 1914 edition. The Jesuit founder's program of prayer and discernment. This book preserves that influential method. The file is now open to the public.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-14:
After the sickness years, grim resolve marks Volume 14, from 1898. Thwaites spans Huron country and Quebec in the wake of great loss. The mission staggers under grief, yet it does not fall apart.

Priests bury their converts, then baptize new ones among those who live. Letters home weigh what was lost against what faith still demands. Food runs short, help runs late, and fear lingers in the towns. Faith here is tested by disaster and hardens rather than breaks. The volume's quiet grit gives the whole series much of its power. Endurance, more than triumph, is its theme.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luria-10114:
Luria is the name of a far-flung family treated in a group entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The article, written by six contributors, describes the family as wide in its branches. Several members were known for mystical leanings and for deep rabbinic learning. The entry then profiles individual Lurias one by one.

The hosted text opens with Abraham ben Nissan Luria, a Russian rabbi and grammarian. His 1821 work studied the grammar found in Rashi's Bible commentary and in older Mishnah commentaries. Next comes David ben Aaron Luria, a Russian educator born in Minsk about 1800. He took over the city's Talmud Torah in 1843 and rebuilt it as a modern school. His success won support from former opponents and even from the government. When officials closed his schools, he retired to his books. The entry shows how one family produced both scholars and reformers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyons-israel-10:
Israel Lyons the younger, an English astronomer and botanist, is the subject of a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Cambridge in 1739, he was the son of the Hebrew teacher Israel Lyons. He showed a gift for study, above all mathematics, from his earliest youth. He began studying botany in 1755 and kept at it all his life. He died in London in 1775.

The article lists work done at a remarkable pace. At nineteen he published a treatise on fluxions, an early form of calculus. A catalogue of plants around Cambridge followed in 1763. Sir Joseph Banks, once his pupil, invited him to lecture at Oxford. In 1773 Lyons sailed with Captain Phipps on a voyage toward the north pole. He died about a year after his return, while editing papers of Edmund Halley. The entry preserves a short, bright scientific career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mako-10314:
Mako, a town in Hungary's Csanad county, is given a community entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Of its 33,722 people, 1,642 were Jews in 1900. Jews began settling there around the middle of the eighteenth century. The Bishop of Csanad, Stanislavich, protected them and assigned them a special quarter in 1740.

The article traces the community's growth and leaders. A burial society existed by 1747. The first rabbi, Judah ben Abraham ha-Levi, served from 1778 to 1824. Salomon Ullman followed, writing a commentary printed at Vienna in 1854. Anton Enoch Fischer then introduced German, and later Hungarian, into his sermons. The town kept a Jewish school founded in 1851, a women's association, and a students' aid society. One teacher, Marcus Steinhardt, had served the school for forty years. The entry portrays a protected settlement grown into a full communal life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayer-elkan-105:
Elkan Mayer was a German army physician of the eighteenth century. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. He was born in Frankfort-on-the-Main, where his father practiced medicine, and he took his degree at a German university. The entry survives because his career ran into a wall of law. In 1753 the council of Frankfort refused his petition for permission to practice in his own city.

Seven years later an imperial infantry regiment appointed him its military physician. His commander praised him warmly. The contrast between the welcome of the army and the refusal of the city fed a long public argument. The council of Frankfort and the Jewish congregation argued for years over whether Jews had any right to practice medicine at all. For its evidence the entry points to the history of Jewish physicians by Landau, published in 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-memorial-dates-:
Memorial Dates are the days Jewish communities chose to remember. Joseph Jacobs and I. George Dobsevage survey them in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Birthdays, the article notes, went almost wholly unrecorded. Death-days were noted only rarely. Cases include the fast of Gedaliah on the third of Tishri, and the pilgrimage to Simon ben Yohai's tomb on Lag be-Omer. Eastern European Jews paid Jahrzeit visits to the graves of great rabbis, seeking their intercession.

Most of the entry is a working calendar of fasts and feasts rooted in history. The Ninth of Ab marks the Temple's two destructions. Hanukkah marks the Maccabean rededication. The Rhineland fasts mark the Crusade martyrs. The Polish fast of the twentieth of Siwan marks the Cossack massacres of 1648. Local Purims run from Crete to Frankfort. Then, following Zunz, it prints a month-by-month list of notable dates for almanacs and the press.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-j:
Meshullam ben Joel ha-Kohen was a Galician Talmudist. He died at Lemberg on September 25, 1809. Gotthard Deutsch and A. Peiginsky profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His career was a progress through Galician pulpits. He was first rabbi at Zurawno, then called to Koretz to succeed his brother Isaac. Then came Bolechow, and at last Lemberg. His standing among contemporaries is measured by their requests for his responsa. One responsum was printed in his ancestor Naphtali ha-Kohen's "Sha'ar ha-Hakanah." Another appeared in the Vilna Gaon's "Shenot Eliyahu."

His own book is the "Pithe Niddah," comments on the laws of Niddah. It was printed at Lemberg in 1802. It also carries a specimen of his Pentateuch work, "Likkute Yom." A further responsum survives in his brother Isaac's "Zikron Kehunnah." So the entry maps a family of rabbinic authors. The family spans two generations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mogador-or-suer:
Mogador, the Moroccan Atlantic seaport founded in 1759 by Sidi Mohammed ibn Abdallah, had ten thousand Jews in a population of nineteen thousand, as Gotthard Deutsch and M. Knafo report in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town was built in three parts: the Ḳaṣbah of officials and merchants, the Moorish Medinah, and the Mellah, the Jewish quarter behind two fortified gates.

The entry stresses that Mogador's Jews fared better than most in the empire, favored by the Sherifian sultans and encouraged in commerce. The dark exception was Muley Yazid, who tortured ten Jews for ten days in a dry cistern to force conversion; some died before his own death freed the rest. In 1807 the governor founded the present Mellah expressly for the Jews' security.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morgenland-alte:
Morgenland, Altes und Neues, the Orient, old and new, was a monthly magazine published at Basel. Samuel Preiswerk edited it. It gets a four-line entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It ran for six years, from 1838 to 1844. Its contents were exclusively exegetical, the study of Scripture verse by verse.

The periodical was designed, its prospectus said, for the friends of Holy Writ. That meant a Christian readership for biblical study. It was the age when the Orient meant the Bible's lands. The entry is among the shortest in this stretch of the encyclopedia. It rests on no cited bibliography. A title, an editor, a city, and six years are most of what survives of the venture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munajja-abu-al-:
Abu al-Faraj ibn Sadakah Munajja, called Ibn al-Sha'ir, was a Samaritan writer of the twelfth century, probably at Damascus. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His father was a renowned poet, which explains the son's byname, son of the poet. Munajja wrote commentaries on the Pentateuch.

Samaritan writers cite those commentaries as standard works. He also wrote a polemic against Karaites and Rabbanites, aimed above all at Saadia Gaon. Only its second part survives, in twenty-three chapters on commandments where Samaritans and Rabbinites differ. There he charges that the rabbis' readings fight the Law, while his ancestors' readings upheld it. His son Sadakah became physician to a sultan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-herz-b: Naphtali Herz ben Zebi Hirsch Halberstadt was an eighteenth-century rabbi at Dubno in Russia. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer give him a brief Jewish Encyclopedia notice. His name survives through responsa on the famous Cleve divorce case, printed in Israel Lipschütz's Or Israel in 1770. Two brothers were also rabbis, Solomon at Glogau and Simhah at Dessau.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nega-im-plagues:
Nega'im is the treatise on plagues and leprosy. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It belongs to the order Tohorot, on cleanness. Its rules rest on Leviticus chapters thirteen and fourteen. Most editions place it fourth in that order. Fourteen chapters hold one hundred fifteen paragraphs.

Priests inspect spots, but never on their own bodies. Signs show whether a spot is clean or unclean. Whole-body spread can, strangely, count as clean. Boils, burns, and scall of head and beard follow. Garments can carry the plague, and so can houses. One proverb warns, woe to the wicked's neighbors. The last chapter gives the leper's cleansing rite. Birds, shaving, and an offering complete that rite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neymarck-alfred:
Alfred Neymarck was a French writer on money matters. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Châlons-sur-Marne on Jan. 3, 1848. In 1868 he edited the Revue Contemporaine. In 1869 he founded Le Rentier, a financial paper.

He still managed Le Rentier in the year 1904. Paris's Statistical Society crowned him laureate in 1889. He was first to win its Prix Bourdin as well. The Academy gave him the Prix Wolowski in 1891. Honors followed: Academy officer, then Legion of Honor officer. His books treat Colbert and Turgot in two volumes each. A manual of political economy appeared in 1898. He sits on the Jewish Consistory of Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novy-dvor-11614:
Novy-Dvor is a village in the Grodno district. Herman Rosenthal and George D. Rosenthal wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jews formed a settled community in the 1500s. Some of them owned farms around the village. Records also show friction with the local priests.

The quarrels turned on the oath Jews must swear. In 1540 the Jew Khatzka appealed one ruling. The priest Clement wanted the solemn synagogue oath. Khatzka held the common oath fitted his case. His son Simon read the Russian documents aloud. Queen Bona received the case beyond local courts. A census of 1558 shows Jewish property there. Three streets held their houses and garden land. In 1897 Jews numbered 500 of 1,282 souls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottolenghi-dona:
Donato Ottolenghi was an Italian author from Acqui. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Acqui on November 7, 1820. He died at Alessandria on October 5, 1883. He had lived at Alessandria since the year 1848.

Donato was a keen lover of his land of Italy. He wrote by mail to great men of his age. He was a rich man with a large store of wealth. He gave all his strength to lift the poor of Alessandria. He made his plans known through the daily press. He made them known through his own books as well. His works treat the cause of the poor at length. One puts forth a plan for a chief board of aid. One treats want and aid in Alessandria as a whole.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parma-11914:
Parma is an Italian city, once chief of a duchy. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It held a Jewish group from a very old date. When the plague swept Italy in 1348, Jews died there. The mob blamed them for the spread of that plague.

In the next age, famed Jewish doctors lived at Parma. One was Elijah, a doctor to the Duke of Parma. He had taught in the schools of Pavia in past years. One was Giacobbe, who may have cured a great duke. One was Abramo of Prato, named in the year 1480. In 1449 the town gave itself up to Francesco Sforza. One term of that pact kept Jewish rights in full force. Jews who came new to the town were to gain those rights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pe-ot-plural-fo:
Pe'ot are the side-locks worn by many Jewish men. The word is the plural of pe'ah, meaning side or border. Cyrus Adler and S. Mannheimer wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The custom rests on a verse in Leviticus.

That verse bars rounding off the corners of the head. Strict Jews let the hair fall in curls at both sides. Some rabbis barred the razor but allowed scissors. In 1845 Czar Nicholas the First banned the locks by decree. Force was used, yet the custom survived in eastern Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-phinea:
Phineas Phillips was a Polish merchant of Krotoschin. He led its Jewish community about the year 1775. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The ruling prince esteemed him highly there. His town was a fief of Thurn and Taxis.

The prince trusted Phillips with personal errands of state. Phillips traded at the great Leipzig fairs each year. In 1775 he extended his travels to England. He settled in London and dealt in indigo and gum. His son Samuel stayed on in London. Samuel's line produced two lord mayors of the city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plungian-12214:
Plungian was an old town in Russia's Kovno government. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its people were mostly Jewish in the 1800s. In 1897 the town counted 3,583 inhabitants. Learned rabbis served its pulpit for centuries.

Jehiel Heller was its best known rabbi of the century. He died in post there in 1861. Zechariah Plungian wrote a book of ethics and folk cures. Its many editions spread far beyond the town. Mordecai Plungian, born there in 1814, became a famed Maskil. The town court's record book survives in New York.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pseudepigrapha-:
Pseudepigrapha means books that bear false names of authors. Crawford Howell Toy and George F. Moore wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The names are put on by fraud or by plain error. Greek writers knew the trick well. One of them speaks of false speeches laid on Demosthenes.

Such speeches were rolled into sets of that great speaker's works. They were not his, for all that. A bishop of Antioch makes the same point on a gospel. Serapion, who held that see about the year 200, treats the Gospel of Peter with care. The article lists such books and asks who truly made them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinowitz-elij:
Elijah David Rabinowitz was a Russian rabbi of the Kovno land. Joseph Jacobs and Benzion Eisenstadt wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Pikeln in 1845. His father was rabbi of three towns in turn. The boy learned Talmud and rabbinics at his father's side. By fifteen he knew a great deal of both.

In 1873 Poneviezh called Rabinowitz to its rabbinate. He served that town for a full twenty years. He was then named rabbi of Mir in his place. The entry traces a life spent in two pulpits. It shows the slow rise of a Talmud boy to fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romano-leone-ju:
Leone Romano was an Italian scholar born at Rome in 1292. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Rome after 1350. His full name is Judah b. Moses Romano.

The article calls him a gifted thinker and fine Latinist. He knew scholastic philosophy well. With Benjamin b. Judah he centered Roman Jewish learning. His cousin Immanuel became his devoted pupil despite being older. Romano translated major medieval philosophy into Hebrew. By 1328 he had finished the Liber de Causis. He rendered Aquinas, Averroes, and Albertus Magnus as well. He compiled a Hebrew Italian glossary of philosophy terms. King Robert of Naples studied under him at court. The entry shows Latin learning opened to Hebrew readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rouen-hebrew-an:
Rouen is the ancient capital of Normandy, set on the right bank of the Seine. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews likely settled there as early as the Roman period.

The first record tells of a harsh persecution early in the eleventh century. King Robert the Pious sought to force baptism on all Jews on his lands. Many were killed or took their own lives rather than convert. Jacob ben Jekuthiel won the pope's help to stop the attacks. In 1066 many Rouen Jews followed William the Conqueror to England.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salaman-charles:
Charles Malcolm Salaman was an English journalist and dramatist born in London on September 6, 1855. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a son of the composer Charles Kensington Salaman.

Salaman wrote verses for many of his father's best known songs. He also supplied words for music by Macfarren and by Osborne. His own plays include the farcical comedy Deceivers Ever, staged in 1883. Dimity's Dilemma played the Gaiety, and A Modern Eve the Haymarket. He edited Pinero's published plays and wrote Woman, Through a Man's Eye-glass.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jose: Samuel ben Jose ben Bun, or Abun, was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In his time, it is said, the Jerusalem Talmud was arranged and completed by his father, Jose. A few of Samuel's own sayings survive in that Talmud, in Rosh ha-Shanah, Berakot, Sotah, and Kiddushin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sason-jacob-ben:
M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Jacob ben Israel Sason, a Palestinian Talmudist. He flourished at Safed at the end of the seventeenth century. Sason studied under Isaac Alfandari. Safed was still a famed center of Jewish learning. His career was cut short by an early death.

Sason wrote Bene Ya'aḳob, printed at Constantinople in 1714. The book comments on part of Isaac ben Abba Mari's Sefer ha-'Iṭṭur. It also holds fourteen responsa and new readings. Those treat Maimonides' code and Jacob ben Asher's four Ṭurim. Death stopped the work before it was done. Sason was only thirty-one years old. The entry draws on Azulai, Conforte, and the standard catalogs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schreiber-simon:
Bernhard Friedberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Simon Schreiber, an Austrian rabbi. He was born at Presburg, in Hungary, in 1821. He died at Cracow on March 25, 1883. Simon was a son of Moses Schreiber, the famed Moses Sofer. In 1842 he became rabbi of Mattersdorf.

In 1857 Schreiber declined a call from the congregation of Papa. In 1860 he accepted Cracow's invitation instead. He became the top leader of Galicia's Orthodox Jews. His word carried weight in worldly matters as well as religion. His shrewdness won him a seat in the Austrian Parliament in 1879. In 1880 he founded the Hebrew weekly Maḥaziḳe ha-Dat. It is still published at Lemberg in 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semites-origina:
Semites, first called Shemites, names the peoples listed in Genesis as descendants of Shem. Emil G. Hirsch and George A. Barton wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the term. Genesis names Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram among those descendants. The entry tests that old list against history and language.

Elam, for one, was old and warlike, yet its language was not Semitic. The authors suggest it entered the list through Semitic settlers there. They also weigh rival views on the hard name Arphaxad. Readers get an early scholarly attempt to match a biblical family tree with real peoples of the ancient Near East.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shulamite-r-v-s:
Shulamite is the name given to the heroine of the Song of Songs. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on her. The name appears only once in the whole poem. That single mention comes near the Song's end.

Some modern critics read her as a shepherd's bride. Solomon's desire for her drives their reading of the poem. She resists his bid to place her in his harem. Her name likely means a native of Shulem. Eusebius matched Shulem with the town of Shunem. The Greek version supports that link, the entry argues. Some critics then identify her with Abishag of Shunem. Abishag had served David and figured at his court. The entry weighs a one-word name against a full love story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-samu:
Simeon ben Samuel was a philosopher and cabalist of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was of French or German birth, they report. His book Adam Sikli is also called Hadrat Kodesh.

Written in 1400, the work treats the Ten Commandments at length. It covers God's thirteen attributes and the thirteen articles of faith. A commentary called Gillayon accompanies the main text. A cabalistic meditation in prayer form follows it. Its title's letter values carry mystic meaning, he explained. Later scholars printed extracts of the work abroad. Hottinger used it in a grammar of four languages. Wolf added a Latin translation to the extracts. The entry preserves a late medieval blend of faith and mysticism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-snail-13814:
Snail is the English rendering for the Hebrew word shabbelul. Emil G Hirsch and I M Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The word occurs only once, in Psalm fifty-eight. The Targum and Talmud agree with that rendering. The Septuagint and Vulgate give wax instead.

The psalm speaks of the snail melting away as it goes. That image may come from its trail of slime. It may also come from its retreat into cracks and crevices. Many mollusks live in Syria and Palestine, the entry notes. The shabbelul was used as a cure for boils. Other Talmudic notes deal with the snail's egg and shell.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-soncino-13914:
Soncino was an Italian family of Hebrew printers of great fame. M Seligsohn and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The family took its name from the town of Soncino. It traced its line back to a Moses of Speyer. Israel Nathan ben Samuel first set up the family press.

He opened his Hebrew press at Soncino in 1483. His first work, the tractate Berakot, appeared in 1484. The press moved often, to Naples, Brescia, Fano, and Pesaro. Branches later worked at Constantinople and at Salonica in Turkey. Soncino prints were prized for fine type and correctness. The first Hebrew Bible was printed by that house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinhardt-jose:
Joseph Steinhardt was a German rabbi born about 1720 and active in Alsace and Bavaria. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He served as chief rabbi of Upper Alsace early in his career. In 1763 he was called as rabbi to Fürth. He stayed there until his death in 1776.

Steinhardt ranked among the foremost Talmudists of his time. Scholars sent him questions from Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, and Switzerland. He held very conservative views on religious practice. His chief book, Zikron Yosef, printed at Fürth in 1773, collects his responsa and rulings. Later works add notes on the Pentateuch and on a Talmud tractate. The entry preserves the record of a widely consulted rabbi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sun-rising-and-:
Knowing sunrise and sunset fixes the hours of Jewish observance. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Sabbath and festival times depend on those moments. Strict reading makes each day run sunrise to sunset. Ibn Ezra supports that view in his commentary.

Hebrew has rich words for dawn and dusk. One term names the rising of the morning before sunrise. Poets call dawn the brows of the morning. The morning star bears two Hebrew names in sources. Twilight, between the suns, troubled the rabbis most. They could not tell if it belonged to day or night. So they guarded it against trespass on either side. The entry explains the clock that governs sacred time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-talmud-commenta:
Commentaries on the Talmud explain its dense text for later readers. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Richtmann wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Such works form only a small part of legal literature. Responsa and code commentaries bulk far larger. Early scholars felt no need to write them.

When the Talmud closed, its tradition still lived in memory. The first gaonate period wrote no commentaries either. Paltoi Gaon first glossed passages inside his responsa. His son Zemah paraphrased hard texts he quoted. Zemah also built a lexicon to aid Talmud study. Saadia Gaon is said to have commented on the Talmud. The last great geonim added much more in this field. Sherira mostly explained difficult terms for readers. The entry traces commentary from glosses to a genre.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ten-14314:
Ten, as a number in the Bible and rabbinic writing, is surveyed here. Wilhelm Bacher and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Counting began with fingers and toes, they note. The Hebrews used the decimal system, and ten stayed a base unit.

Ten shapes the measures of Noah's ark and the Tabernacle. It gives the count of the commandments and of Egypt's plagues. Passover and the Day of Atonement fall on the tenth day. Abraham gave a tenth, and tithes followed that pattern. The article also tracks ten in the Talmud and Midrash. There it marks completion and perfection again and again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-triesch-14514:
Triesch, a city in Moravia, owed its Jewish congregation to exiles from Iglau. Gotthard Deutsch and M. L. Stern wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Those exiles likely arrived shortly after 1426. They traded in Iglau by day and slept outside its limits. Wool was their chief ware, sold to Iglau cloth-makers.

Freedom of residence in 1848 shrank the congregation. Czech national feeling later hurt Jewish trade standing. Jews still led in cloth, furniture, and match making. Its rabbis included the cabalist Mordecai Bet ha-Levi. His manuscripts burned in the great fire of 1824. Eleazar Löw served twice around 1800 to 1820. About 300 Jews lived among 5,000 residents in 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-usque-14614:
Usque was a family named for Huesca in Spain, famed for the Ferrara Bible. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its members fled the Inquisition through Portugal to Italy. Abraham Usque, born Duarte Pinel at Lisbon, heads the entry. He reached Ferrara sometime after 1543.

At Ferrara he built a large printing house. Its imprint was a globe with a verse from Isaiah. Between 1551 and 1557 it issued some twenty-eight Hebrew books. Judaeo-Spanish rituals and Portuguese works appeared there too. His chief work was the Ferrara Bible of 1553. It revised an older Spanish rendering of the Hebrew. One issue honored the Duke, another Dona Gracia Nasi. New editions ran at Salonica and Amsterdam for decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vital-14714:
Vital was an Italian family of scholars and mystics. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its best known member is Hayyim Vital. Hayyim was born at Safed in 1543. He died at Damascus on May 6, 1620. His father was Joseph Vital.

Legends fill Hayyim's life story. A dream of the prophet Elijah turned him toward Kabbalah. He studied alchemy for over two years. Then he became the chief disciple of Isaac Luria. Hayyim wrote down Luria's teachings for later readers. That record made him central to Jewish mysticism. The entry tells his visions alongside the plain facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-15014: Worms, as a family name, is traced by Joseph Jacobs for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The kin came from Frankfort-on-the-Main and from England. Their line runs back to Aaron Worms of Frankfort in the mid 1700s. A great-great-grandson won a baron rank in Austria in 1871. A later kin, Baron Henry de Worms, rose to the British peerage as Lord Pirbright. The short entry gives the line and points to a family tree.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yod-15114: Yod is the tenth sign of the Hebrew letter set. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broyde wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name seems tied to the word yad, meaning hand. The old Phoenician sign looks a bit like a hand. The sound is that of the English letter y. With the vowel i it melts into a long i sound. As a count sign it holds the worth of ten. The name of God is at times shown by this sign.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeebi-israel-15:
Israel Zeebi (1651-1731) was a top Talmud man of Hebron in Palestine. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lazarus Grunhut wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Benjamin Zeebi of that town. On his mother's side he came from Abraham Azulai.

His sire died when the boy was four years of age. His mother raised him and saw to his school work. At age eighteen he wed a girl of a good house. For near thirty years he led the Jews of Hebron. He is said to have backed Nehemiah Hayyun in his day. He wrote to five great sages of his age on the law. His full name was Abraham Israel in his late years. His son brought out two books of his work in 1758.
jonson-bartholomew-fair-1614:
Ben Jonson wrote Bartholomew Fair for the London stage in 1614, setting the whole comedy at Smithfield's famous cloth fair. Jonson loved to mock pretension, and the fair gives him a whole city of targets. The play opens with a famous induction that teases the audience itself.

At the fair, a stiff Puritan named Zeal-of-the-Land Busy denounces the fun while enjoying it. Pickpockets, puppet shows, ballad singers, and a foolish justice fill the scene. A puppet play within the play settles several quarrels at once. Jonson's sprawling comedy shows Jacobean London at its loudest, full of appetite, folly, and noise.
journal-of-discourses-vol-14:
Federal pressure on plural marriage opens in Volume Fourteen, from 1872. Court cases loom as Washington turns its guns on Utah's ways. The Saints brace for a long legal war over their faith.

Young defends religious liberty with all his famous force and scorn. Sermons frame the fight as a test of America's own first freedoms. Speakers urge calm, unity, and strict obedience to church counsel. The kingdom's long stand for its way of life begins here. Readers hear a prophet turn lawyer, patriot, and war chief at once in these talks. The legal fight he foresaw would run for two long decades.
joyce-dubliners-1914:
James Joyce published Dubliners in 1914, his fifteen stories of Dublin paralysis, ending with The Dead in snow. The book that reinvented the short story had waited nine years, fought printers and censors, and seen an edition burned. Joyce called his method a style of scrupulous meanness, aimed at a chapter of his city's moral history.

The Sisters, Araby, and Eveline trace childhood, youth, and public life in a city of missed chances and drink. A Little Cloud, Counterparts, and The Boarding House weigh clerks, drunks, and matchmakers in Dublin's lower middle class.
