Gabriel Conroy, in The Dead, learns at a Christmas party that his wife loved a dead boy more than him. Snow, general all over Ireland, closes a story many rank the greatest in the English language. Joyce's epiphanies, moments that reveal a soul, changed fiction's craft for good.
lamarck-zoological-philosophy-1914:
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck published his theory of how animal life changes in French in 1809. Hugh Elliot translated that work into English in 1914 as Zoological Philosophy. Lamarck argued that living things pass on changes gained through use, need, and habit.

His best-known example involves giraffes stretching toward higher leaves over many generations. He also set out a broad account of how species descend and change over time. Charles Darwin later offered a different mechanism, but Lamarck came first. Readers get the first full theory of evolution, stated before Darwin was born.
lawrence-prussian-officer-1914:
Lawrence's first story collection appeared in 1914, led by the title novella of a Prussian cavalry officer and his orderly. Their relation of discipline, resentment, and buried feeling hardens until it breaks in violence in a lonely forest.

The volume also holds 'Odour of Chrysanthemums', his great story of a miner's wife waiting for a husband who comes home dead, and 'The Christening'. Many pieces draw on the mining country of his youth in Nottinghamshire. Lawrence writes working lives from inside, without pity or polish. These stories announced a major talent and still stand among his finest work in short fiction.
mach-sensations-williams-1914:
Mach's Analysis of Sensations, in the 1914 English translation by Williams and Waterlow, asks what the world is made of at bottom. His answer is plain sense data: colors, sounds, pressures, heat, and cold. Mind and matter, he argues, are two ways of grouping the same basic stuff.

A table, a body, and a thought all count as bundles of such elements in different patterns. That view, later called neutral monism, refuses to split the world into two rival kinds of thing. Thinkers in physics and in the study of mind both drew on the book for years.
maier-arcana-arcanissima-1614:
Michael Maier read the myths of Egypt and Greece as coded alchemy in Arcana arcanissima, published in 1614. Maier, a physician at the court of Rudolf II and a voice for the Rosicrucians, decodes hieroglyphs and the fables of the golden age. Every god and hero hides, in his reading, a step in the making of the stone.

The Latin text piles symbol on symbol with a scholar's glee, daring the reader to follow. Maier's grand claim, that ancient fable is veiled chemistry, shaped how his age read both myth and matter. The work stands as his mytho-alchemical masterwork, central to the strange learning of the Rosicrucian years.
mckechnie-magna-carta-commentary-1914:
William Sharp McKechnie published Magna Carta: A Commentary on the Great Charter of King John in 1914, in its second edition. McKechnie, a Glasgow professor of law, took the charter of 1215 clause by clause. His aim was to show what each clause meant to the barons who forced it on King John.

McKechnie separated the charter's real medieval sense from the grand meanings later ages read into it. Famous clauses on judgment by peers and no sale of justice get careful, sober treatment. He printed the Latin text and tracked each clause's later fate. The book became the standard scholarly commentary on Magna Carta, the reference against which popular claims about the charter are still checked.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-14: Fourteenth in line, volume fourteen bears etext number 3564. The title in its head note carries the year 1815. Bourrienne wrote the memoirs, and Widger produced this Gutenberg file. Beyond those head facts, the sample gives a reader only terms of use and fund appeals. The narrative that should follow is absent from the sample held here. For that reason this entry describes the file, not the volume's contents.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-14:
The Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, closes with volume fourteen, Chrysostom's homilies on the Gospel of John and on the Epistle to the Hebrews. Philip Schaff's set ended here in 1886. Eighty-eight homilies cover John's gospel, preached at Antioch in his early years.

Chrysostom treats John as the most spiritual gospel, aimed against heretics who shrank Christ. The thirty-four Hebrews homilies, preached later at Constantinople, take up the high priesthood of Christ and the call to endure. His voice darkens as exile nears. The volume ends both the Chrysostom block and the whole first series. Schaff's second series, on the Greek and Latin fathers after Nicaea, stands separately.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-14:
The second series of the Nicene Fathers closes with volume fourteen: the canons and decrees of the seven ecumenical councils. Schaff and Wace's 1890 series ends on the documents that defined orthodox faith for east and west alike. From Nicaea in 325 to the second council of Nicaea in 787, the councils span four and a half centuries.

Each council's creeds, definitions, and canons stand here in English, with the letters and debates that explain them. The reader watches the church fix the Trinity at Nicaea, Christ's two natures at Chalcedon, and the fate of icons at the last. Few volumes pack so much consequence into official prose. It is the legal spine of ancient Christianity.
norwegian-constitution-1814:
Norway's constitution was signed at Eidsvoll on 17 May 1814. Norwegians seized the moment when Denmark, beaten in the Napoleonic wars, had to hand Norway to Sweden. An assembly of 112 men wrote the charter in a few spring weeks, claiming their country's freedom on the model of America and France.

The text makes Norway a free, independent, and indivisible kingdom with a limited hereditary monarchy. Power is split among the king, the Storting as legislature, and independent courts, and a wide share of men gained the vote for the age. Sweden forced Norway into a union that year, but let the constitution stand almost untouched. Norwegians celebrate the 17th of May as their national day. The charter is among the world's oldest written constitutions still in force.
openalex-w2011868814:
Samira Miyamoto, Imperio Lombardi, Katherine Berg and colleagues created a Brazilian version of the Berg balance scale. Their paper appeared in 2004. The scale tests functional balance in older people. Clinicians needed a sound Portuguese version for Brazil. The team tested whether its scores were reliable.

Two bilingual translators rendered the scale into Brazilian Portuguese. A panel settled differences, and back translation checked the work. Older patients and therapists tried the draft version. Items that many found unclear were rewritten and retested. Six questions changed during that process. Later tests on older patients showed very high agreement. Scores matched closely within and between testers. The version was judged ready for clinical use.
openalex-w2016899314:
Julie Perez and Cyrille Goarant worked on faster identification of Leptospira bacteria in New Caledonia. Their paper appeared in BMC Microbiology in 2010. Leptospirosis is a disease spread through water and animal urine. The standard lab test has known weaknesses. Knowing the infecting strain helps track outbreaks.

The team tested whether PCR product sequences could name the strain. Two standard test products showed useful sequence differences. They checked the method against a fuller typing method. Samples from local patients and animals matched well. They found one group with no known reference strain. They also found a group only in introduced Rusa deer. That deer is likely its animal reservoir in the area.
openalex-w2207949614:
Jacqueline Kerr, Jennifer Emond, Hannah Badland, and colleagues published this study in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2015. The IPEN study asked how neighborhood features, as residents perceive them, relate to walking and cycling for transport. Rates of both habits are low and vary widely between countries, which makes choosing design fixes hard.

Self-reported data came from nearly fourteen thousand adults in seventeen cities across twelve countries. Participants rated their neighborhoods on a standard walkability scale and reported recent travel habits. Walking for transport was linked to perceived housing density, mixed land use with good access, connected streets, looks, and safety. The team modeled the strength and shape of each link, city by city.
openalex-w2299123914:
G. Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this performance study in the European Physical Journal C in 2016. Muons are among the cleanest signals at the Large Hadron Collider, central to Higgs and new-physics searches. The paper documents how well ATLAS finds and measures them in its first thirteen-TeV proton collision data.

Decays of J/psi and Z particles into muon pairs served as the yardsticks. Reconstruction efficiency came out near ninety-nine percent across most of the detector's range. Isolation efficiency ran between ninety-three and one hundred percent, depending on settings. Momentum was measured to within about two percent in the detector's heart, and simulations matched the real data closely throughout.
openalex-w2972679514:

Pankhurst led the Women's Social and Political Union in Britain, whose members chained themselves to railings, broke windows, and endured prison hunger strikes. Prison scenes, forcible feeding, and the death of Emily Davison at the Derby mark the campaign's hardest years. She judged each act by one test: did it win attention for the vote? The memoir remains the leader's own account of the suffragette fight.

plos-pbio-0020014:
Christiane Landgraf, Simona Panni, Luisa Montecchi-Palazzi, and others presented a protein mapping method in PLOS Biology in 2004. Many proteins link up through short stretches that fit into small pockets on partner proteins. The team scanned whole sets of proteins with short peptides to find those links.

Each scan tests huge numbers of pairs at once, far more than one-by-one lab work allows. The result is a network map of which proteins can touch which. Such maps help predict how signals travel through a cell and where a fault might cause disease. They also give drug makers a list of contacts that a well aimed compound might block or boost.
plos-pone-0000014:
Lili Yu, Valter Tucci, Shuji Kishi, and co-authors made zebrafish into a model for the aging mind in a 2006 paper. Zebrafish are small, cheap to keep, and share much of their basic brain biology with humans. The team asked whether old fish show the same slide in learning and memory that marks cognitive aging in people.

They tested fish across ages on learning tasks, looking for decline that mirrors human patterns. A fish model that ages mentally like we do would speed up research: drugs and genes could be screened in months, not decades. The study lays the groundwork, showing what changes with age in the zebrafish brain and how to measure it.
plos-pone-0000114:
Elin Lehrmann, Carlo Colantuoni, Amy Deep-Soboslay, and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It asks whether cocaine, cannabis, and phencyclidine, three very different drugs of abuse, leave a shared mark on the human brain. The team looked for gene activity changes common to all three.

A central goal of addiction research is finding brain changes shared across drugs, since those may drive dependence itself. The authors compare transcription patterns linked to each drug and pull out the overlap. Work like this points drug research toward the common machinery of addiction rather than the quirks of one substance.
plos-pone-0000214:
Pekka Janhunen, Hermanni Kaartokallio, Ilona Oksanen, and colleagues published this Earth history paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It concerns the Neoproterozoic icehouse, a time hundreds of millions of years ago when ice may have covered much of the planet. The authors argue biological feedbacks both caused and ended that deep freeze.

The paper also looks ahead: cold conditions may carry astrobiological lessons, including prospects for faster evolution. The authors link microbial life, climate, and planetary change in one loop. Their argument treats the snowball Earth episode not just as a climate event but as a turning point for life itself.
plos-pone-0000314:
Kevin C. Leonard, Dino Petrin, Stuart G. Coupland, and colleagues published this eye research paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited disease that kills photoreceptors, the light-sensing cells of the retina, causing blindness. The authors study XIAP, a protein that blocks cell death, and its protection of photoreceptors in animal models of the disease.

Slowing photoreceptor death could preserve sight even without fixing the faulty gene. The authors test whether boosting this natural brake on cell death saves the cells. The work supports gene therapy approaches that deliver protective proteins to the retina.
plos-pone-0000414:
Yanling Zhang and colleagues studied a protein that helps kidney cells keep their shape and tiny hair-like sensors, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The protein, collectrin, is a target of the gene regulator HNF-1β. The team examined collecting duct cells, which line the kidney's final urine-handling tubes.

They focused on collectrin's role in maintaining primary cilia and cell polarity. A primary cilium is the single antenna-like hair most cells carry. Cell polarity is the cell's sense of top and bottom. When cilia or polarity fail, kidney cysts and other defects can follow. The work links a diabetes-related regulator to the basic architecture of kidney cells.
plos-pone-0000514:
Nadia A. Ayoub and colleagues read the full genes behind spider silk, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dragline silk, the spider's lifeline and web frame, outperforms most human-made fibers for its weight. The team produced the blueprint for this high-performance biomaterial: full-length spider dragline silk genes, which are enormous and repetitive and had resisted complete sequencing.

The repeat structure is exactly what makes silk strong and elastic, and exactly what made the genes hard to read. Full sequences let engineers copy the design into microbes or materials with the proportions right. Biomaterials work of this kind aims to manufacture silk's properties without farming spiders.
plos-pone-0000614:
Peter R. Teske, Isabelle Papadopoulos, Christopher D. McQuaid and colleagues turned to a very old fashion question in PLOS ONE in 2007. Shell beads made from the southern African tick shell are the earliest known ornaments worn by humans. Beads from about 75,000 years ago, found in a cave on South Africa's south coast, were larger than later ones.

Three explanations compete in the title itself: climate change, genetics, or human choice. The authors compare Pleistocene shells with Holocene ones to weigh why the size shifted. A change in taste would say something about early human culture. A change in climate or genes would point to the shells' own biology instead.
plos-pone-0000714:
Yale J. Passamaneck, Anna-Katerina Hadjantonakis and Anna Di Gregorio filmed muscle cells building a sea squirt's tail, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Axial elongation, growth along the body's length, shapes developing organisms. In the ascidian Ciona intestinalis, the larva's tail extends in a striking example of this process. Muscle cells set along the tail's sides elongate and differentiate on their own schedule.

The team describes dynamic, polarized behaviors in those cells as the tail forms. Polarized means the cells have distinct fronts and backs guiding their movement and shape. Such cell-level detail explains how a simple larva builds a working swimming tail so quickly and reliably.
plos-pone-0000814:
Qi Wang and Christopher Lee worked on a trap in the study of how proteins change, using HIV as their case. Scientists often infer that two sites in a protein work together when they change together over time. But shared ancestry can fake that pattern. Sites can look linked just because they were inherited in the same viral line, a problem classed as background linkage disequilibrium.

Their study sorts true linked change from that background effect. The test proteins were HIV protease and reverse transcriptase, the two enzymes most HIV drugs target. The stakes are practical: falsely linked sites can mislead work on how the virus escapes drugs. A cleaner method points drug design at real weak spots.
plos-pone-0000914:
Ana-Belen Martin-Cuadrado, Purificacion Lopez-Garcia, Juan-Carlos Alba and co-authors sampled the gene pool of the deep Mediterranean Sea, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Metagenomics reads DNA straight from the environment, revealing microbes that never grow in a lab. Most sea studies of this kind had focused on sunlit surface waters.

The deep Mediterranean is different: a warm bathypelagic habitat, far below the light. Reading its microbes shows what life does where food is scarce and pressure is high. Work of this sort keeps rewriting basic ideas in microbial ecology. It shows how much of the living world stays hidden until its DNA is read directly.
plos-pone-0001014:
Tina Rich and Archana Varadaraj tested how fusion partners change the harm done by a repeated protein stretch, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Clumps of protein inside the nucleus mark several folding diseases. Much of what we know comes from glowing fusion proteins carrying polyglutamine repeats, the same repeats behind Huntington's disease.

Ataxin-1 is one such protein. The pair ask whether the partner fused to it changes how lethal the repeat is and how it aggregates. If partners change the outcome, then lab results depend on the test construct, not just the repeat. That caution matters for every study built on fusion proteins.
plos-pone-0001114:
Nearly a fifth of human cancers around the world are linked to infections, Xing Guo Wang and co-authors note in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their examples include liver cancer tied to hepatitis B and C viruses, and cervical cancer tied to human papilloma virus. The authors argue that these virus-linked tumors need fresh lines of attack.

Rather than treating such cancers only as growths to cut or poison, the authors propose a different target. They would go after the viral proteins, called antigens, that sit inside the tumor cells. Those antigens could serve as targets for new treatments. The same targets might also help prevent tumors of viral origin before they form.
plos-pone-0001214:
Cell-mediated immunity is needed to stop HIV spreading from cell to cell, and killer T cell responses are central to it. Ammar Achour and colleagues tested an unusual vaccine candidate in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The candidate is a synthetic peptide called B1, built by mathematical transformation of HIV protein structures rather than copied from them.

The peptide shares no sequence homology with HIV, yet earlier work hinted it could still provoke immunity. The authors report HIV-1 envelope-specific cell-mediated immunity induced by this non-homologous peptide. If it holds up, the design route behind B1 could widen the search for vaccine parts.
plos-pone-0001314:
Epigenetic changes, especially DNA methylation, are among the earliest abnormalities in tumor formation. Jared Ordway and colleagues searched breast cancer for methylation changes that occur at high frequency, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Cytosine methylation is thermodynamically stable, which makes it attractive as a biomarker that can survive in clinical samples.

The authors report identification of novel high-frequency DNA methylation changes in breast cancer. Changes present in most tumors are the most useful for detection tests. Their catalogue adds candidate markers for the long-running effort to catch breast cancer from a blood or tissue sample.
plos-pone-0001414:
Matthias Schaefer, Julia Steringer, and Frank Lyko wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on an enzyme in fruit flies called Dnmt2. Enzymes of this family are kept across many species, yet their true job was in doubt. This one bears all the marks of a DNA tagging enzyme. Still, tests kept pointing to a role with RNA instead.

The team found the fly enzyme bound to the scaffold inside the cell nucleus. It could reach DNA while the cell was dividing. Those facts keep both roles in play and refine where to look next. Sorting this enzyme out matters for the wider tale of how gene tags evolve.
plos-pone-0001514:
Birte Meyer and Jan Kuever wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that models an enzyme of sulfur germs. The enzyme drives a step in how some germs burn or store sulfur. It works forward in sulfate eating germs and in reverse in sulfur burning ones. No lab shape for it existed, so the pair built a model from kin enzymes.

Their model maps the enzyme's shape and its key working parts. Those parts include a flavin helper and two iron sulfur clusters. A sound model lets labs guess how mutations will shift the enzyme. It also aids study of sulfur cycles in soil and sea.
plos-pone-0001614:
Michael Bethune and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a monkey model for gluten sensitivity. In celiac disease, gluten in food sparks gut harm, poor food uptake, and loose stools. A faithful animal model had been lacking, which slowed work on the ill. The team tested whether rhesus monkeys can fill that gap.

Some monkeys did show the gut harm, blood marks, and signs seen in human celiac disease when fed gluten. That makes them a rare model that mirrors the human course. With it, labs can test diets, drugs, and the ill's first steps in a close kin. Ethical care bounds such work, which adds to its value.
plos-pone-0001714:
Karin Dedek, Chethan Pandarinath, Nazia M. Alam, and their co-authors asked how the retina adapts between night and day in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The visual system adjusts to its setting. Retinal ganglion cells, which send the eye's output to the brain, shift their spatial tuning when light changes. That shift is thought to come from changes in how horizontal cells are coupled to each other.

The team tested whether horizontal cell coupling plays a causal role in ganglion cell adaptability. The full text gives the retina preparations, the coupling measurements, and the tuning shifts. The coupling acts like a switch that reconfigures the eye's circuits for dim or bright scenes, a design that artificial vision systems also exploit.
plos-pone-0001814:
Shashank Gupta, Sabine Höpner, Bernd Rupp, and their co-authors studied how immune display molecules swap their cargo in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Class II MHC molecules display peptides on cell surfaces for surveillance by CD4 T cells. A complex processing pathway delivers only stable peptide-MHC complexes to the surface, so the display reflects the cell's contents.

The team reports that anchor side chains of short peptide fragments trigger ligand exchange of class II MHC molecules. The full text gives the binding experiments and the structural evidence. Understanding exchange rules helps vaccine designers load chosen peptides onto MHC molecules deliberately, rather than by trial and error.
plos-pone-0001914:
Naeem Ali and co-authors reported that a protein long cast as a mere holder has its own immune effects, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, called latency associated peptide, binds TGF-beta1 and holds it in a latent, inactive form. Most work assumed the peptide's only job was to keep that signal locked away.

Past work had shown the peptide can make lining cells move, but effects on white blood cells were unknown. The team tested the peptide in lab dishes and in living animals, apart from TGF-beta1. They report immune effects of its own. If a holder protein also acts alone, immune models need a rewrite.
plos-pone-0002014:
Cory Toth and co-authors studied a protein that helps severed nerve fibers regrow, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Axons, the long fibers of nerve cells, regrow poorly after injury. Blame falls on both a hostile scar setting and a weak inborn drive to regrow inside the neuron. The steps of that weakness were unclear.

The team focused on Ndel1, a protein tied to how cells build their inner frame. As the title states, Ndel1 promotes axon regeneration via intermediate filaments, one class of that frame. A regrowth lever inside the cell is a hope for spinal and nerve repair.
plos-pone-0002114:
Maorong Chen and co-authors found the rings that make a major potassium channel one-way, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. BK channels are large-conductance channels opened by calcium and voltage, and they serve many tissues. Their auxiliary beta subunits add much of the channels' diversity, which is fundamental to their right function in each tissue.

The team describe a feature of the human beta two subunit's outer segment: rings rich in lysine, a charged building block. As the title states, these extracellular rings confer the outward rectification of BK channels, a bias to pass current one way. Form explains function here, residue by residue.
plos-pone-0002214:
Linea Melchior, Toomas Kivisild, Niels Lynnerup, and co-authors extracted DNA from Viking Age skeletons in Denmark, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ancient human DNA is easily swamped by modern DNA from handlers, so results in this field have often been doubted. Strict lab rules exist to guard against such contamination.

The team's skeletons had stayed untouched by humans for about 1,000 years until careful excavation. That rare history let them argue their DNA results were authentic. Verified Viking DNA can test sagas against genetics. It traces kinship and migration in early medieval Scandinavia with a firmer hand than most ancient studies can claim.
plos-pone-0002314:
Hidehito Takayama, Prashen Chelikani, Philip Reeves, and co-authors produced and purified a human membrane protein called CD81, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Membrane proteins are prime drug targets, but studying their structure requires making large amounts in a working form, which is notoriously hard. CD81 belongs to the tetraspanin family and is also the entry receptor used by hepatitis C virus.

The team built a mammalian cell line that makes CD81 at high level under a switchable promoter, then purified it in a single affinity step. They characterized the protein to confirm it stayed functional. A clean supply of CD81 enables structural work and screens for entry blockers.
plos-pone-0002414:
Work from Addessi and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Elsa Addessi, Alessandra Mancini, Lara Crescimbene, and others. Its subject is preference Transitivity and Symbolic Representation in Capuchin Monkeys ( Cebus apella ). Can non-human animals comprehend and employ symbols?

The most convincing empirical evidence comes from language-trained apes, but little is known about this ability in monkeys. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002514:
In 2008, Lundby and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Alicia Lundby, Hiroki Mutoh, Dimitar Dimitrov, and others. Its subject is engineering of a Genetically Encodable Fluorescent Voltage Sensor Exploiting Fast Ci-VSP Voltage-Sensing Movements. Ci-VSP contains a voltage-sensing domain (VSD) homologous to that of voltage-gated potassium channels.

Using charge displacement (‘gating’ current) measurements we show that voltage-sensing movements of this VSD can occur within 1 ms in mammalian membranes. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002614:
A research team led by Pantano reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Sergio Pantano, Francesco Zonta, Fabio Mammano, and others. Its subject is a Fully Atomistic Model of the Cx32 Connexon. Connexins are plasma membrane proteins that associate in hexameric complexes to form channels named connexons.

Two connexons in neighboring cells may dock to form a “gap junction” channel, i.e. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002714:
Yoshimi Endo led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was role of sox-9, ER81 and VE-Cadherin in retinoic Acid-Mediated Trans-Differentiation of breast cancer cells. Authorship is credited in the record to Yoshimi Endo and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Many aspects of development, tumor growth and metastasis depend upon the provision of an adequate vasculature. The summary also notes a further point. This can be a result of regulated angiogenesis, recruitment of circulating endothelial progenitors and/or vascular trans-differentiation. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002814:
Joseph Alan Wamstad led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was role of the transcriptional corepressor bcor in embryonic stem cell differentiation and early embryonic development. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Joseph Alan Wamstad, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Bcor (BCL6 corepressor) is a widely expressed gene that is mutated in patients with X-linked Oculofaciocardiodental (OFCD) syndrome. The summary also notes a further point. BCOR regulates gene expression in association with a complex of proteins capable of epigenetic modification of chromatin. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002914:
Todd Harshbarger and Allen Song probed the tail end of the brain's blood signal in 2008. In fMRI scans, the BOLD signal rises with activity and then dips below baseline, a phase called the post-stimulus undershoot. That dip is perhaps the least understood part of the signal.

By adding diffusion weighting, which is sensitive to small water movement, the team tried to separate blood vessel effects from neuron effects. The PLOS ONE paper links the dip's sensitivity to a hierarchy of vessels and neurons. Scan analysts can use that to read fMRI results with more care.
plos-pone-0003014:
Vincenzo Penteriani and Maria del Mar Delgado proposed in 2008 that owls signal breeding status with droppings and prey feathers. Many animals mark key spots in their home range with materials that carry information. Visual signaling had already been shown to play a once-unrecognized role in eagle owl communication, both territorial and parental.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors argue faeces and prey feathers may signal current reproduction in these owls. That would let rivals and mates read breeding state at a site without the owner present. Field biologists get a testable reading of marks once dismissed as mere mess.
plos-pone-0003114:
Brent Bill, Darius Balciunas, Joshua McCarra and co-authors studied choroid plexus development and Notch signaling in zebrafish in 2008. The choroid plexus is an epithelial and vascular structure in the brain's ventricles and a critical part of the blood-brain barrier. It produces and regulates cerebrospinal fluid and blocks entry of harmful substances.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team sets out development of the zebrafish plexus and its requirements for Notch signaling, a core cell-to-cell pathway. Knowing the signals that build the plexus helps explain disorders where fluid balance in the brain goes wrong early in life.
plos-pone-0003214:
Yaoxing Huang, Michael Krasnitz, Raul Rabadan and colleagues describe a recoding method for an HIV DNA vaccine in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The manuscript describes a novel strategy to improve HIV DNA vaccine design. Using a new information theory based bioinformatic algorithm, the team identify a set of nucleotide motifs common in the coding region of HIV but under-represented in highly expressed genes.

The aim is a recoding method to improve the humoral immune response to the vaccine. Readers see vaccine design treated as a sequence engineering problem. Changing silent parts of the code may raise antibody output without changing the protein the immune system must learn.
plos-pone-0003314:
Jehangir S. Wadia, Monica Schaller, R. Anthony Williamson and colleagues study how the harmful prion protein enters cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies are fatal neurodegenerative disorders. They include variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans. They also include bovine spongiform encephalopathy in cattle. In these diseases, the host cellular prion protein misfolds into an infectious form.

The title reports that pathologic prion protein infects cells by lipid-raft dependent macropinocytosis, a drinking-like uptake route. Readers see prions use a bulk entry pathway rather than a single receptor. That route may suggest new points to block prion spread between cells.
plos-pone-0003414:
Chun-Hua Yuan and co-authors reported a new toxin family from tarantulas in this 2008 paper. Kunitz-type toxins were known from snakes, cone snails, and sea anemones. These proteins first evolved to block enzymes that cut other proteins. Some later gained the power to block ion channels as toxins.

The tarantula versions formed a distinct superfamily of their own. Finding them widened the known reach of this toxin clan. Venom proteins like these are prized as tools for probing nerves and pain. The paper gives toxin hunters a fresh set of spider compounds to study.
plos-pone-0003514:
Hiu-Kwan Chow and co-authors built hybrid gene-switch proteins in this 2008 paper. They fused parts of two protein families, bHLH and bZIP. Each part brings a skill: binding DNA or pairing with a partner. The hybrids were designed to grip one DNA site called the E-box.

The hybrids behaved one way in test tubes and another in living cells. Binding measured in vitro did not predict binding in vivo. Context inside a cell changes how such tools work. Engineered gene regulators must be tested where they will actually serve. Living cells add salts, partners, and crowding that no test tube can copy.
plos-pone-0003614:
Isabella Irrcher and co-authors studied an endurance gene's switch in muscle cells in this 2008 paper. PGC-1α helps build mitochondria and is central to muscle adaptation. How its gene expression is controlled in skeletal muscle was largely undefined. An energy sensor called AMPK was the candidate regulator.

They used AICAR, a compound that activates AMPK, in their tests. AMPK activation switched on the PGC-1α promoter. A 2.2 kb fragment of that promoter carried the response. The pathway explains part of how activity reprograms muscle. Endurance training works through this same pathway in human muscle too.
plos-pone-0003714:
Zhenbin Chen, Jinong Feng, Carolyn H. Buzin, and colleagues published this lung cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Some DNA changes come in pairs that arise at the same moment, in what are called chronocoordinate events. In normal mouse tissue, such doublet mutations seem to follow that pattern.

The authors surveyed doublet and multiplet mutations in human lung cancers. They found evidence that a subset of these paired changes arises by chronocoordinate events, sometimes in showers across long DNA stretches. The pattern suggests some tumor mutations are born as twins, not as two separate accidents.
plos-pone-0003814:
Ziyin Li, Takashi Umeyama, and Ching C. Wang published this parasite study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite behind sleeping sickness, divides with machinery that differs from ours in key ways. Its Aurora B-like kinase, TbAUK1, runs both mitosis and the final split into two cells.

The team shows the chromosomal passenger complex and a mitotic kinesin interact with the parasite's Tousled-like kinase. Together they regulate mitosis and cytokinesis in the procyclic form. These handshakes reveal how the parasite runs cell division, and where drugs might jam the works.
plos-pone-0003914:
Bethany J. Slater, Karen J. Liu, Matthew D. Kwan, and co-authors described skull growth in a frog in 2009. Their PLOS ONE article uses Xenopus laevis, the African clawed frog. Vertebrate skulls vary hugely in shape, set by differing growth programs. Learning those programs can clarify human face and skull defects.

The authors tracked how skull bones form and how the seams between them develop. The frog offers a simple system where each step can be watched. Its seams differ from those of mammals in useful ways. The work sets a base for comparing skull growth across backboned animals.
plos-pone-0004014:
Timothy J. Bauler, Wiljan J. A. J. Hendriks, and Philip D. King tested two enzymes in T cell signaling in 2008. PTPN3 and PTPN4 are closely related phosphatase enzymes. Both carry extra domains that anchor them in cells. They were thought to damp early T cell receptor signals.

Their PLOS ONE article reports both are dispensable for that signaling. Removing them did not break the receptor's message chain. Negative results like this prune wrong assumptions from immune models. They redirect attention to phosphatases that truly govern T cell activation. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004114:
Mubashir Hanif, Ylva Rosengardten, Hanna Sagelius, and co-authors tracked nuclear proteins through the hair cycle in 2009. Lamin A and C mutations cause disorders with strong skin signs. They include Hutchinson-Gilford progeria, a premature aging syndrome. Hair cycling offers a window on skin renewal over time.

Their PLOS ONE article reports A-type and B-type lamins differ across the cycle. Their expression rose and fell at different phases of hair growth. Such timing may explain why lamin disorders strike skin so hard. It also adds basic data on the hair follicle's clock. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004214:
Fritzie Arce and colleagues published this motor control study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Models of motor control often explain the straightness of reaching movements as the product of optimal control. On that view, curved reaching paths count as sub-optimal.

Arce and colleagues question that assumption, asking whether people may instead choose curved trajectories on purpose. They show how differences in context and feedback lead to different paths and different adaptation strategies. The work suggests the brain treats reaching as a flexible choice, not a fixed ideal line. In other words, a curve can be a choice, not a mistake.
plos-pone-0004314:
Claudia Hohn and colleagues published this zebrafish immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The innate immune response is the first line of defence against invading pathogens, and active endocytosis, cells eating particles, is one of its mechanisms. Endocytosis can serve as a reliable measure of immune defence activity.

The team studied phagocytes, eating cells, in the zebrafish kidney. They report that these cells use macropinocytosis, a gulping of fluid, and calcium-dependent endocytic mechanisms. Knowing how a model fish's immune cells feed helps researchers compare fish immunity with our own. Zebrafish are a standard lab model for such work.
plos-pone-0004414:
Immune cells that eat germs also make stress chemicals. Michael Flierl, Daniel Rittirsch, Brian Nadeau, and co-authors extend that finding in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. Their past report showed these cells are a new source of catecholamines, the body's stress signals.

Here they show two such chemicals switch on a key control gene in macrophages. That switch leads to more release of signals that drive inflammation. Raising these cell-made chemicals boosts the acute inflammatory response. The loop may help explain why severe inflammation can spiral in sepsis. The team built on its own past work on these white blood cells.
plos-pone-0004514:
Seaweed growth does not make a Caribbean coral disease worse, field tests by Ivana Vu, Gillian Smelick, Sam Harris, and co-authors found, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease is Caribbean yellow band disease. A popular idea held that overfishing removes the animals that graze seaweed, called macroalgae. More seaweed was then blamed for driving coral disease and death.

The team ran three field manipulations to test that chain of reasoning directly. Macroalgae had no effect on how severe the disease became or how it progressed, as the title states. A clear negative result is valuable here. It tells reef managers that cutting seaweed alone will not cure this disease, and pushes attention to other causes.
plos-pone-0004614:
Antibodies that grab a virus protein can also be used to purify it, show Sarah Duellman and Richard Burgess in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is EBNA1, the nuclear antigen 1 of Epstein-Barr virus, a virus that infects most humans and can drive several cancers. The team overexpressed EBNA1 in E. coli bacteria and purified it.

They then prepared mouse monoclonal antibodies that react with EBNA1, recovering eleven high-affinity ones. Nine were of one antibody class and two of another. The paper describes the antigen-binding properties of this set. The best use is immunoaffinity chromatography: using an antibody as a selective net to fish out pure EBNA1. Reliable antibodies are workhorse tools for every lab studying this virus.
plos-pone-0004714:
Stéphane Martin and colleagues studied how the stress hormone corticosterone shifts synaptic strength in the brain, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The hormone can both boost and blunt learning and memory. That two way effect has long puzzled researchers who study stress and the brain.

The team traced the effect to movement of a key receptor in nerve contacts. When the hormone moves those receptors, synapses can grow stronger or weaker with more ease. The finding gives a clear cell step behind stress effects on memory. It may guide work on stress linked illness. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004814:
Yuka Nadai and colleagues reported that the HIV-1 epidemic in the Caribbean is dominated by subtype B, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Molecular epidemiology of HIV-1 in the Caribbean had been described using partial genome sequencing. Subtype B was the most common in multiple countries, and nearly full genome amplification, sequencing. Review were conducted to expand knowledge of circulating strains and their relationships.

Full genomes confirm dominance and reveal recombination patterns. Regional data guide vaccine and diagnostic design. Subtype matters for some drug and test performance. Caribbean specific surveillance remains key for control. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004914:
Dongmei Wu and colleagues showed a conserved Shp2 step controls human and mouse embryonic stem cell pluripotency, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Recent studies suggested distinctive properties between human and mouse embryonic stem cells. The team reports that Shp2, a tyrosine phosphatase, plays a shared role in both species. It steers the signals that decide if stem cells stay pluripotent or start to specialize. That shared role bridges an apparent divide in stem cell biology.

Conserved nodes simplify translation between models. Shp2 balances self renewal against specialization. Culture protocols can target shared machinery. Species differences are real but partial. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0005014:
Protected reserves are the main tool for saving the Amazon. Whether they truly work is still debated. Marion Adeney, Norman Christensen and Stuart Pimm tested them in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used fire as their yardstick. In the Amazon, fires are closely linked to deforestation.

Satellite fire data let them compare reserves with unprotected land. Fires burned less inside reserves. That means reserves do hold the line against forest loss. At least they resist fire-driven clearing. The study gives conservation a hard measure of success. It also shows where protection is weakest. Such evidence helps decide where new reserves will do the most good.
plos-pone-0005114:
Optineurin is a busy protein found in all cells. Its production rises with inflammation signals. Cherukuri Sudhakar and colleagues studied how it is regulated in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on the alarm factor NF-kappa B. Tumor necrosis factor alpha triggers that alarm. The question was how the two factors relate.

NF-kappa B mediates optineurin's induction by the tumor signal. Optineurin then acts as a negative regulator of NF-kappa B. The alarm builds its own brake. That feedback loop limits inflammation's run. The finding maps a self-limiting circuit. Such circuits fail in chronic inflammatory disease. Knowing the wiring shows where the failure could sit. It also names optineurin as more than a bystander.
plos-pone-0005214:
On Mount Carmel in Israel, two slopes face each other across a small canyon with sharply different climates. One slope is hot and dry, the other cooler and greener, only meters apart. Raz and colleagues surveyed scorpions there, in a site known as Evolution Canyon, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The survey recorded which scorpion species live on each slope and how the groups differ. Contrasts packed into a tiny area let researchers watch divergence as it happens. Sites like this are natural labs for testing how local conditions split populations apart over time.
plos-pone-0005314:
Animals of the same species cope with stress in different styles, bold or shy, and style shapes how genes respond to challenges. MacKenzie and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that screening for coping style boosts gene expression studies, using common carp as the example.

Fish with different coping styles shifted gene expression in strikingly different ways under the same challenge. Sorting animals by style before analysis sharpens the signal. Ignoring behavior adds noise, so a simple behavioral screen can make expensive gene studies far more powerful. Fish farms and labs both gain from this trick, since calm fish and bold fish do not read as one group. And a mixed group can wash out a real gene effect.
plos-pone-0005414:
Mouse coat color is used as a readout in many studies, from transgene expression to chimerism and epigenetics. Scoring coat proportions by eye is subjective and varies between observers. Ounpraseuth and colleagues presented a quantitative method in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their method measures the proportions of coat colors objectively from the animals. Replacing estimates with numbers makes results comparable across labs and time. Small measurement upgrades like this one quietly improve every study that relies on the readout. A scale that two labs can share beats the eye of one skilled man. The same mouse should show the same coat in Maine and in Kyoto, so work from both labs can stand side by side in print.
plos-pone-0005514:
Nicolas Berthelemy and co-authors tested oxygen as a guide for stem cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Certain early cells in blood can mature into the cells that line blood vessels or the muscle cells that wrap them. Growth factors are usually used to steer that choice.

The team asked whether oxygen level alone could steer it. Changing the oxygen around the cells pushed them toward one fate or the other. A simple physical cue like oxygen could make vessel repair treatments easier to prepare and control. Oxygen is cheap and easy to control in a lab, which makes this route attractive for growing repair cells.
plos-pone-0005614:
Wolf Mehling and co-authors examined measures of body awareness in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Noticing one's own body signals can be helpful or harmful, depending on how it is done. Raising healthy body awareness has been proposed as a treatment aid for chronic pain, obesity, and post-traumatic stress.

The team checked how well existing self-report scales on body awareness hold up when tested. Sound measures are needed before clinics can tell whether a therapy truly changes body awareness. The work sorts stronger scales from weaker ones for future trials.
plos-pone-0005714:
Shinya Watanabe and co-authors charted in 2009 the many forms of a clotting protein made by Staphylococcus aureus. This germ causes a wide range of infections, and its staphylocoagulase makes blood clot around it. The protein comes in at least ten types that differ in how the immune system sees them.

The team compared the genes behind those types to learn how they diverged. Such variety in a surface factor can help the germ dodge immunity. Tracing its family tree may explain how S. aureus keeps reinventing itself. It may also guide vaccines that must cover many types at once.
plos-pone-0005814:
Koichi Ushizawa and co-authors described in 2009 a new member of an old protein family found in cow placentas. The Ly-6 family shares a distinct knot of cysteine bonds; its members sit on cell surfaces or are secreted. The new member, SOLD1, has an unusual origin in a retrotransposon.

The team characterized SOLD1 and tracked where and when it appears in placental villi. Proteins born from mobile DNA scraps are a growing theme in placenta biology. The placenta evolves fast, and borrowed genes may help it invade and feed the calf. SOLD1 is a case ready for functional tests.
plos-pone-0005914:
Gabriel Lidzbarsky, Tamar Shkolnik, and Eviatar Nevo sampled wild yeast in 2009 from a canyon famous for sharp contrasts in sun and drought. Natural populations face constant environmental stress, and UV radiation is a chief threat to yeast growth. The canyon's two slopes offer a ready-made experiment in adaptation.

Forty-six natural yeast strains from the site were tested for their responses to DNA-damaging agents. Strains from harsher slopes responded differently, evidence of adaptation in the wild. Such natural experiments show evolution's handwriting without lab contrivance. They also stock strain collections with hardy variants for industry.
plos-pone-0006014:
Each person's inner clock runs a touch longer than a day, and the exact length differs by person. Mark Smith, Helen Burgess, Louis Fogg and colleagues asked in 2009 whether it also differs by race. Their PLOS ONE paper measures the endogenous circadian period, the free-running length of the body clock, in different groups.

That length helps set whether someone leans toward mornings or evenings. A group difference, if real, would shape how sleep advice and shift schedules should be tuned. The study treats the clock as a trait that varies across humanity, and it gives sleep medicine hard numbers where guesswork about race and rhythm had stood before.
plos-pone-0006114:
Group B Streptococcus can infect a baby before birth, inside the womb itself. Izabela Sitkiewicz, Nicole Green, Nina Guo and colleagues asked how the germ adapts to that setting in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper maps the transcriptome, the full set of genes switched on, as the bacteria grow in human amniotic fluid.

The fluid is the germ's first home during intrauterine infection, and its growth program there was poorly known. A full gene map shows which tools the bacteria raise to survive the womb. That knowledge can guide both prevention and treatment of infections that end in fetal harm, where time for testing is short.
plos-pone-0006214:
Bacteria pump out unwanted chemicals using large transporter proteins in their membranes. Aurelien Deniaud and colleagues compared two such pumps, CusA and AcrB, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Until recently AcrB was the only member of its family with a solved structure, and it formed crystals under many conditions.

CusA behaved differently, and the authors trace the contrast to how flexible each protein is. Flexibility shapes whether a protein will sit still for crystal imaging. The lesson helps structural biologists plan work on other stubborn membrane proteins. Those structures, in turn, support drug design against resistant bacteria.
plos-pone-0006314:
Glioblastoma is the most frequent and most malignant primary brain tumor. Peter Huszthy and colleagues attacked it with suicide gene therapy in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Lab models often lack key features of the human disease, which has slowed translation of new strategies.

A lentiviral vector delivered the suicide gene into cancer stem-like tumor grafts. Treatment drove those invasive grafts into remission in the model. Cancer stem-like cells are thought to regrow tumors after standard therapy. Hitting them directly is the study's central idea, with remission as encouraging evidence.
plos-pone-0006414:
Two proteins secreted by tuberculosis bacteria are key targets of the immune response. Ray Waters and colleagues studied cells carrying SIRPa, a signal regulatory protein, during responses to ESAT-6 and CFP-10 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The proteins help the bacillus escape the cell compartments meant to digest it.

SIRPa-positive cells feature in the adaptive response to those mycobacterial proteins. Bovine tuberculosis, caused by a close relative, frames part of the work. Understanding which cells answer the antigens aids vaccine and diagnostic design. The antigens are already used in TB blood tests.
plos-pone-0006514:
Weihong Pan and colleagues redirected a virus toward cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Re-engineering the tropism of viruses, what cells they infect, is an attractive strategy for targeting cancer. The Ras signaling pathway is a central hub for a variety of signals, and it is often overactive in tumors. The team utilized Ras signaling to direct selective replication of herpes simplex virus-1.

A virus that replicates only where Ras is overactive would multiply in tumor cells and spare healthy ones. That selectivity is the core challenge of oncolytic virus therapy. Their approach uses the cancer's own signaling flaw as the trigger. It is a step toward smarter virus-based treatments.
plos-pone-0006614:
Christopher Carr and Jeremy McGee studied walking in space suits in PLOS ONE in 2009. How space suits affect the preferred walk-run transition is an open question with relevance to human biomechanics and planetary extravehicular activity. Walking and running cost different amounts of energy, and people switch gaits at a characteristic speed. A stiff suit changes that calculus.

They propose the Apollo number, a measure capturing suit self-support and its effect on the walk-run transition. Apollo astronauts famously loped on the Moon. A predictive number helps design suits and plan surface missions. The study turns mission anecdotes into biomechanics.
plos-pone-0006714:
Arnaud Saimpont, Thierry Pozzo, and Charalambos Papaxanthis tested mental rotation of hands in younger and older adults in PLOS ONE in 2009. Normal aging changes both movement and thinking. Less was known about how aging affects imagining an action. Mental rotation of a hand picture taps that imagination quietly. Twenty young adults and nineteen older adults took part.

Participants judged left and right hands shown at different angles. Performance differences revealed how aging alters implicit motor imagery. Imagined movement shares machinery with real movement. Declines here can hint at wider motor planning problems. The results help separate normal aging from early disease in action simulation.
plos-pone-0006814:
Peter J. M. Van Haastert and Leonard Bosgraaf studied how amoeboid cells search for food in PLOS ONE in 2009. Search strategies decide success in patchy environments. Some animals use special random walks with occasional long runs. Others keep moving in a preferred direction. Starving cells face the same strategic problem at microscopic scale.

Starvation changed the cells' movement pattern. It induced an extension of run lengths, making searches wider. Longer runs help leave exhausted areas for fresh ground. The strategy mirrors optimal foraging ideas from animal ecology. It shows search rules can be tuned by hunger itself, even without a brain.
plos-pone-0006914:
James C. Johnston and colleagues pooled world data on treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in PLOS ONE in 2009. Outcomes for this disease are generally poor. Drug-sensitive tuberculosis cures far more reliably. The authors sought overall outcome estimates across studies. They also hunted risk factors tied to poor outcomes.

Their systematic review and meta-analysis combined many treatment cohorts. Pooling clarifies success, failure, and death rates honestly. Risk factors point to patients needing extra support. Programs can use the numbers to set realistic targets. The synthesis is a reference for a disease where every percentage point matters.
plos-pone-0007014:
Bernhard Englitz, Sandra Tolnai, Marei Typlt, and colleagues tested a giant hearing synapse in PLOS ONE in 2009. The synapses of Held are huge nerve junctions in the auditory pathway. They support faithful, rapid hearing signals. They also serve as a model for central synapses in general. Whether their signals can fail was an open question.

The team recorded these synapses in living animals during sound stimulation. That in vivo test is stricter than work in brain slices. Reliability here underpins the timing precision hearing needs. The results help define the limits of even the strongest synapses.
plos-pone-0007114:
Ammar Al-Chalabi, Alexandra Dürr, Nicholas Wood, and colleagues studied a rare brain disease's genetics in PLOS ONE in 2009. Multiple system atrophy is a progressive disorder of movement and body control. It mixes parkinsonism, balance problems, and autonomic failure. Its cause is obscure, but its hallmark is clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein in support cells.

The team tested variants of the alpha-synuclein gene, SNCA. Variants were associated with the disease. A link to the very protein that clumps is a strong lead. It suggests the gene helps set risk, not just supply the raw material of the clumps.
plos-pone-0007214:
Sabyasachi Halder, Masanao Murakami, Subhash C. Verma, and colleagues built a tool to watch early Epstein-Barr virus infection in 2009. The virus is closely linked to many human cancers. Studying its first steps inside cells could reveal weak points for treatment or prevention.

The team made a self-recombining bacterial artificial chromosome carrying the viral genome. They use it to monitor early cellular and viral events in primary B cells. Their PLOS ONE paper describes the system and its use. Virologists get a controlled way to follow infection from its first hours.
plos-pone-0007314:
Cheng-Han Lee, Subbaya Subramanian, Andrew H. Beck, and colleagues profiled microRNAs in ovarian cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. MicroRNAs are tiny non-coding RNAs that block translation of target messages. They have been implicated in the development of many human cancers, including ovarian malignancies in several studies.

High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma is the most common and lethal ovarian cancer subtype. It can occur in women carrying BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, or without them. The authors profile microRNAs in both groups. Their comparison asks whether inherited mutation status leaves a distinct microRNA signature in tumors.
plos-pone-0007414:
Joachim Lange, Marc de Lussanet, Simone Kuhlmann, and colleagues tested motion perception in people who cannot recognize faces in 2009. Prosopagnosia is a deficit in recognizing people from their faces. Congenital prosopagnosia is not caused by a brain lesion and has presumably been present since early childhood in affected people.

Face recognition might share machinery with biological motion perception, the ability to read movement of living beings. The authors test that perception in congenital prosopagnosia. They report impairments of biological motion perception. Their finding suggests the condition reaches beyond faces into wider social perception.
plos-pone-0007514:
Guillaume Jacquot and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Vpr, a multi-purpose protein of HIV-1. Vpr shows many functions in laboratory tests, but which of them matter during real infection is less clear. The team characterized Vpr variants taken from two patients. One patient's disease progressed rapidly, while the other controlled the virus for years. Two single-letter changes, Q65R and R77Q, drew their focus.

The variants behaved differently in functional tests. Those small substitutions changed what Vpr could do. That suggests the protein's fine details help shape how infection unfolds in a person. Comparing natural variants is a way to let the virus reveal its own priorities. The work connects laboratory functions to clinical courses. It may help explain why HIV progresses at such different speeds in different people.
plos-pone-0007614:
Xiao-Juan Jiang and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a family of brain-wiring genes in a reptile. Protocadherins are adhesion molecules found mostly in the nervous system. They are thought to help establish the complex neural network during development. Their genes sit in a distinctive cluster in vertebrate genomes. The team identified and analyzed that whole cluster in the green anole lizard, then compared it across vertebrates.

The lizard's set fills a missing branch in the family's story. Comparing reptile, bird, and mammal clusters shows which genes were gained, lost, or kept. Adhesion molecules with many variants may give each neuron a surface identity. Evolution's handling of the cluster hints at how that identity system grew. The study is comparative genomics aimed at the wiring of brains.
plos-pone-0007714:
Gisella Puga Yung and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns Crohn's disease in children, a long-term gut inflammation. The disease is thought to arise when the immune system reacts wrongly to gut microbes. Heat shock proteins are among the targets it may attack.

The authors found that T cells react to small pieces of heat shock proteins. Those reactions add to the autoimmune inflammation in young patients. Pinpointing such targets, called epitopes, helps explain why the gut stays inflamed. It may also guide gentler treatments that calm only the harmful response.
plos-pone-0007814:
Tammy-Claire Troy and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies skin barrier failure in engineered mice. Healthy skin blocks infection, water loss, ultraviolet light and temperature swings. That barrier weakens as skin ages, for reasons not fully known.

The team altered a protein called claudin 6 in the mice's outer skin. The mutant protein lacks its tail end. The mice developed dermatitis and barrier problems like those of aging. Their skin offers a model for studying how the barrier breaks down. It may also help test creams or drugs that restore it.
plos-pone-0007914:
Irene De Biase and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explains one layer of gene silencing in Friedreich ataxia. More than fifteen inherited diseases come from repeated DNA letters expanding. In this disease, a GAA repeat in the FXN gene grows too long in both copies.

The expanded repeat cuts the gene's transcription, starving cells of its protein. The authors link the silencing to loss of CTCF, a protein that binds DNA at a marker sequence. Antisense transcription across the region also plays a part. The findings suggest routes to switch the gene back on.
plos-pone-0008014:
Payel Bhanja and colleagues tested a gut growth factor against radiation harm in mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. Hard radiation kills the gut's lining cells and the cells that renew them. The result is diarrhea, fluid loss, infection, and often death.

The factor, R-spondin1, feeds the gut's own stem cells. Mice given it kept more of their gut lining and lived through doses that killed untreated mice. A shield built on the body's own repair crew could serve after accidents or attack, and perhaps ease cancer radiation care as well.
plos-pone-0008114:
Anfumbom Kfutwah and colleagues studied the placenta's signal mix in Cameroonian mothers with HIV and malaria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Placental cytokines, small signal proteins, keep pregnancy steady and shield the unborn child. Both infections were already suspected of stirring that mix.

In women carrying both infections, malaria measurably threw the signal mix off balance. A skewed mix can weaken the placenta's guard and harm birth outcomes. The result helps explain why mothers facing both ills fare worse, and it argues for malaria protection as part of HIV pregnancy care.
plos-pone-0008214:
Diana B. Peckys and colleagues presented a microscopy method in PLOS ONE in 2009 for imaging whole cells. Scientists need nanoscale views to see single proteins at work. They also need them to watch nanomaterials interact with living systems. The team imaged whole fixed cells while the cells sat in liquid. They used a scanning transmission electron microscope for the job.

A liquid enclosure kept the cells wet inside the microscope. That is hard, because electron microscopes normally require a vacuum. Imaging cells in a near natural state preserves fine detail. The method opens new ways to study cell structure at very small scales.
plos-pone-0008314:
Richard T. Frank and colleagues used stem cells to carry cancer drugs in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Monoclonal antibodies have become tools for cancer therapy. Their large size limits how well they penetrate solid tumors. It also blocks them from crossing into the brain. A delivery vehicle that homes to tumors could solve both problems.

Neural stem cells naturally migrate toward tumors. The team used them as a platform to deliver therapeutic antibodies. Tumor-specific delivery would concentrate treatment where it is needed. It could also reduce side effects elsewhere in the body.
plos-pone-0008414:
Nargis Nasrin and colleagues studied an enzyme partnership in cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. SIRT1 is a deacetylase that regulates many pathways, including stress protection. It acts on substrates such as histones, FOXOs, PGC-1 alpha, and p53. Those actions lead to cellular protection against damage. The team identified a functional interaction involving the kinase JNK1.

JNK1 phosphorylates SIRT1 and promotes its enzymatic activity. A stress kinase thus switches on a stress protector. That pairing helps cells coordinate their defense programs. It adds a control point to pathways tied to aging and survival.
plos-pone-0008514:
Joao Dias and co-authors solve a tick protein structure in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Chemokines are signals that guide inflammatory cells to tissues. They act through receptors on cell surfaces. Blocking a chemokine and its receptor can reduce inflammation. Ticks make a protein called Evasin-1 that soaks up chemokines. It keeps tick bites from provoking a strong host response. The team crystallize Evasin-1 bound to the chemokine CCL3.

Their crystal structure shows exactly how Evasin-1 sequesters CCL3. That atomic view explains its tight and selective binding. It offers a template for designing anti-inflammatory drugs. Nature's own blocker becomes a blueprint for medicine.
plos-pone-0008614:
Michael Berney and co-authors study energy flexibility in mycobacteria in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mycobacteria are obligate aerobes that require oxygen for growth. Paradoxically, they can survive and metabolize under hypoxia, or low oxygen. The mechanisms behind this metabolic plasticity were unknown. That survival lets tuberculosis germs persist in low-oxygen lung lesions. The team report on adaptation of Mycobacterium to starvation and hypoxia together.

They find unique flexibility in energy metabolism under those stresses. The germ rewires how it generates ATP when oxygen and food are scarce. That flexibility explains its legendary persistence in hosts. It also exposes metabolic weaknesses that drugs might exploit.
plos-pone-0008714:
Patrick Ott, Anne Hamilton, Amanda Jones, and colleagues ran a phase II trial of a cancer drug. Their report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drug, ixabepilone, steadies the cell's inner scaffolding so cancer cells cannot divide well. Lab work had hinted it might help against melanoma that has spread. Phase II trials test whether such hints hold in patients.

Patients with metastatic melanoma received the drug at several centers. The team tracked tumor shrinkage and side effects. Even a modest response can matter when few options remain. The results help decide whether bigger trials of this drug are worthwhile.
plos-pone-0008814:
Rachel Sarig, Ora Fuchs, Lilach Tencer, and colleagues tested whether committed muscle cells can change identity. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells are usually thought locked into their chosen fate. Reports of fate switching often turn out to involve cell fusion instead. Cloned myogenic cells, with known single-cell origins, offered a rigorous test. Placing them in a nerve-friendly setting posed the challenge.

Inside living hosts, the muscle clones became neuron-like cells. Careful checks ruled out fusion as the explanation. Genuine reprogramming in the body raises hopes for repair therapies. It also reopens basic questions about how fixed cell identity really is.
plos-pone-0008914:
Michael Boivin, Paul Bangirana, and Rebecca Smith compared two kinds of working memory in African schoolchildren. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Working memory holds sights and sounds briefly while the mind works. Earlier work in Congo found the two spans independent in children. American and Lao children, by contrast, showed linked spans when older. Culture and schooling may shape that link. Children in Senegal and Uganda formed the new test groups.

Tests measured visual-spatial and auditory-verbal spans side by side. How the spans related bore on universal claims about memory development. Local data keep child psychology honest about its sample base. Most classic studies draw on a narrow slice of the world's children.
plos-pone-0009014:
Coralie Spiegelhalter and co-authors joined live filming of cells with freeze-frame electron pictures, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cell biologists need both movies of living cells and fine structural detail. Light microscopes give the movies; electron microscopes give the detail. Matching the same moment across both views is technically hard.

Their method films cells, then freezes them under high pressure at a chosen instant. The frozen cells then go to electron microscopy for three-dimensional structure. Events caught live can be inspected at near-atomic neatness afterwards. The pipeline turns a passing moment in a cell's life into a lasting specimen.
plos-pone-0009114:
Bryan Clarkson, Wendy Gilbert, and Jennifer Doudna asked whether yeast's two protein-making starters can cover for each other, in PLOS ONE in 2010. eIF4G is a scaffold that gathers an RNA message for translation. It reads tags at both ends of the message to recruit the ribosome. Many eukaryotes carry several versions of this factor.

Baker's yeast has two eIF4G isoforms with partly shared duties. The team tested how much their functions overlap. Each could substitute for the other across much of the workload. Backup copies like these keep protein production running when one fails.
plos-pone-0009214:
Antoine Nougairède and colleagues published this flu surveillance report in PLOS ONE in 2010. It covers the first months of the 2009 swine flu pandemic in south-eastern France. The new virus, influenza A H1N1sw, was first detected in France in April 2009. Reference labs across the French Defence Zones ran the testing.

The authors report virus test results from the public hospital labs of the region, from April through August 2009. Their data trace how the new flu arrived and spread during its first season. Such regional records show how a pandemic unfolds on the ground. They also document how lab surveillance worked while the outbreak was still new.
plos-pone-0009314:
Elias César Araujo de Carvalho and co-authors published this data sharing paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Research on disease patterns and clinical care produces valuable data sets. Yet sharing between research groups is poor at best. That hoarding slows science and wastes the effort of the patients and communities who supplied the data.

The authors describe a web application built to share information about such data sets. They also present the policy model that governs who may see what. Describing a data set's contents, without exposing private records, makes collaboration easier. The paper offers a working pattern for opening research data safely.
plos-pone-0009414:
Andreas Androutsellis-Theotokis and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Growing one pure cell type from the adult brain is valuable for therapy and drug hunting. The adult brain does hold neural stem cells, in zones that make neurons and in zones that do not. Coaxing them to grow in dishes was the challenge.

The team found that angiogenic factors, signals that grow blood vessels, stimulate those stem cells. Under their influence, adult neural stem cells grew more readily. The overlap between vessel growth and nerve growth hints the two systems share a niche. It also gives labs a practical lever for expanding cells needed in research.
plos-pone-0009514:
Alex Boyko and co-authors asked whether plants pass stress memory to offspring in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some effects of the environment can last into the next generation without DNA changes. The team worked with Arabidopsis, a small plant used in labs worldwide. Parents were exposed to stress, and their offspring were tested. The team also used plants that lack key tools for chemical DNA tags.

Offspring of stressed parents adapted better to the same stress. That gain vanished when DNA methylation or Dicer-like proteins were missing. So the memory depends on those tools. The result matters for farming, since crops face more stress as the climate shifts.
plos-pone-0009614:
Ningxin Zhang and co-authors studied a fast changing gene in a yeast in PLOS ONE in 2010. Candida albicans is a yeast that can infect people. Some of its genes mutate very fast, which constantly creates new variants. The gene PNG2 is one of those high change genes. The team asked whether the yeast's wider genetic background shapes which PNG2 variants win out.

They found that background does steer which alleles are selected. So rapid change does not play out the same in every strain. That matters for how the yeast adapts and dodges immunity. Rules like these could help predict how this pathogen evolves during long infections.
plos-pone-0009714:
Brain disorders often share symptoms, from anxiety to psychosis, across different diagnoses. Anthony Deo and colleagues proposed a new way to trace those symptoms back to genes. Their analytical framework appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Behavioral symptoms are often harder to map than the diseases themselves.

The method dissects genetic architecture, the pattern of gene effects behind a trait. It aims to link gene patterns with behavioral symptoms seen in neuropsychiatric disorders. A shared framework could show which symptoms share genetic roots. That would help researchers group patients by biology rather than labels alone.
plos-pone-0009814:
Depo-Provera is a widely used hormone-based contraceptive shot. Meritxell Genescà and colleagues asked whether it weakens vaccine protection against SIV in female monkeys. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The monkeys had been immunized with an attenuated AIDS virus.

Attenuated means the vaccine virus was weakened so it could protect without causing disease. After treatment, the monkeys still held protection from an intravenous SIV challenge. That answer matters because contraceptive use is common where HIV risk is high. A vaccine that fails alongside contraception would be far less useful.
plos-pone-0009914:
Systematic reviews gather all evidence on a medical question, but evidence keeps growing. Chantelle Garritty and colleagues surveyed how review teams around the world keep reviews updated. Their international survey appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Reviews guide treatment choices for millions of patients.

Updating a review means folding new studies into old conclusions. The survey asked teams when they update, how, and what blocks them. Outdated reviews can mislead doctors who trust them as current. The answers point to habits the whole field could adopt. The survey reached teams on several continents.
plos-pone-0010014:
Derya Shimshek, Matthias Mueller, Christoph Wiessner, and co-workers tested a hoped-for Parkinson's treatment in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. In Parkinson's disease, a protein called alpha-synuclein folds badly and clumps in the brain. Heat-shock proteins help refold proteins or clear them away, so they looked like a natural way to cut that clump load.

The team raised levels of the chaperone HSP70 in a mouse model of alpha-synuclein disease. Their title gives the plain result: HSP70 was not beneficial there. A clear negative finding like that saves other groups time and steers the search toward other routes.
plos-pone-0010214:
The authors were Carinne Piekema, Mark Rijpkema, Guillén Fernández, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used brain scans to separate two kinds of memory binding. Working memory must bind features into single items and items into sets. A brain region called the medial temporal lobe was thought to maintain those bound representations while we hold them in mind.

Building on earlier scan work, the team dissociated the brain activity for each binding type. Intra-item binding links features of one object, while inter-item binding links objects together. Showing separate neural support clarifies how short-term memory builds a coherent scene.
plos-pone-0010314:
The authors were Tanja Woyke, Damon Tighe, Konstantinos Mavromatis, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study sequenced a whole genome from one bacterial cell. Most finished microbial genomes came from bacteria grown in culture. Yet the vast majority of microbes refuse to grow in laboratories. Their genomes stayed out of reach for complete sequencing with standard methods.

Working from a single cell, the team recovered one complete genome. That proof opens the uncultured majority of microbial life to full genome study. Cataloging those hidden genomes can reshape understanding of ecosystems and evolution.
plos-pone-0010414:
Teresa Rodríguez-Calvo and co-workers designed a new kind of vaccine from broken virus genomes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vaccines against fast-changing RNA viruses are hard to build. Foot-and-mouth disease, a livestock scourge, shows the problem well. The standard vaccine uses whole virus killed by chemicals. It works, but production carries risks and costs. The authors tried genomes that are defective on purpose.
