Their design mixes features of live-weakened and killed vaccines. A defective genome can enter cells and stir immunity without spreading disease. That middle path could be safer to make and store. Livestock vaccines protect food supplies and farm incomes, not just animals. A better design would matter across the farming world.
plos-pone-0010514:
Gaya Hettiarachchi and colleagues tested pumpkin-shaped molecules as drug carriers in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some ring-shaped molecules can hold a drug inside, like tiny buckets. One such family is already used in many medicines. A rival family grips its cargo even more tightly. Before doctors could use it, its safety had to be checked. The team ran safety and delivery tests on these carriers.

Tight gripping can help drugs that barely dissolve in water reach the body. Safety data decide whether that promise can leave the lab. These carriers are quiet workhorses of modern drug making. Comparing the families side by side helps makers choose well. The study adds the safety side of the ledger for the newer family. It also shows where the carriers might work best.
plos-pone-0010614:
Svitlana Garbuzova-Davis and colleagues looked for vessel damage in ALS, in PLOS ONE in 2010. ALS slowly kills the nerve cells that control muscles. Animal work had suggested the barrier around the brain and spinal cord breaks down during the disease.

The team counted vessel-lining cells circulating in patients' blood. Counts were lower in ALS patients than in healthy controls. Fewer free cells fit with the idea that vessel walls are injured or repairing poorly. The finding widens ALS research beyond nerve cells and points to blood vessels as part of the story.
plos-pone-0010714:
Tarek Elsaba and colleagues tested a marker claim about colon cancer stem cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A surface protein called CD133 was said to mark the stem-like cells that seed tumors. Reports disagreed sharply on how useful the marker really is.

The team sorted colon cancer cells by whether they carried CD133. Cells with the marker formed colonies more readily and moved more than cells without it. Those two traits fit a more aggressive cell type. The marker's value in this cancer looks real but partial: it flags behavior worth targeting without capturing the whole stem cell story.
plos-pone-0010814:
Natalia Pitala and colleagues weighed growth against immune defense in wild birds, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Young animals must split limited food between growing and fighting infection. Field studies often count only the cost of immunity. Its benefit shows only when parasites are actually common, so the team varied parasite exposure directly.

Nests were treated to raise or lower the load of biting ectoparasites. Chicks shifted spending between growth and defense as the load changed. Where parasites were rare, heavy defense wasted resources. Where they were common, defense paid for itself. The study gives the trade-off real numbers from the wild, where the balance evolved.
plos-pone-0010914:
Jean-Edouard Ombetta, Natacha Thelier, Chang Zhi Dong and co-authors published this drug design study in PLOS ONE in 2010. An enzyme called group IIA phospholipase A2 helps produce prostaglandin E2, a major driver of pain and swelling in rheumatic joint disease. Blocking that enzyme is a long-standing goal, and the team used computer modeling to improve a known blocker.

They designed seven new variants of a starting compound, simulated how each would grip the enzyme, and then synthesized and tested them. The modeling rankings held up in lab assays, and one variant, C8, proved the strongest blocker of the set. It also suppressed prostaglandin release from joint cartilage cells. Ombetta and colleagues show a full design loop, from screen to cell, for a possible new class of anti-inflammatory drugs.
plos-pone-0011014:
Yonghe Li, Wenyan Lu, Taj King and co-authors published this cell signaling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Wnt signals guide development and are restrained by Dkk1, a secreted blocker that grabs the Wnt co-receptor LRP6. Earlier reports said Dkk1 drags LRP6 inside the cell for destruction, at least when a partner receptor is present, but this team observed the opposite.

Adding Dkk1 made LRP6 accumulate, both at the cell surface and in internal compartments, and extended the receptor's life, even as Wnt signaling itself was inhibited. Adding the partner receptor Kremen2 erased that accumulation effect. Li and colleagues show the blocker's effect on its target depends on which partner proteins are around. Such context effects matter because Wnt blockers are being explored as drugs for cancer and bone disease.
plos-pone-0011114:
Ushiki, Kizaka-Kondoh, Ashihara and colleagues reported transplant imaging in PLOS ONE in 2010. After a bone marrow transplant, donor cells must travel to and settle in the marrow. The team wanted a gentle way to watch that homing soon after transplant, without harming tissue.

Using light based imaging that works through the body, they tracked donor cells as they settled. Seeing homing directly could warn doctors early when a graft is failing to take hold. It also helps researchers test ways to improve settling. Better settling means faster recovery of blood and immune function for transplant patients.
plos-pone-0011214:
Terao, Watanabe, Yagi and colleagues tested moving eyes and color in PLOS ONE in 2010. When eyes smoothly follow a moving target, vision does not simply blur. The team asked whether that smooth pursuit changes how finely people can judge color changes over time.

Pursuit eye movements improved the time resolution of color perception in their tests. Motion and color, long studied apart, turn out to interact. That interplay matters for basic vision science. It also informs display design, where screens must match how the eye truly samples a moving colored world.
plos-pone-0011314:
Hurt, Torrone, Green and colleagues tracked drug use and HIV in North Carolina for PLOS ONE in 2010. They studied young men newly diagnosed with HIV between 2000 and 2005. Records let them measure how many reported methamphetamine use around the time of diagnosis.

Stimulant use shadowed a notable share of new cases in this group. That behavioral overlap points to where prevention can do most good. Programs that address drug use and sexual risk together may reach these young men better than separate efforts. The study gives HIV prevention a defined, at risk population in the state.
plos-pone-0011414:
Sebastian Padayatty and colleagues surveyed alternative medicine practitioners in 2010 about giving vitamin C by intravenous drip. High-dose vitamin C through a vein is offered for cancer and other conditions, despite thin evidence and little tracking of harm. Because the practice sits outside standard medicine, no registry recorded how it was used or what went wrong.

The survey asked practitioners how they prepare and dose the vitamin and what adverse effects they had seen in patients. Gathering those reports maps real-world habits and harms that trials had missed. Patients considering the therapy gain a clearer picture of its risks, and regulators gain data where before there were only claims. The study is a model for studying popular alternative treatments honestly: ask the practitioners, record the harms, and publish both.
plos-pone-0011514:
Noelia Valbuena and Sergio Moreno showed in 2010 how fission yeast merges two keep-off signals into one decisive stop. Fission yeast mate and enter meiosis only when food is scarce, and two nutrient-sensing pathways, TOR and PKA, normally block mating in good times. The puzzle was whether the two blocks are independent backups or parts of one mechanism.

Both pathways proved to converge on a single protein, the Ste11 transcription factor, which is the switch that turns on mating genes. Together they hold that switch off more firmly than either could alone. Convergence of this kind is an elegant design: several senses of plenty vote on one switch, so a single faulty sensor cannot trigger mating by mistake. The study explains, in one clean circuit, how cells make a life-or-death decision robust.
plos-pone-0011614:
Benoit Guénard and Robert Dunn reported a hidden ant invasion in eastern North American forests, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Introduced ants threaten native wildlife in many places, yet few foreign species manage to invade cool temperate forests. One ant long treated as a normal forest resident turns out to be something else.

Careful identification showed the ant is an introduced species that arrived long ago and spread widely unnoticed. Because it is now abundant, its effects on forest floors, seeds and other insects may be broad. The case warns that other supposed natives may also be overlooked invaders.
plos-pone-0011714:
Mounia Alaoui-El-Azher and co-authors traced how a gum germ's toxin kills mouth lining cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The toxin, called CDT, comes from the oral germ Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans. It halts the cell cycle and triggers set cell death in several cell types.

With chemical blockers and gene silencing in human gum cells, the team mapped the death route step by step. It runs through the ATM and checkpoint kinase 2 pathway, the cell's DNA damage alarm. Charting each step shows how this mouth poison does its work, and where a drug might cut in.
plos-pone-0011814:
Aaron White and co-authors tied a broad fuel shift to Salmonella group behaviour, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Germs can build complex group patterns set by timed waves of gene use, most often under one master control path. For group builds such as biofilms, the switches that start the process were partly known.

Their work links a sweeping change in fuel use to Salmonella's shift into group life. As the germs band together, their whole energy plan is recast. That fuel switch shows the power plan behind biofilm cities, which are famed for being hard to treat with drugs.
plos-pone-0012014:
Glenda Canderan and colleagues presented in 2010 a recipe for growing a patient's own tumor-fighting T cells in the lab. Expanding killer CD8 T cells that recognize a patient's own non-small cell lung cancer is a goal of tumor immunology, both for research and for therapy. The hard part is doing it efficiently and keeping the cells specific.

Their strategy induces and maintains such T cells in vitro, using the patient's own tumor as the target reference. A dependable recipe matters because cell therapy fails when the product cannot be made the same way twice. Lung cancer is common and often drug-resistant, so a workable autologous cell approach has wide relevance.
plos-pone-0012114:
John Fieberg, Kyle Shertzer, Paul Conn, and co-authors built a model of Minnesota's black bear population for PLOS ONE in 2010. Counting wild bears directly is costly and hard, but records from hunted bears, such as age and sex, are easy to gather. The team combined those harvest records with other data in one model of the whole population.

A single model that uses every data source at once gives a clearer picture than each source read alone. It can estimate how many bears there are and how fast the population is changing. Wildlife managers can then set hunting limits and watch trends with more confidence, using data they already collect each year.
plos-pone-0012214:
Enrico De Franchi, Claire Schalon, Mirko Messa, and co-authors predicted side targets of kinase-blocking drugs by computer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Kinases are switch enzymes that many modern cancer drugs aim to block, but a drug shaped for one often fits others, causing surprise side effects. Their method compares the three-dimensional pockets where drugs bind, measuring how similar one kinase's pocket is to another's.

Similar pockets predict cross-reactions, and the team followed their predictions by testing drugs against an unexpected target, a scaffold protein in nerve endings. Catching off-target binding on a computer, before patients do, is cheaper and safer. The approach can also rescue shelved drugs by revealing new uses.
plos-pone-0012314:
Raúl Guantes, Javier Estrada, and Juan Poyatos analyzed signal detection by genetic circuits in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells run small gene circuits that detect signals. Some read a signal's size. Others read how fast it pulses. All of them must work amid molecular noise. That noise is the random jitter of small numbers of molecules. The authors asked what trade-offs such detection imposes. They also asked how noise limits it.

Their study of a simple circuit shows where two goals pull apart. Those goals are sensitivity and reliability. People who build cell sensors need these limits before they build. The work also explains why natural circuits take the shapes they do. Evolution had to pay the same trade-offs.
plos-pone-0012414:
Noha Youssef, M. Couger and Mostafa Elshahed surveyed microbes at an Oklahoma sulfur spring in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Zodletone Spring hosts a rich mix of bacteria in sharp chemical layers. Deep DNA sequencing now reads far more species than older surveys, letting the team ask how much of the local variety comes from rare species found only in one layer.

Most of the fine-scale variety came from the rare biosphere, species present at very low numbers. Each layer kept its own rare cast. The result warns that shallow sampling misses most diversity and shows why rare microbes, though scarce, may hold unique chemistry worth protecting and studying.
plos-pone-0012514:
Thomas Fischer, Robert Langner, Kersten Diers and colleagues tracked brain waves while people waited for a signal, in a 2010 PLOS ONE EEG study. When a warning cue promises a coming event, the scalp EEG shows a slow negative drift called the contingent negative variation. Its early part reflects anticipation, and faster beta waves ride alongside it.

The team mapped where and when beta activity changed during that early anticipation phase. The pattern locates the brain systems that prepare action before events happen. Anticipation faults appear in conditions from ADHD to Parkinson's disease, so a fine time-space map of normal anticipation is useful reference data.
plos-pone-0012614:
Leimu and Fischer crossed plants from separate populations and watched what happened to their defences. Mixing populations can add fresh genetic variety, which often helps a group survive. It can also backfire, a problem called outbreeding depression, when local traits no longer fit together.

Their 2010 study went beyond plant growth and checked how the crosses handled insect attack and damage. Outbreeding changed both resistance and tolerance, the two ways plants cope with being eaten. The results warn conservation workers that mixing plant populations alters more than size or seed count.
plos-pone-0012714:
Miquel, Peyretaillade, Claret and co-authors published the full genome of a Crohn's disease linked E coli strain. The strain, LF82, clings to and invades gut cells and is found in the ileum of many Crohn's patients. Their 2010 paper reads its complete DNA, letter by letter.

A full genome lets researchers list every tool the strain carries for sticking, invading and surviving inside cells. Comparing it with harmless gut E coli shows which parts are unusual. That inventory guides the search for what makes this strain a Crohn's partner.  The genome is now public for any group to mine.
plos-pone-0012814:
Gessmann, Kourtis, Petratos and co-authors modelled the touch-sensing ion channels found across animals. The DEG/ENaC family of channel proteins serves roles from salt balance to the sense of touch. Their members appear in all animal groups, humans included, yet their detailed shapes long stayed unclear.

Their 2010 modelling study set out the shared structural features of these channels and how those features fit their jobs. A channel that opens under pressure is the basis of touch itself. Models like theirs guide the hunt for drugs acting on pain and blood pressure.
plos-pone-0330014:
Mirte Boelens and colleagues refined a questionnaire that measures health broadly, not just the absence of disease. They asked the people who would use and answer it. Their 2026 study convened nine focus groups and an expert interview. Seventy-six participants spanned healthcare, welfare, policy, and research. Citizens, including those on low incomes, took part too. All critiqued the thirty-two-item instrument their team had built earlier.

Items were cut, merged, and added, landing at twenty-eight. Participants pushed for questions about felt experience, like feeling happy or healthy. They pushed against wording that smuggles in judgments. Items on exclusion and belonging sparked genuine disagreement, settled by a preset decision rule. The revised questionnaire is offered for use across health, welfare, and policy settings.
plos-pone-0331514:
Takakura and colleagues, in a 2026 study in Japan, compare quitting smoking by telemedicine against doing it face to face in clinics. Clinic programs work but demand repeated trips, which many smokers find bothersome. The online program ran four video sessions over eight weeks with drug support, and followed patients for a year.

Thousands of smokers applied online, and a large group was analyzed against clinic patients drawn from a health ministry database. The share who finished treatment was far higher online than in the clinic comparison. Long-term abstinence a year later is the paper's headline measure, set against the burden of travel. The authors frame telemedicine as a way to keep smokers in treatment long enough for the drugs and coaching to work. They note the comparison is retrospective, so the groups were not assigned at random.
plos-pone-0339014:
Yan Zhang and co-authors studied a chemical arms race in ginger fields, where growing ginger year after year breeds a devastating wilt fungus. Ginger roots release natural compounds, called autotoxins, that slow the crop itself, and the team asked what those same compounds do to the fungus. Their 2026 lab study exposed the pathogen to four ginger autotoxins and tracked its growth, reproduction, and attack tools.

Each compound hit the fungus differently. One strongly curbed growth and spore sprouting yet provoked the fungus to make more wall-chewing enzymes and toxins. Another suppressed nearly everything, including toxin genes. In several cases the fungus answered chemical pressure by raising its own weapons. The authors describe a two-way interaction in which plant defenses and pathogen counterattacks shape the disease.
plos-pone-0339114:
Mohammad Abuawad and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One study of meningioma in Palestine. Meningioma is the most common primary brain tumor. The team worked from records at Al-Makassed Hospital. That hospital is the country's main referral center for brain surgery. They profiled just over two hundred confirmed cases from 2018 to 2023. They logged age, sex, tumor grade, symptoms, and care.

The typical patient was about fifty-one years old. Women were affected at roughly twice the male rate. The authors stress that their rate estimate is a floor, not a true population rate. Most tumors were the lowest grade. Higher grades were more common in men. Local nerve symptoms were the usual first complaint. Nearly all patients were treated with surgery alone. The authors call for registry-style research to firm up the picture.
plos-pone-0342114:
Victoria Miller and co-authors reviewed court cases about retinoblastoma, a childhood eye cancer, in work published in 2026. Late diagnosis can cost a child an eye or worse, and the team asked what goes wrong often enough to end in malpractice suits.

A legal database search found thirteen cases covering fourteen children, most of them girls, and all alive at trial. Several suits claimed doctors failed to warn parents about inherited risk, or missed signs. Specialties named ranged from eye doctors to pregnancy care. Though the set is small, it shows families and courts focus on warning, screening, and fast referral.
plos-pone-0347014:
Zhenyao Jin and Lei Yang present a system that turns ordinary images into consistent cartoon scenes, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Automated cartoon making often drifts in style from frame to frame or warps shapes, which limits its use in film and games. Their model joins an improved adversarial network, where two programs compete to sharpen output, with a retention network that holds onto structure across the image.

Extra parts handle style variety, judging, and geometric consistency, including a module that keeps surfaces from bending wrongly. Tested on two public scene datasets against three mainstream rivals, the model scored well on image quality, structure preservation, speed, and modest memory use. Its cartoon output stayed close to the original layout. The authors pitch it as a cheaper automated route for animation, game art, and digital content production.
plos-pone-0347214:
Iqra Shafique led a team of eight authors on this 2026 lab study attacking drug-resistant typhoid bacteria without antibiotics. Resistant Salmonella typhi strains pump drugs back out of their cells and form protective films. The team tested two plant compounds, schisandrins from a vine, against resistant and sensitive clinical strains.

Schisandrin B disrupted bacterial membranes, blocked the pumps, and stopped most film growth in the lab, slowing the bacteria rather than killing them outright. Shafique argues such non-antibiotic helpers could one day restore the power of failing typhoid drugs, pending much more testing.
plos-pone-0348014:
Josna Soyuz and Anish V Cherian led a review of teen suicide research. They focused on a method called psychological autopsy. In it, experts rebuild a young life from records and talks with kin. The aim is to learn what led to the death. The team gathered fifteen such studies. They then drew out the shared themes across them.

Four theme groups came up again and again. The first is the teen's own state: illness of mind, drug use, past self-harm. The second is family strain: sick parents, abuse, neglect. The third is hard life events: school failure, fights, early trauma. The fourth is the world around them: means at hand, media sway, no care near. The team says guard work must act on all four.
plos-pone-0348214:
Qike Fu and colleagues test a malaria drug cousin against diabetic liver damage in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The drug is artemether, kin to the malaria cure artemisinin. Early work hinted it eases high blood sugar. The liver suffers quietly in type 1 diabetes. No targeted treatment exists for that injury.

In diabetic mice, the drug eased liver harm. It also fixed two deeper faults. The power plants inside liver cells kept a healthier shape. The cells' core fuel chemistry ran more smoothly too. These power plants are the mitochondria. The findings rest on animals only. Still, they point to guarding cell power as a path worth testing.
plos-pone-0348414:
Suhyun Hwangbo, Yoojin Choi, and Jae Yong Ryu built prediction models for triple-negative breast cancer, the subtype with the fewest treatment options and the grimmest outlook. Pooling several gene-expression datasets, they searched for a compact set of genes whose activity forecasts survival, aiming to beat the accuracy ceiling that earlier models had hit.

Their nine-gene signature pushed predictive performance above the level previous studies had managed, and it held up when applied to five independent datasets. Most of the nine genes are individually tied to survival in this cancer. The authors propose the panel as a prognostic marker set to guide follow-up and trial design, pending clinical validation.
plos-pone-0348514:
Huifu Li and colleagues asked whether building a digital economy cleans the air in China's in-between places, the cities sitting on provincial borders, which often become pollution havens nobody governs well. Panel data from one hundred and eighty-eight border cities over a decade were used to test the link, and to check whether cleaner air spills across borders into neighbouring regions.

Digital development did improve local air quality, with the strongest gains in poorer, less connected border areas. Benefits also leaked helpfully into adjacent regions rather than merely pushing pollution onto them, the opposite of the haven fear. Two channels did the work: digital tools broke down segmented local markets that shelter dirty industries, and they sharpened environmental monitoring and enforcement. The authors offer the findings to developing countries wrestling with the same border problem.
plos-pone-0348614:
Younes Beniaich and co-workers record sleep and movement in newborn lambs across their first three days and again weeks later. As lambs begin chewing the cud, their digestion matures and their days may reorganize. Their 2026 study fits eight lambs with gentle brain and body recorders for three-day stretches at birth and after cud chewing begins.

Newborns were most active around dawn and dusk and slept in many short bouts, more at night. Weeks later, daytime activity rose and total sleep fell by hours, squeezed by time spent chewing the cud. Wake time itself barely changed. Chewing the cud seems to compete directly with sleep as young ruminants grow, a trade-off farmers and vets rarely count.
plos-pone-0348714:
Xiaomin Liang and colleagues examined how the tiniest pores inside coal govern how easily trapped methane escapes, a question that matters for both gas production and mine safety. Coals of three ranks, from soft lignite to hard anthracite, were measured for pore size, surface, and connections, then watched as they released methane. The team sorted micropores by how they sit: attached to channels, clustered in networks, or isolated.

Micropores supplied nearly all the surface area, and their arrangement changed with rank. Lignite's attached pores let methane slip straight into flow paths, giving the fastest release. Coking coal's tangled clusters slowed diffusion, and anthracite's isolated pores trapped gas worst of all. The authors link pore layout directly to release behaviour, offering guidance for choosing where and how to drain gas before mining.
plos-pone-0348814:
Alejandro Morales-Huitrón and colleagues mapped friendship and hostility among roughly four thousand three hundred students in nine schools in Yucatán, Mexico. From these maps they built two smaller networks: one around students who name many enemies, and one around students who are named as enemies by many others. They then compared the shape of the two networks and how groups formed inside them.

The two networks turned out to overlap heavily, sharing about three fifths of their members, so the same students often appear on both sides of conflict. Girls' networks were generally denser than boys'. The authors connect their measures to roles seen in bullying, and they pin down when these attack and defense networks are defined sharply enough to mean something.
plos-pone-0349014:
Jasmijn E Klapwijk and a large team gave fifty-one medical students a set of imaginary cases from prenatal genome testing, where results during pregnancy often come back uncertain. Students judged how uncertain each result felt, decided whether they would pass it to the expectant parents, and rated their confidence in that choice. Their personal tolerance for uncertainty was also measured.

Students passed on fewer of the highly uncertain results and felt shakier about those decisions, confirming a widely held hunch with real data. Surprisingly, students who personally disliked uncertainty behaved no differently from tolerant peers, and anxiety about parents considering ending a pregnancy did not sway reporting either. The authors say counselling training should prepare clinicians for the discomfort of uncertain results, since instinct alone trims what parents get told.
plos-pone-0349114:
Limin Yu, Zhe Chen, and Zeyu Qin tackle a grading problem: hands-on courses taught through real projects need fair marks, yet judges often disagree and their scores carry doubt. Their framework grades students in stages, moving from a pass check to a score and then a final grade. It uses a maths tool built to hold both a judgement and how reliable that judgement is.

Marks came from classmates, teachers, and industry experts for a class of twenty-four students. The weight of each criterion was set by how much it varied and overlapped with others. Repeated checks suggested the method stays stable under changed assumptions. The authors say it can make project course grading clearer and more open, while noting that wider testing in other courses is still needed.
plos-pone-0349314:
Abdulrahman Alasmari and colleagues tested an alcohol extract of the plant Otostegia fruticosa against aggressive breast cancer cells in the laboratory. Their 2026 study used MDA-MB-231 cells, a standard model of triple-negative breast cancer, a form that is hard to treat. They measured whether the extract could kill the cells or slow their spread.

The extract did kill the cancer cells, largely by raising reactive oxygen species, unstable molecules that damage cell power plants and trigger cell death. Treated cells also moved and invaded less than untreated ones. The work is early and limited to cells in dishes, but it marks the plant as a candidate for further study.
plos-pone-0349414:
Maiya G Block Ngaybe and colleagues interviewed twenty experts and peer leaders in Uganda in March 2024 about HIV prevention choices for groups at highest risk. A long acting injectable prevention drug has been approved but not yet rolled out in Uganda, and a future vaccine may follow. Talks covered current habits and what people would want from injectable options.

Condoms and daily prevention pills were the most mentioned current tools. Barriers named included dosing burden, access, cost, and stigma. Long dosing gaps made injectables attractive, provided supply and privacy hold. Rollout plans that listen to peer leaders first, the authors argue, will decide whether a promising drug is actually used.
plos-pone-0349514:
Karolina Pawłowska-Cyprysiak and colleagues asked what shapes whether people with disabilities in Poland take part in training for computer skills. Their 2026 PLOS One survey gathered answers from about four hundred fifty people with different kinds of disabilities.

One factor stood out sharply. When training looked hard to access, through distance, cost, or rooms and materials that ignore disabled users, the chance of taking part fell by more than seventy percent. Other traits mattered far less by comparison. The authors say the lesson is simple: making courses genuinely reachable does more for equal chances than urging people to sign up.
plos-pone-0349614:
Chao Zhang and colleagues trained an artificial intelligence system to spot stomach cancer that has quietly spread to the abdominal lining, a finding that changes whether surgery makes sense. Standard scans often miss this spread in advanced cancers. The team tested several image-reading networks on pre-surgery CT scans and then added attention modules that teach the network where to look hardest.

The best design, a deep network sharpened by a squeeze-and-excitation module, distinguished spread from no spread with excellent accuracy, and its risk estimates matched real outcomes closely. Decision analysis suggested using it would help more patients than it harmed. The authors recommend that patients the system flags as high risk receive a keyhole inspection before any major operation, sparing others futile surgery.
plos-pone-0350014:
Gustavo A Ballen, Klára Hedvika Mühlová, and Jan Hajič jr. applied tools from evolutionary biology to one of music history's puzzles: recovering the earliest forms of Gregorian chant melodies. Early chant notation does not record pitch precisely, so original melodies must be inferred. Legend credits Pope Gregory the First with receiving the chant from a dove, but the tunes evolved over centuries of singing and copying.

The team first converted family trees of chant versions into timed, directed trees, separating elapsed time from rate of change. They then reconstructed likely ancestral melodies at each branching point. Applied to a Christmas Vespers dataset, the results lined up well with what music experts had rebuilt by hand at Solesmes. The authors see the method as a promising way to trace how culture is transmitted through time.
plos-pone-0350314:
Retraction notice: The PLOS One editors retracted a study claiming that the best stiffness of a three-dimensional gel for keeping cancer stem cells alive depends on the tissue the cancer came from. Editors found multiple figure panels that looked more similar than independent results should, regions within images that appeared discontinuous, and overlap with material published earlier under a restrictive license. The corresponding author attributed the similarities to uniform cell appearance under standardized imaging.

The editors judged the supplied image data incomplete and the explanations insufficient, leaving the reliability of the results in doubt. All authors disagreed with the retraction and stand by their findings, a disagreement the notice records. Because its figures cannot be trusted, the article's claims about matrix stiffness and cancer stem cells should not be relied on.
plos-pone-0350414:
Jean A Hall, Leslie B Hancock, and Elizabeth M Morris fed cats with early kidney disease two special diets to see how the balance of calcium to phosphorus affects blood calcium control. Cats with kidney disease can develop high blood calcium, and diet is a suspected driver. Their 2026 trial rotated nine older cats between a moderate-ratio food and a higher-ratio food, with washout periods between, sampling blood and urine throughout.

Blood calcium stayed within the normal range on both foods, and most calcium-related measures did not differ by diet. The higher-ratio food did lower parathyroid hormone and showed trends toward raising two other markers, all still in normal ranges. The authors conclude that dietary calcium ratio alone is likely not the sole cause of high blood calcium as kidney disease advances, though the shifts they saw deserve further study.
plos-pone-0350514:
Tu Trang and five colleagues ask the staff who used genome-guided tuberculosis treatment what they really thought of it. Their 2026 study sits inside the SMARTT trial. The trial tested whether whole-genome sequencing, translated into drug recommendations, could improve care for rifampicin-resistant TB. Eleven health workers who managed trial patients joined a focus group. Their experiences were sorted by theme, letting patterns emerge from the conversation itself.

The technology mostly won them over. Sequencing simplified drug susceptibility testing and was seen as good for patients. It did not threaten the workers' professional judgement or autonomy. Trust still cracked in places. Slow result turnaround, advice deviating from guidelines, and disagreement between testing methods all hurt confidence. A few patients' poor outcomes lingered in minds. Stock-outs, patchy internet, and training gaps completed the obstacle list. Genomic medicine's promise, the workers suggest, will live or die on logistics.
plos-pone-0350614:
Hriddhi Sarker and co-authors searched for drug targets shared by breast, ovarian, and colorectal cancers in 2026. Cancers differ, yet shared growth pathways may allow one drug to strike several types, a cheaper road than one drug per cancer.

Three gene data sets yielded a common set of changed genes. Network ranking lifted three cell division genes to the top as targets. Pathway and regulator analysis sketched the shared machinery, and docking tests ranked candidate drugs, with one compound binding most strongly. Computer evidence only, but it gives labs a short, shared target list to test in cells.
plos-pone-0351014:
Putri Amelia and co-authors reviewed the records of child heart patients in Indonesia in 2026, studying three things together: nutrition, the burden of illness, and how much health care the children used. Their retrospective cross-sectional study covers pediatric outpatients living with congenital heart disease, heart defects present from birth. Such children often grow poorly, because a struggling heart burns energy and feeding is hard.

Looking at nutritional status beside clinical burden and clinic use shows where the strain concentrates and which children return most often. That picture helps hospitals plan nutrition support and follow up where it will matter most. The study also adds Indonesian evidence to a literature dominated by wealthier health systems.
plos-pone-0351114:
Dana Islam and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One systematic review of immersive virtual reality in stroke rehabilitation. The reviewers gathered randomized trials, thirty-four studies with about twelve hundred survivors in total, testing fully immersive headsets alone or alongside standard therapy for arm movement, balance, walking, and quality of life.

Virtual reality, usually added to conventional rehabilitation, improved upper-limb motor impairment on the standard assessment scale, and small gains appeared in some walking measures. Results for everyday function, balance, and life quality were mixed and hard to pin down. The authors judge the evidence promising but weak, graded low to very low certainty, and call for larger, better-standardized trials before immersive therapy becomes routine.
plos-pone-0351214:
Hongzhen Yin and colleagues reviewed forty one adults treated for a foreign body stuck in the airway at a Chinese hospital across nearly twelve years. Swallowed or inhaled objects in adults are rare but can kill. Records covered imaging, removal method, breathing support, brain outcome, and survival to twenty eight days.

Flexible scope removal was tried first in nearly all patients and worked in about four fifths. Most patients needed only nasal oxygen, while about one fifth needed stronger support including one case of full life support. Survival at twenty eight days passed ninety percent, and most survivors left with good brain function. A clear pathway keeps rare emergencies calm and successful.
plos-pone-0351314:
Le, Nhu, and Thong built a hybrid AI framework to predict drug and protein pairings in a 2026 study. Knowing which proteins a drug touches speeds discovery and reuse of old drugs. Their system reads drug shapes with one network and protein sequences with another, then lets the two views attend to each other.

Tests used two standard benchmark sets under three splits, including hard cases with unseen drugs or unseen proteins. Performance matched leading rival methods across those tests. Gains came from joining shape and sequence views rather than relying on either alone. Better pairing predictions cut the number of lab tests wasted on hopeless combinations.
plos-pone-0351414:
Anemia stays common in India even though a national program has pushed iron supplements since 2018. Priyanka Gupta Bansal and colleagues describe the PRAKASH study, a 2026 PLOS One protocol for testing better ways to deliver proven anemia care in real districts.

The plan covers young children, school-age children, teenagers, women of childbearing age, and pregnant women. Its parts include testing and treating until anemia clears, iron and folic acid pills, fortified rice, more iron-rich foods, and public campaigns. Repeated community surveys will measure anemia rates, while interviews probe what helps or blocks the work. The goal is prevalence at or below one fifth.
plos-pone-0352014:
Claire Peneycad and co-authors studied a plant compound called isoginkgetin, taken from ginkgo leaves, and its odd effect on metal-handling genes. The compound was already known to block cells from making new proteins. The team found it also switches on genes for metallothioneins, small proteins that bind metals, and for a zinc transporter.

The switch runs through a known metal-sensing factor, and the gene messages rose in several cell lines. Yet the matching proteins did not increase, because the compound blocks translation, the step that builds proteins from messages. A reporter test confirmed messages were being read less, not more. The work warns that a rise in gene messages does not always mean more protein, a trap for anyone reading drug effects from RNA alone.
plos-pone-0352314:
Mohammad Fathi and seven colleagues train a machine-learning model to grade how badly intensive care patients' kidneys are failing, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Standard staging uses two measures and misses much of the clinical picture. Working with records of more than two thousand patients from a large critical-care database, the team fed dozens of routine variables into a gradient-boosted model and asked which ones carried the signal.

The model sorted patients into the correct severity stage about four times in five, performing best at the extremes — no injury and the most severe injury. Pre-existing kidney disease, sepsis, a liver pigment, and several blood-pressure drugs topped the predictor list. Such models could flag deteriorating kidneys hours before the standard thresholds trip.
plos-pone-0352514:
Stepanian and colleagues, in a 2026 study, sort breast tumors using both their full gene activity and the ancestry of the patients. Breast cancer is the top cancer killer of women worldwide, and precise subtypes guide treatment. Standard subtyping uses a short gene list and can wobble depending on the batch of samples fed in.

The team read RNA from about two hundred seventy tumors and a few healthy samples from varied places. From the same data they extracted enough genetic markers to infer broad ancestry, and they recovered European, African, Asian, South Asian, and mixed American roots. Clustering on complete expression profiles grouped tumors in ways the short list only partly matched. Computer drug tests then pointed to medicines that might work on specific clusters. The authors argue that ancestry-aware, whole-profile subtyping could make breast cancer care fairer and sharper, provided research cohorts grow more diverse.
plos-pone-0353214:
Eleftheria Michalaki and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study of a strikingly cheap device for delivering RNA vaccines without the fatty carriers used today. The gadget, adapted from a lighter and costing under a dollar, uses tiny needles and a small electric pulse to push naked RNA into skin cells. Carrier-free RNA is normally destroyed quickly and enters cells poorly, so it had been written off.

With the device, naked RNA produced strong gene activity and immune responses in animals, matching carrier-based delivery at low doses, without the body-wide inflammation those carriers cause. The team tested several RNA designs and confirmed the approach works in living human skin samples. They pitch it as a low-cost route for routine shots and fast pandemic response.
plos-pone-0354014:
Lei Ma and four co-authors build a gene-based prediction model for Alzheimer's disease from tiny parcels that cells release into the blood, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. These parcels, called exosomes, carry molecules tied to the disease. Working only with public datasets, the team sifted exosome-related genes for a small set that could flag the disease.

Five genes formed their final model. Computer simulations then linked those genes to several existing drugs and mapped where drug molecules might bind on the resulting proteins. Everything here is computational, with no patient testing yet. Still, a blood-based gene signature of this kind is exactly what early Alzheimer's diagnosis research is hunting for.
plos-pone-0354114:
Heribert Stich, Angelika Deisling, and Fabian Standl report infection screening results for unaccompanied refugee minors arriving in one Bavarian district of Germany. Long journeys can expose young travelers to infections, and German law requires health checks on arrival. The team reviewed standardized assessments gathered over thirteen years for more than two hundred minors. Tests covered tuberculosis, hepatitis types, scabies, and gut parasites. Journey links were then explored in the subgroup with travel details recorded.

At least one infection was found in about three in five minors screened. Prevalence patterns were broadly similar across journey features in this early analysis. Stich and colleagues argue the high overall rate alone justifies careful screening and fast treatment pathways for this vulnerable group, whatever route they traveled.
plos-pone-0354514:
Eline Meireson and five colleagues published this 2026 ultrasound study of the unborn baby's heart. A technique that tracks tiny speckles in ultrasound images can measure how the heart muscle stretches, but doctors worry different users get different numbers. Healthy pregnant volunteers had scans every four weeks, and observers re-measured the same heartbeat blind.

Agreement was steadier for the left side of the heart than the right, and it weakened after about thirty-two weeks of pregnancy. Meireson sees real promise in the method, but says the measurement routine needs tightening before clinics rely on it.
plos-pone-0354714:
Makoto Nishimori and colleagues taught deep learning systems to grade heart muscle inflammation from biopsy slides. Myocarditis can kill quickly, yet the gold-standard biopsy lacks an objective severity score. Their 2026 study used slides from several hundred patients at a national heart centre, with severe cases defined by shock, support machines, or death.

One model scored severity from the density of immune cells counted by a detection system. A second model, reading the most telling slide patches with a transformer, separated severe from milder cases almost perfectly in testing. Its attention maps highlighted both inflammation and muscle injury. Nishimori and colleagues propose the score as a standardised tissue index, pending wider validation.
plos-pone-0354814:
Solomon Gedfie led a team of eight authors on this 2026 systematic review of leukemia across Africa. Scattered hospital studies had given conflicting pictures of how common this blood cancer is. The team searched several databases, followed standard review guidelines, and pooled the results with statistical models.

Their combined estimate put leukemia at about five percent in the general population studied, lower in children. Living in a rural area and being older were both linked to higher odds. Gedfie and colleagues argue the pooled picture gives cancer planners a firmer base for deciding where diagnosis and treatment services are most needed.
plos-pone-0354914:
Min Sup Lim and four colleagues published this 2026 paper on a faster test for respiratory syncytial virus, a major cause of chest infections in babies and older adults. Standard gene testing needs complex machines, which many clinics lack. Their method copies viral genes at one steady temperature and uses two probes to tell subtype A from subtype B.

The test caught nearly all true cases of both subtypes and never fired on other common respiratory viruses. Lim sees it as a fit for small clinics and field settings, once wider trials confirm the lab results.
plos-pone-0355214:
Farhad Udwadia, Annudesh Liyanage, and Gary Yang study device sales staff in 2026. They ask if a rep in the room changes surgery results. The surgery repairs a swollen belly artery from inside. Reps teach device use and help fix problems. Their presence also raises worries about bias. Records covered ninety planned cases at one busy centre.

A rep was present in most of the cases. No clear gaps appeared in surgery time. Imaging time and extra device use matched as well. Hospital stay and leak rates were alike. Death rates also matched at six months. Routine rep support showed no clear gain here. The authors call for more selective use of reps.
plos-pone-0355314:
Andrés Velasco-Cárdenas and co-authors sprayed cut-flower plants with natural defence triggers to blunt a major thrips pest. Western flower thrips damage ornamental crops worldwide, and insecticides are losing ground to resistance. Their 2026 study applied two elicitors, methyl jasmonate and a floral scent compound, to Alstroemeria plants and measured feeding damage.

Both triggers cut thrips feeding consistently across doses and time points. The strongest, most repeatable effects came from the higher jasmonate dose and the mid scent dose. Thrips on treated leaves showed shifted detox enzyme activity, and plant chemistry profiles separated clearly by treatment. Velasco-Cárdenas and colleagues present elicitor priming as a residue-light complement to chemical control in floriculture.
plos-pone-0355614:
Catiana Engelhardt and colleagues randomly assigned anxious adults to two talking therapies delivered in online groups. Cognitive behaviour therapy is the standard; positive psychotherapy instead builds on strengths and good experiences. Their 2026 trial ran both for ten weeks and measured anxiety, happiness, quality of life, and distress up to three months later.

Patients improved clearly in both groups, with medium to large gains over time. Almost no measure favoured one therapy over the other; a single fear questionnaire was the lone exception. Follow-up scores held the gains. Engelhardt and colleagues read the result as evidence that positive psychotherapy can stand beside the standard approach for anxiety, at least in an online group format.
plos-pone-0355714:
Shahida Ferdousee and co-authors stressed four high-yield tomato varieties with salt and with a drought mimic to compare their defences. Salinity and drought are intensifying with climate change and slash tomato harvests. Their 2026 study tracked growth, leaf water, pigments, and protective chemistry across the varieties under both stresses.

No single tolerance pattern emerged; each variety answered differently. One kept growing taller shoots and stockpiled the protective compound proline. Another held its green pigment and leaf water while keeping a damage chemical lowest. Detox enzyme activity shifted with variety, treatment, and their combination. Ferdousee and colleagues say breeders should match variety choice to the stress a region expects most.
plos-pone-0356614:
Sinan Eliaçık and Nouman Ali designed new drug candidates by computer in 2026 for restless legs syndrome, a disorder that drives an urge to move the legs, worst at night. Their target receptors are dopamine D1 and D3, since dopamine signaling is deeply involved in the condition. Starting from rotigotine, a drug already used for it, they aimed to design improved derivatives from scratch, a process called de novo design.

Their pipeline combines a three dimensional convolutional network with a generative model and a sequence model to propose and refine candidate molecules. Computer design of this kind can explore far more chemical possibilities than a laboratory, leaving bench scientists a short list worth making and testing.
plos-pone-0356914:
YiZhong Yang leads a team of five teaching a camera system to sort construction waste on sites, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rubble heaps mix categories that look alike, hide under each other, and bend out of shape, while site computers are weak. Their algorithm trims a detection network for lightness. It adds spatial attention so the model notices where things are. It also redesigns the detection head, aligning what the model sees with what it is asked to find.

On the team's ten category dataset, the system beat its parent network on detection quality and precision while shedding about a fifth of its parameters. The model weighs four megabytes, small enough for cheap site hardware to run in real time. Tests on public datasets backed its ability to generalize beyond its home set. For an industry drowning in debris, automated sorting at the source starts with eyes this cheap.
plos-pone-0357014:
Irène Godéré led a team of eight authors working on microplastics in giant clams, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Giant clams filter seawater for food and swallow plastic particles along the way. Counting those particles inside the clam Tridacna maxima is slow by hand, so the team tested a staining dye called Nile Red with machine learning.

Godéré's combined method aims to spot and count microplastics faster and more reliably. Marine scientists tracking plastic in filter feeders need that speed to survey wide areas. Giant clams are also valued reef animals, so knowing their plastic load serves both pollution science and their protection. The approach could extend to oysters and other filter feeders people eat.
plos-pone-0357214:
Nidal S. Khatib and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on reading cerebral palsy risk from the way young babies kick. Clinicians score infants' spontaneous movements with a trained eye, a scarce skill, so objective measures could widen screening. Twenty-six babies under three months wore motion-capture sensors while kicking; models estimated joint movements and muscle forces, and waveform analysis measured how varied the patterns were.

Variation told the story. Babies whose movements scored as healthier showed richer variation in knee and hip motion and in several muscle forces, while restricted variation tracked with the poor-repertoire pattern that flags risk. Some measures also shifted with age, matching the known path toward more complex movement. A statistical classifier separated normal from poor-repertoire babies with good accuracy using those measures alone. Such measurements, they argue, could support earlier, cheaper risk screening and give physiotherapists concrete targets.
plos-pone-0357714:
Itamar Shatz published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies procrastination among college students in the United States, putting off tasks despite expecting harm from the delay. The author measures how common it is and weighs its impact.

The comparison set is other common health and life issues students face, which puts procrastination's weight in perspective. If its impact rivals better-known problems, colleges have reason to treat it as a health concern, not a character flaw. Student support staff and researchers of self-control are the readers for prevalence figures framed this way.
plos-pone-0357814: Odonkor, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on health systems in Sub-Saharan Africa facing diseases that return after fading. The cross-country analysis traces pathways that build health resilience, the power to absorb a new outbreak and keep care running. Comparing countries side by side can show which investments, like labs or local staff, pay off when a known disease resurges.
plos-pone-0359314:
Leila Sharda and a broad team of co-authors published in 2026 the protocol for a scoping review about dementia care across language and culture. The review will gather what is known about how such care is handled for members of minoritised ethnic groups who have dementia or milder problems with memory and thinking. Language barriers and cultural differences can distort memory tests and delay diagnosis in these communities.

A protocol paper fixes the review's questions and methods in advance, so readers can later judge whether the team followed its own plan. The planned review maps a scattered literature rather than testing one treatment. Its findings should help clinics adapt their assessments so that a person's background does not decide the quality of their dementia care.
plos-pone-0359714: Dejen and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a review on malaria that shows no symptoms. School-aged children can carry the malaria parasite while feeling fine, and still spread it. The plan sets out a systematic review and a pooled analysis of past studies. It aims to size the hidden burden in this age group. Hidden carriers are a key obstacle to wiping out malaria.
pmc-10202314: A 2023 note thanked the editorial board of Dementia and Neuropsychology, the acknowledgment, the journal record. The archive preserves it. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
pmc-13238514:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes judges a food enzyme made by a modified fungus. The enzyme, beta-glucosidase, is produced by a genetically modified Trichoderma reesei strain for Genencor International. Such enzymes help release flavours and process plant materials in food making, and each new production strain must pass a safety check before use in Europe.

The panel found the genetic changes raised no safety concerns. The enzyme product held no living cells of the fungus and none of its DNA. On that basis it could be cleared for the two food processes proposed. The evaluation shows the standard EFSA route for enzymes from modified microbes.
pmc-13240914:
Gaál Kovalčíková and colleagues in Bratislava asked whether neutrophil extracellular traps drive adenine-induced kidney disease in mice. The traps form when a PAD4 enzyme is active. Mice lacking that enzyme were compared with normal littermates. Both groups received daily adenine injections for fourteen days.

Adenine slashed body weight by a fifth and doubled kidney creatinine in normal mice. Injury markers like lipocalin-2 soared more than twenty-fold. Knockout mice fared no better, and their creatinine actually rose sooner. Neutrophils clearly activated, but trap production itself appears uninvolved in this model's damage.
pmc-13241014:
Scarlett's team surveyed open source contributors across the University of California system for its program office network. Two hundred ninety-four students, faculty, researchers, and staff took part. The survey probed both daily contribution hurdles and what support would help most. It also sized up how deeply open source runs on campus.

Over ninety percent of students and researchers called open source important to their work. Well over half of experienced contributors had run a project of their own. Lack of time, especially for documentation, was the top frustration. Respondents prioritized solid computing environments and dedicated sustainability grants.
pmc-13242114:
Chekav and colleagues in Bushehr tested whether picture stories can teach diabetes self-care past low health literacy. One hundred fifty patients were randomized into three equal groups. Two groups took five theory-based training sessions; one added an AI-designed photo-novel and plain-language materials. The third got routine care.

Both teaching groups gained knowledge, confidence, and self-care over three months. The photo-novel group gained far more on nearly every measure. Only felt social support refused to budge between groups. Chekav recommends pairing behavioral theory with visual literacy tools for such vulnerable patients.
pmc-13242514:
Huixia Savannah Wang, Anna Rieckmann, and Maria Josefsson asked whether social and health risks harm memory equally across Europe. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. They drew on a cross-national survey of adults aged fifty and older, covering more than one hundred thousand people in twenty countries. Five risks were tested against memory scores: living alone, inactivity, obesity, depression, and heart and metabolic conditions.

All five risks were tied to worse memory on average, but the strength of several links changed by region, and a few even flipped direction. Living alone, obesity, and inactivity behaved least consistently across northern, western, eastern, and southern Europe. Results also shifted with education and age in parts of the analysis. The authors warn that dementia prevention plans imported wholesale from one region may misfire in another. Local context, they argue, should shape which risks a program targets first.
pmc-13244514:
Zhenyuan Yu, Shuwei Zhang, and Ze Lu reviewed the two-way traffic between iron and mouth bacteria in gum disease. Their narrative review appeared in the Journal of Oral Microbiology in 2026. Periodontitis is driven by oral pathogens, yet it also tracks with body-wide disease. Iron sits at the crossroads: too much free iron feeds radical damage and a form of cell death called ferroptosis.

In periodontitis, blood iron and its carrier transferrin fall while storage and control proteins rise, a signature of iron locked away by inflammation. That misdistribution shelters pathogens, fans inflammation, kills ligament cells by ferroptosis, and eats into jaw bone. The same iron disorder ties gum disease to anemia and other systemic conditions. Chelating or rebalancing iron looks promising as therapy, the authors say, but solid clinical trials are still missing. The review frames gums as an iron story, not only a plaque story.
pmc-13246514:
Lee and Leite published this publisher correction in Behavior Research Methods in 2026. It corrects their earlier article on propensity score analysis, a statistical method for comparing groups in observational studies, when some data are missing in ways that depend on the missing values themselves. Their paper had introduced a method called dual-forest proximity imputation for filling in such gaps.

A publisher correction is a formal notice that something in the published record was wrong and has now been fixed, so that readers and future citations rest on the corrected version. The notice itself presents no new data or analysis. Readers who use the dual-forest method should check the corrected article to see exactly what changed.
pmc-13247314:
Zhang, Zhao, and Liu re-examined how a protein switches on, in this 2026 Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal study. Proteins are often pictured flipping between two fixed shapes, but the authors suspected the innate immune adaptor STING works more subtly. Using long molecular-dynamics simulations and network inference, they watched how binding a small signaling molecule reshaped the protein's whole range of motion.

The ligand did not simply snap STING from closed to open. It reweighted the energy landscape, suppressing stretched-out shapes and favoring activation-ready intermediates, while communication routes inside the protein condensed from scattered paths into shorter, focused channels that transmit signals more efficiently. The authors propose allosteric activation as landscape reweighting, a model that may explain regulation in many flexible proteins.
pmc-13248314: Dwivedi and colleagues published this correction notice in 2026 in the Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology. It fixes their earlier paper on gene activity and chemical marks on DNA in cows with subclinical mastitis, a hidden udder infection. Two values in Table 1 were printed wrong for the gene OXCT1, one for its measured activity change and one for a methylation change at its promoter. The notice records the correct figures and leaves the study's findings and conclusions unchanged.
pmc-13250214:
Kola and co-authors set out a plan for reviewing survival when patients with lung scarring need a breathing machine. Their 2026 BMJ Open protocol covers interstitial lung diseases, a group of disorders marked by lung inflammation or scarring. Patients in sudden breathing failure often enter intensive care, yet evidence on whether invasive ventilation helps them is thin.

The review will search four databases for trials and observational studies in adults receiving invasive ventilation. Main outcomes are deaths in hospital and at one year, with time off the ventilator and length of stay also tracked. Planned subgroup checks include disease subtype, lung pressure problems, and timing of ventilation. Study quality will be graded with standard tools before results are combined where the data allow.
pmc-13251614:
Nijina Li and Hao Zhang trace a molecular driver of atrial fibrillation in this 2026 study. The common irregular heartbeat disorder scars the heart's upper chambers and disrupts their energy factories, and a chemical tag placed on RNA may help drive that damage.
