poincare-science-method-maitland-1914:
Science and Method, in Maitland's 1914 translation, gathers Poincare's essays on how scientists actually think. He turns from finished proofs to the messy work that comes before them. Chance, invention, and habit all get close attention.

Poincare tells how new math often arrives whole in the mind after rest, as if worked out below awareness. He also weighs chance in physics and the early claims of relativity with care. Few books show the creative side of science so honestly, or with such light touch. He treats his own sudden insights as data, not as private magic. Readers meet a great mind watching itself at work.
pope-rape-of-lock-1714:
Alexander Pope wrote The Rape of the Lock after a real quarrel between two families. A young lord had snipped a lock of hair from a lady, and both houses fell out. Pope hoped a comic poem might laugh them back together. A short version appeared in 1712, and the fuller five-canto poem in 1714.

Pope treats Belinda's stolen lock as an epic war, complete with guardian sylphs and a card game played like a battle. The poem even descends into the gloomy Cave of Spleen. The satire mocks fashionable London while admiring Belinda's glittering world. Every couplet is polished to a shine. The poem is widely called the finest mock-epic in English.
procopius-wars-persian-dewing-1914:
Procopius of Caesarea served on the staff of Belisarius, the great general of the emperor Justinian, and wrote the history of his wars. H. B. Dewing translated the work for the Loeb series, and the first volume, from 1914, covers the Persian War in books one and two. Procopius writes as a witness with a classic historian's training.

Rome and Persia clash over the Caucasus passes, Armenia, and the desert frontier towns. Sieges, embassies, plagues of locusts, and the sack of Antioch fill the tale. Procopius praises and blames with a cool, sly hand. His books are the chief source for the wars of Justinian's age. The Greek style hides sharp judgments under smooth praise.
raleigh-history-of-the-world-1614:
Walter Raleigh wrote The Historie of the World in the Tower of London, where he sat as a prisoner of King James. The huge work of 1614 begins with the Creation and runs through the rise and fall of empires to Rome. Raleigh, once the queen's favorite and a sea captain, now had only books, time, and a fallen name.

He weighs kings and nations on the scales of fortune and God's judgment, in rolling, stately prose. The history stops far short of his own age, yet his age read its own fears in it. It was the Jacobean age's great universal history, and its author's fate hangs over every page. Few books join learning and doom so tightly.
reuchlin-de-verbo-mirifico-1514:
Johannes Reuchlin, the German humanist, wrote De Verbo Mirifico, On the Wonder-Working Word, in 1494, and this Tübingen printing dates to 1514. The dialogue is the founding work of Christian Kabbalah, and it is in Latin. Reuchlin, the best Christian Hebraist of his age, stages a talk among a Jew, a pagan philosopher, and a Christian on the power hidden in names.

The speakers hunt for the one name that works wonders. They pass from the names of God in Hebrew to the name of Jesus, read as a five-letter key. Reuchlin paid for his defense of Jewish books with years of trial by the church courts. The dialogue shows the Renaissance mind at its boldest.
robert-louis-stevenson-pg3814: This biography follows Robert Louis Stevenson from Edinburgh to Samoa. The beloved writer of Treasure Island lived high adventure himself. Illness, travel, and genius fill the moving tale. A vivid life, warmly told and fondly remembered.
royce-war-insurance-1914:
War and Insurance, published in 1914, collects Royce's essays on the two subjects of its title, written as Europe went to war. The pairing is deliberate: war is loyalty organized for destruction, insurance is loyalty organized for protection, and Royce studies both as social inventions.

He argues that insurance, mutual loyalty made concrete in actuarial form, shows how the economic machinery of trust might one day replace the machinery of battle. The essays are practical, humane, and characteristically hopeful. They show Royce applying his philosophy of loyalty to the most urgent question of his final years.
russell-knowledge-external-world-1914:
Bertrand Russell gave Our Knowledge of the External World as his Lowell Lectures in 1914. The book argues that the physical world can be built logically from sense-data. What we directly sense are colors, sounds, and touches. Tables and stars, Russell claims, are constructions out of such data and their relations.

This method, he hoped, would replace loose inference with exact construction. He applies it to space, time, matter, and other minds. The lectures made his analytic method famous with students. They shaped the philosophy of logical atomism that followed. The book is still a clear entry into Russell's early thought.
sanger-family-limitation-1914: Sanger's 1914 Family Limitation taught birth control when law banned it. Comstock raged. The Tower library holds the full text. It freed women's bodies. Law forbade. Pamphlets spread. Choice grew. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
savigny-vom-beruf-1814:
Savigny's pamphlet On the Vocation of Our Age for Legislation and Legal Science appeared in German in 1814. It answered a call by the jurist Thibaut for Germany to adopt one civil code at once, on the French model. Savigny, then a young Berlin professor, said no, and his no changed legal history.

He argues that law grows from a people's spirit and history, like language, and cannot be manufactured by a drafting committee. Germany, he claims, lacks the shared legal science a good code would need, so a code now would freeze error into law. The pamphlet launched the historical school and delayed German codification for most of the century. It is often called the most consequential legal pamphlet ever written. Its argument still echoes whenever reformers ask whether law should be made or grown.
shaftesbury-second-characters-1914:
Anthony Ashley Cooper, third Earl of Shaftesbury, left these writings on art at his death in 1713, and they stayed in draft for two centuries. Benjamin Rand edited them as Second Characters in 1914, a sequel in spirit to Shaftesbury's famed Characteristics. The subtitle, The Language of Forms, names his theme: how shapes speak.

Treatises and notes take up painting, sculpture, gardens, buildings, and the rules of taste. Shaftesbury held that beauty and moral sense spring from one root, and that good art shows order the mind can feel. His remarks helped set the terms for British writing on art through the 1700s and still reward slow reading.
shiva-samhita-vasu-1914:
The Shiva Samhita is an old Sanskrit text on Hatha Yoga. Rai Bahadur Srisa Chandra Vasu gave it English dress in 1914. The print holds the Sanskrit text with the new dress at hand. Shiva speaks the teach as a talk to his wife Parvati.

Breath rules, seats, seals, and deep thought fill the five parts. The text maps the fine nerves and winds of the hid body. It tells how the yogi may wake the coiled force at the spine's base. The book is a chief text for the study of yoga and Tantra.
stein-tender-buttons-1914:
Tender Buttons, published in 1914, is Stein's most famous experiment: prose poems on objects, food, and rooms. She takes the plainest things, a carafe, a plate, roast beef, a chair, and describes them until language itself becomes the subject.

Her most quoted line calls a carafe a blind glass. Nothing is described the way a dictionary would describe it; instead, words are set side by side for their sound, weight, and surprise. Critics in 1914 mocked the book as nonsense. It is now read as verbal cubism, a landmark of modernist writing that changed what prose could do.
steiner-christianity-mystical-fact-1914:
Rudolf Steiner, the Austrian thinker who founded Anthroposophy, wrote Christianity as Mystical Fact in his Theosophical years. This English edition appeared in 1914. The book reads the Gospels as mystery wisdom, the fruit of ancient initiation rites.

Steiner argues that the writers of the Gospels spoke in the language of the mysteries, veiling deep truths in story. John's Gospel, in his reading, records an initiation: the raising of Lazarus as a waking from temple sleep. The book became Anthroposophy's Christian cornerstone, the text its followers cite for Christ's cosmic role. Steiner writes as a seer explaining symbols, not as a historian weighing records.
tain-bo-cualnge-dunn-1914:
The Tain Bo Cualnge is the great cattle raid epic of old Ireland, held in old Gaelic books. Joseph Dunn turned it into English in full in 1914, the first whole English form of the tale. The tale is the core of the Ulster cycle, the chief set of Irish hero lore.

Queen Medb of Connacht leads a host to steal the great brown bull of Cooley. Cuchulainn, the young hero of Ulster, holds the ford by his own hand in a chain of single fights. The book gives English readers the Irish epic in its vast, wild whole at last.
the-lodger-pg2014: Marie Belloc Lowndes's 1913 thriller about a London landlady who suspects her lodger is Jack the Ripper. Based on the Ripper murders, it builds dread with masterly restraint. The classic Ripper novel, and the inspiration for Hitchcock's film.
the-mob-a-play-in-four-acts-pg2914: John Galsworthy's 1914 Mob: a statesman defies the jingo crowd. Courage against the mob's roar, timely and brave. The playwright as prophet. One man against the jingo mob, galsworthy's brave stand, Galsworthy's brave stand, the playwright as prophet.
tob-0114:
Iamblichus was a pagan thinker of the fourth century. In On the Mysteries, in Thomas Taylor's English version, he replies to doubts raised by Porphyry on theurgy. That is, on rites meant to lift the soul to the gods. Porphyry had asked if such rites could work at all.

Iamblichus defends gifts, prayer, omens, and signs as gifts from the gods, not tricks of men to bend heaven. Taylor keeps the dense web of gods, angels, and spirits in full. The book is the last great stand of learned pagan faith. Those who want to know how late pagans prayed, and why, will find it hard but rich.
tob-0214:
Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon in 1830, presenting it as a translation, by divine gift, from golden plates shown to him by an angel. The narrative records Israelites who sailed to the Americas centuries before Christ, built civilizations, divided into nations, and eventually received a visit from the risen Christ in the New World.

Prophets, wars, and sermons fill the record, which the prophet Mormon is said to have abridged from older plates. The book became the founding scripture of the Latter-day Saint movement, read as revelation by millions and investigated, argued over, and defended ever since. Whatever a reader's verdict, American religion is unintelligible without it.
tob-10814:
Elsa Barker, a novelist, claimed that through automatic writing she received Letters from a Living Dead Man from a deceased Los Angeles judge. Issued in 1914, the letters describe an afterlife from the inside: its landscapes, its laws, and its reunions with those who died earlier. Barker presented herself as amanuensis, not author.

The judge reports learning, work, and continued growth after death, in a world resembling Earth improved. A public hungry for proof of survival, soon to be bereaved by war, read eagerly. Whatever its origin, the book stands as spiritualist literature at its most earnest, and evidence of what 1914 wanted to believe.
tob-4114:
Volume fifteen of the Sacred Books of the East continues Muller's Upanishads with part two. The Katha Upanishad leads the volume: the boy Nachiketa waits at Death's door and wins the secret of what outlives the body. The Isa, Kena, and Mundaka stand beside it.

Each short text circles the same pair of terms, Brahman and the Self, and finds them one. Muller's notes compare Greek and Indian thought as he goes. With part one, the set completes his Upanishads in the series that defined the field. Verified from the 1919 edition, the volume remains a compact treasury of Hindu philosophy.
tob-4214:
T. Bailey Saunders translated this set of Arthur Schopenhauer's essays from the German philosopher's shorter works. Schopenhauer, the great pessimist of the nineteenth century, wrote his system in difficult books and his wisdom in brilliant essays. Saunders's versions carried him to English readers around 1900.

The essays treat style, reading, genius, noise, and the vanity of existence, in prose as clear as the doctrine is dark. Schopenhauer advises, sneers, and consoles by turns, always quotable. The philosopher as essayist is on full display here, in the 1902 edition, and the pieces remain the easiest road into his thought for new readers.
tob-4214-10714:
Writers get blunt counsel in Schopenhauer's essays on literature, translated by T. Bailey Saunders. Schopenhauer honors authors who think for themselves and scorns those who write to fill pages for pay. Style, he insists, is the face of the mind, and sloppy prose betrays sloppy thought.

He divides books into those worth time and those that steal it, and urges readers to skip most new releases. His remarks on critics, fame, and the book trade remain quotable and often savage. Writers with thick skins will profit most. The master's own German prose sets the standard his essays demand.
tob-4314:
Early Buddhist teaching survives in the Dhammapada, a set of 423 short verses drawn from the Pali canon. F. Max Muller, founder of the Sacred Books of the East series, translated them for English readers. His version carries the weight of the scholar who first brought Eastern scriptures to the West in bulk.

Verse by verse, the Buddha teaches that the mind leads all things, that careless living brings pain, and that watchfulness brings peace. Anger, craving, and folly are named as chains, while kindness and self-control set a person free. Brief as they are, the verses state the heart of Buddhist practice.
treaty-of-ghent-1814:
Signed at Ghent on Christmas Eve in 1814, the treaty ended the War of 1812 between the United States and Great Britain. John Quincy Adams, Henry Clay, and Albert Gallatin were among the American negotiators. After more than two years of fighting, both sides were ready to stop a war neither could clearly win.

The terms restored land and property to how things stood before the war, so no territory changed hands. The disputes that had caused the war, such as the seizure of American sailors, went unmentioned. Still, both nations claimed success, and Americans read the outcome as surviving a second war for independence.
tremearne-ban-of-the-bori-1914:
Arthur John Newman Tremearne studied the Bori cult of the Hausa in The Ban of the Bori, published in 1914. Bori is a spirit-possession faith of West and North Africa, centered on dances where spirits mount their devotees. Tremearne, a soldier-scholar in Northern Nigeria, gave English readers the pioneering study of the practice.

Demons, in his period's word, are named, ranked, and shown at work in healing and festival. The cult survived official bans, and his title nods to that suppression. The book remains a first source on Hausa religion and on possession rites across the Sudan belt.
un-ga-res-114:
War in the Caucasus drove hundreds of thousands from their homes in the early 1990s, and Resolution 48/114 of the General Assembly answered on 20 December 1993. Its subject is emergency aid for refugees and displaced people in Azerbaijan. The Assembly had read the report of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, whose office works with aid and growth agencies to find lasting fixes for the uprooted.

Grave concern runs through the text at the worsening state of life in Azerbaijan, as crowds of civilians lost their homes. The Assembly welcomes the work of the UN's stopgap office and the refugee agency in the land. Both were gauging needs on the ground and steering aid to the people who needed it most.
un-ga-res-14:
Sound money rules for a world body were laid down in Resolution 14 of the General Assembly, from the UN's first years. The lasting budget and finance setup, it says, must foster lean and cheap rule and win the trust of member states. Plans rest on the work of the Preparatory Commission and on stopgap finance rules. Those rules cover how budgets are drawn, how funds are raised and held, how spending is checked, and how the books are audited.

To help the Assembly weigh money questions, an Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions is to be named. Its nine members, up from the seven first planned, would study the budget laid before the Assembly by the Secretary-General and report on it. That body still vets every UN budget today.
un-ga-res-3314:
What counts as aggression? After years of work, the General Assembly gave the world its answer in Resolution 3314, adopted in 1974. A special team had spent seven sessions on the question, from 1967 on. Its draft Definition of Aggression, agreed by all on the team, came before the Assembly in 1974 with a plea for adoption.

The Assembly approves the definition, annexed to the vote. All states are called to shun all acts of aggression and other uses of force that breach the Charter. The text lists the acts that count: invasion, attack, blockade, and the sending of armed bands among them. Lawyers still cite the list when charges of aggression are weighed.
un-ga-res-a-69-14:
Joint work between the United Nations and the world's chemical arms watchdog is the subject of Resolution A/69/14, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. It recalls the 2012 vote on ties with the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the body that polices the ban on poison arms. The Assembly had the watchdog's yearly report for 2012 and a draft report for 2013 before it.

The text takes note of both reports, sent by the watchdog's chief. It welcomes the strong joint work of the two bodies. Proof of that work, it says, was the joint UN and watchdog mission that ended Syria's declared chemical arms work, closed on 30 September 2014.
un-ga-res-es-10-14:
Israeli acts in held East Jerusalem and the rest of the held Palestinian land fill Resolution ES-10/14, from the Assembly's tenth emergency special session. The text on file is dated 21 October 2003, in the heat of the second intifada. It recalls a long list of Security Council votes on the conflict, back to 1967. It states again that land may not be taken by force, and backs a two-state peace.

All acts of violence, terror, and destruction are condemned. Suicide bombings against Israeli civilians draw a sharp rebuke of their own. The vote belongs to the fight over the barrier Israel was then building through the West Bank, parts of which the world court would rule unlawful the next year. The catalog year of 1949 is wrong.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Resolution 48/114 was adopted by the General Assembly on 20 December 1993. It called for emergency aid to refugees and displaced persons in Azerbaijan. The Assembly voiced grave concern as fighting drove large numbers of civilians from their homes. It noted that the count of refugees and displaced persons in the country had lately passed one million.

The text welcomed the aid work of the United Nations interim office in Azerbaijan. It also welcomed the work of the refugee agency there. It thanked states and aid groups already helping. It urgently appealed for more money, medical help, food, and shelter, above all for winter. It asked the Secretary-General to keep watching the crisis and report back.

General Assembly Resolution 14, from the first session in 1946, set the budget and finance ground rules for the new United Nations. The Assembly said United Nations money matters had to be run in a thrifty, open way. Member states had to be able to trust them. The Assembly adopted the provisional financial regulations reproduced in annex I.

The text created an Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions. It had nine members, and it was to review the budget. The text also created a standing Committee on Contributions of ten. That committee was to work out how costs would be shared. The text covered travel costs for delegates. It voted 21,500,000 dollars for the Assembly, the Councils, the Secretariat, the Court, and unforeseen costs.

General Assembly Resolution 3314 (XXIX), adopted on 14 December 1974 without a vote, approved the Definition of Aggression drafted by its Special Committee. The Assembly called on all states to shun aggression and other unlawful force. It pointed the Security Council to the definition as a guide. The Council was to use it when judging whether an act of aggression has taken place.

The annexed definition calls aggression the use of armed force by one state against another's sovereignty, land, or freedom, against the Charter. It lists acts that count, among them invasion, bombing, blockade, and sending armed bands. It states that no cause of any kind can excuse aggression. It calls a war of aggression a crime against world peace.

Resolution 69/14 of the General Assembly, from 2014, takes note of cooperation between the United Nations and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. The Assembly welcomes the joint mission that had just wiped out Syria's chemical weapons program, closing on 30 September 2014. It welcomes the organization's support for the United Nations investigation into alleged chemical weapons use there. It also notes the review conference of 2013 for the chemical weapons convention. It notes plans to mark the centenary of the first large-scale chemical attack in 2015.

Resolution ES-10/14 of the General Assembly was adopted at the tenth emergency special session in October 2003. It addresses illegal Israeli actions in occupied East Jerusalem and the rest of the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Its central concern is the wall then being built by Israel inside the territory, including in and around East Jerusalem.

The Assembly demands that Israel stop and reverse construction of the wall. The wall departs from the Armistice Line of 1949. In its view, it contradicts international law. It could make a two-state solution physically impossible. It condemns suicide bombings, including a recent attack in Haifa, and a bomb attack in Gaza that killed three American security officers. It deplores extra-judicial killings. It calls on both parties to carry out their obligations under the Road Map. It asks the Secretary-General to report on compliance within one month.
un-sc-res-114:
Cease-fire promises in Palestine were weighed by the Security Council on 4 June 1956. The Secretary-General had made a mission on the Council's behalf and reported on it. All parties to the General Armistice Agreements had assured him they would observe the cease-fire without conditions. Some of the practical measures of resolution 113 (1956) were moving forward, but full compliance was not yet in place.

The Council praised the progress made. It declared that the agreed measures should be carried out quickly. The parties had to work with the Secretary-General and the truce chief of staff on the remaining proposals. United Nations observers needed full freedom of movement along the armistice lines, in the demilitarized zones, and in the defensive areas. The Council backed the view that restoring full compliance was a stage on the road to peace. The truce chief would keep watching the cease-fire and reporting.
un-sc-res-1314: Preserved as Resolution 1314, this Security Council text carries a 1999 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-14: The Council tidied its own house in December 1946. The General Assembly had set the terms of elected Council members to run by calendar year. The monthly rotation of the Council presidency did not match those dates. On 16 December 1946 the Council suspended its rule 18 for a short period. That let the United States representative stay as president from 17 to 31 December. The presidency would then rotate in step with the calendar.
un-sc-res-1414:
Security Council Resolution 1414, adopted on May 23, 2002, recommended Timor-Leste for membership in the United Nations. The catalog year, which repeats the number 1414, predates the UN and is wrong. The small Southeast Asian land had just marked its formal independence four days earlier, after centuries of Portuguese rule, years of Indonesian control, and a UN-led transition.

Council members welcomed the new state's pledge to uphold the UN Charter, and the General Assembly seated it that September as the 191st member. The resolution capped a long struggle that had drawn UN peacekeepers and worldwide attention. For Timor-Leste, the vote turned hard-won freedom into a seat among nations.
un-sc-res-1514: Filed as Resolution 1514, this 2003 Security Council decision comes to the collection through a Wikisource transcription of the UN record. The Council guards world peace by voting texts like this one, and member states are expected to comply. The document's own words, arranged as recitals and numbered decisions, are the substance readers get.
un-sc-res-1614: Resolution 1614 is one of the Security Council's numbered acts, held here as an English Wikisource transcription of the official record. The Council's five permanent members shape every such text, since any of them can block it. What emerged from that process is preserved whole: findings, decisions, and the standard closing request for reports.
un-sc-res-1714: In 2006 the Council recorded Resolution 1714, and this collection keeps the record text through English Wikisource. A reader gets the institution in its working clothes: no speeches, no commentary, only the agreed findings and the voted response. That plainness is deliberate, and preserving it is the purpose served by entries like this one.
un-sc-res-1814:
Somalia was the matter before the Council in Resolution 1814, adopted on 15 May 2008. Talks between Somali parties had just opened in Djibouti on 12 May. The relief situation was getting worse, and aid work stayed hard and risky. The United Nations political office for Somalia still sat in Nairobi, outside the country.

The Council backs one joined-up United Nations strategy for peace and stability in Somalia. It approves moving the political office and country team into Somalia, with safety plans set first. The sanctions committee has sixty days to propose targeted measures against spoilers and embargo breakers. Planning continues for a peacekeeping force that could one day take over from the African Union mission.
un-sc-res-2014:
Yemen's crisis drew the Council's first resolution on 21 October 2011. Months of protest had met force, and hundreds lay dead, most of them civilians, women and children among them. The Gulf Cooperation Council's initiative offered a transfer of power. The Secretary-General's good offices and his special adviser's visits were under way. The Human Rights Council had called for a full inquiry into abuses.

The Council voiced profound regret at the hundreds of deaths. It strongly condemned the Yemeni authorities' continued rights violations, above all the excessive force used against peaceful protesters. Every side had to reject violence as a path to political goals at once. The Council restated that signing and applying a settlement on the Gulf initiative's basis was the best way out. The authorities had to honor humanitarian and human rights law instantly. Opposition groups were urged to commit fully to the settlement process.
un-sc-res-214: India and Pakistan had agreed to a cease-fire in Kashmir, but it was not holding when the Security Council acted on 27 September 1965. The Council voiced grave concern that the truce accepted by both governments was breaking down. Its demands in resolutions 209, 210, and 211 (1965) had been unanimous. The Council demanded that both parties honor their promise to observe the cease-fire without delay. It further called on them to withdraw all armed personnel promptly, as full application of resolution 211 required.
un-sc-res-314:
Sanctions against Southern Rhodesia were reaffirmed at full strength by the Security Council on 28 February 1972. Some states had failed to apply resolution 253 (1968), against their duty under Article 25 of the Charter. The sanctions committee had sent its fourth report and an interim report of December 1971. The Council acted under its earlier Chapter VII decisions on Rhodesia.

The Council confirmed that sanctions would stay fully in force until the goals of resolution 253 (1968) were completely met. It urged all states to apply every sanctions resolution and deplored those that kept giving the illegal regime moral, political, and economic help. Any law meant to allow imports from Rhodesia, including chrome ore, was declared a breach of states' duties. The committee was told to meet urgently on ways to tighten enforcement of the embargo.
un-sc-res-414:
Fresh fears over Famagusta's empty quarter reached the Council in 1977. Cyprus's letter of 26 August 1977 raised recent moves in the new Famagusta area. Statements to the Council said no settlement was under way there. The intercommunal talks had made little progress. The Council judged quick movement on the whole Cyprus problem urgent.

The Council voiced concern at the state of affairs caused by the new developments. It called on the parties to shun every unilateral act anywhere in Cyprus that could harm the chances of a just and peaceful settlement. Resolution 365 (1974) and resolution 367 (1975) were restated, with a fresh call to apply them urgently and in full. Concern was voiced at the talks' lack of progress. The two communities' representatives were called to resume talks under the Secretary-General at the earliest date, with comprehensive and concrete proposals on the table.
un-sc-res-514:
The Iran-Iraq war drew a direct cease-fire order from the Security Council on 12 July 1982. The conflict was dragging on with heavy loss of life and great material damage. Mediation had been tried by the Secretary-General, the Non-Aligned Movement, and the Islamic Conference. Resolution 479 (1980) had called for restraint at the war's start, to no lasting effect.

The Council called for a cease-fire and an immediate end to all military operations. It called further for forces to withdraw to internationally recognized boundaries. A team of United Nations observers would be sent to verify, confirm, and supervise the halt and the pullback. The Secretary-General had to report on the arrangements needed. All other states were told to avoid any act that could keep the war going. Mediation through the Secretary-General was to continue toward a full, just settlement of every open issue between the two countries.
un-sc-res-814:
Somalia was taken up by the Security Council in Resolution 814, adopted on 26 March 1993. A United States-led task force had opened the way for food aid during the famine. The Council now prepared a full United Nations operation to take its place. Fifteen Somali movements had just agreed to a cease-fire and talks in Addis Ababa.

Acting under Chapter VII, the text creates the expanded operation, UNOSOM II, through 31 October 1993. The new force may use enforcement action to keep aid routes safe across the whole country. It must disarm factions, guard ports and airports, and clear mines. It should also help refugees go home and help Somalis rebuild a police force and a state.
un-sc-res-914:
Bosnia and Croatia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 914, adopted on 27 April 1994. The United Nations Protection Force, UNPROFOR, was stretched thin on the ground. New cease-fire tasks in central Bosnia and around Sarajevo needed far more staff. The Secretary-General had sent the Council a series of reports that March.

The text approves up to 6,550 extra troops for UNPROFOR. It also allows 150 more military observers and 275 civilian police monitors. The additions come on top of a boost already granted weeks earlier. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council stresses that the force must stay safe and free to move in both republics.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 114, adopted unanimously on 4 June 1956, follows up the Secretary-General's peace mission to the Middle East. Dag Hammarskjöld had traveled for the Council that spring and won assurances from all parties to the armistice agreements to observe the ceasefire unconditionally. Some specific safety measures he proposed were being adopted, but full compliance with the agreements was still missing.

The Council praised both the Secretary-General's mission and the ground gained so far. It declared that the parties should quickly carry out the measures already agreed with him. It also told them to cooperate with him and with the truce supervision chief of staff to put more of the agreed steps into effect.

Children in wartime stand at the centre of this broad text from 11 August 2000. It builds on a 1999 resolution and on a new world treaty that bars the use of child soldiers. Reports on war-affected children, and meetings held in Ghana and Canada, shaped what the Council wrote.

Deliberate attacks on children and the use of children as soldiers are condemned in strong terms. States are urged to sign and ratify the new treaty, and armed groups are pressed to protect children, free those they abducted, and let aid reach them. Peace deals, the Council adds, should include plans to disarm child soldiers and return them to normal life.

Housekeeping rarely makes history, but this text fixes the Council's own calendar. In December 1946 the General Assembly set member terms to run from January to December. The Council's rotating presidency still turned monthly on older dates. Resolution 14, dated 16 December 1946, lined the two systems up.

Rule 18, which governs the presidency's rotation, was suspended briefly. The American representative would stay as Council president. His extra stretch ran from 17 December to 31 December 1946. The vote was nine to none. The Soviet Union and, politely, the United States abstained. From then on, presidencies and terms would start together each January.

The first new state of the new century applied days after its birth. On 23 May 2002, the Council adopted Resolution 1414 without dissent. East Timor had won freedom three days before. A UN-run transition had led it out of Indonesian rule. A quarter century of struggle lay behind the vote.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit East Timor. The Assembly seated it that September. Few entries carried such weight of meaning. The UN had run the land's affairs during the change-over years. It then handed over a working state. Membership closed the long arc from occupation to self-rule.

Côte d'Ivoire's special political mission, MINUCI, is extended on 13 November 2003, until 4 February 2004. The mission supports the Linas-Marcoussis peace agreement and the Government of National Reconciliation. The Secretary-General is asked to report by 10 January 2004 on the mission's work and on whether the United Nations presence in the country should be reinforced.

Lebanon's force, UNIFIL, is extended until 31 January 2006 on 29 July 2005. The Secretary-General's July report is endorsed. Grave concern is voiced at the persistence of tensions and recent incidents across the Blue Line, the withdrawal line confirmed after Israel's 2000 pullout.

All acts of violence, including the recent cross-line incidents, are condemned. Lebanon's government is called on to extend its authority fully over the south and do more to secure the area. Both parties are told to give UNIFIL complete freedom of movement and to respect the Blue Line in its entirety. The renewal kept the force's interim mandate in place for another six months.

Sudan is the subject of Security Council resolution 1714, adopted in October 2006. The Council had a large peacekeeping mission in southern Sudan, UNMIS, sent to guard the peace deal that ended the long north-south civil war. Darfur, in the west, was burning at the same time, which sharpened every debate on Sudan.

The resolution extends the mandate of UNMIS and restates support for the peace deal between Khartoum and the south. It also voices concern over Darfur and the safety of aid workers. The text shows the Council trying to hold one peace together while another crisis grew.

Somalia's political process is pushed forward in Resolution 1814, adopted on 15 May 2008. Talks between Somali parties had just opened in Djibouti. The Secretary-General proposed an integrated UN strategy. He also proposed moving the UN Political Office for Somalia, UNPOS, from Nairobi into Somalia. Contingency planning was under way for a UN peacekeeping operation to succeed AMISOM. The humanitarian situation kept worsening.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council backs the strategy and the UNPOS relocation, with security arrangements to be set. It asks UNPOS to help the Transitional Federal Institutions write a constitution and hold a referendum and elections in 2009. It asks the Sanctions Committee to recommend, within 60 days, targeted measures against those blocking peace, threatening the institutions or AMISOM, or breaking the arms embargo. It calls for full AMISOM deployment, protection for World Food Programme shipping, and safe, unhindered aid delivery.

A judge of the International Court of Justice resigned in 2010, and Resolution 1914 deals with filling his seat. The Court is the main court of the United Nations. Judge Shi Jiuyong had resigned, with the resignation due to take effect on 28 May 2010. The Council adopted the resolution on 18 March 2010.

Under the Court's own rules, the Security Council fixes the date of the election for a new judge. The Council set that election for 29 June 2010. It would be held at a meeting of the Security Council and, on the same day, at a meeting of the General Assembly. Both bodies had to vote to fill the vacancy for the rest of the judge's term.

Yemen's political crisis is addressed in Resolution 2014, adopted on 21 October 2011. Months of protests had met force from the authorities, and hundreds of people, mostly civilians, had died. The Gulf Cooperation Council had put forward a plan for a transfer of power. Food and fuel prices were soaring, hunger was spreading, and Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula was gaining ground in parts of the country.

The Council strongly condemns the rights abuses by Yemen's authorities and by other actors and says those to blame must be held to account. It demands that all sides give up violence as a path to political goals. It backs signing and carrying out the Gulf plan at once, for a Yemeni-led shift to a new government and early presidential elections. It demands open access for aid and asks the Secretary-General to report within 30 days and every 60 days after that.

Resolution 214, adopted on 27 September 1965, shows a ceasefire failing in real time. India and Pakistan had accepted the Council's demand for a ceasefire in the Kashmir war, yet the Secretary-General's reports showed it was not holding. The Council expressed grave concern at the breakdown of a pledge both governments had made unconditionally.

It demanded that the parties urgently honor their commitment to observe the ceasefire. It further called on them to withdraw all armed personnel promptly, as the necessary step toward carrying out resolution 211, the Council's fuller ceasefire and withdrawal order from a week earlier. The war ended within days under combined diplomatic and military pressure, and a settlement conference followed at Tashkent.

Resolution 314, adopted on 28 February 1972 by thirteen votes to none with two abstentions, refuses to let Rhodesia sanctions fade. Some states had ignored the mandatory measures imposed in 1968 against the illegal white minority regime, helping it survive. The Council studied the sanctions committee's fourth report and an interim report from December 1971.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council reaffirmed that the sanctions would stay fully in force until their aims were completely achieved. It urged every state to apply all the sanctions resolutions in full, as the Charter requires. It also deplored the attitude of governments that had kept giving the illegal regime moral, political, and economic support.

Resolution 414, adopted without a vote in September 1977, warns against faits accomplis around Famagusta in Cyprus. Cyprus's ambassador had written in August about developments in the new Famagusta area, the resort district of Varosha, emptied in 1974 and held behind fences. Statements to the Council indicated that no settlement of the area was in fact under way, and the parties and the Secretary-General addressed the reports.

The Council expressed concern at the situation and called on everyone to avoid unilateral actions anywhere in Cyprus that might damage the chances of a just and peaceful solution. It voiced concern at the lack of progress in the intercommunal talks and urged the two communities' representatives to resume negotiations under the Secretary-General as soon as possible.

The Iran-Iraq war, then nearly two years old, is taken up again in Resolution 514, adopted unanimously on 12 July 1982. The Council said it was deeply concerned at the conflict's prolongation, the heavy loss of life, and the material damage, all endangering peace and security. Mediation by the Secretary-General, the Non-Aligned Movement, and the Islamic Conference had not stopped the fighting.

The Council called for a ceasefire, with all fighting stopped at once. It further called for forces to pull back behind the borders the world recognizes. It decided to send a team of UN observers to verify, confirm, and supervise both steps, and asked the Secretary-General to report on the arrangements needed.

Somalia's collapse fills Resolution 814, adopted in March 1993. Famine and drought, compounded by civil war, had destroyed the country's means of production. The US-led Unified Task Force, UNITAF, had opened a secure space for relief work under Resolution 794. A transition to an expanded UN Operation in Somalia, UNOSOM II, was now needed, while violence continued and disarmament of the factions remained essential.

The Council approves the Secretary-General's report of 3 March 1993, which set out that transition. It thanks him for convening the Conference on National Reconciliation in Addis Ababa, following the January meeting where Somali parties signed three agreements. It stresses broad representation at such talks, including community leaders, women, professionals, and elders. Throughout, the text insists Somalis themselves bear the final responsibility for reconciliation and rebuilding, and that relief and the revival of institutions and the economy must go together.

UNPROFOR reinforcements are authorized by Resolution 914, adopted on 27 April 1994. The UN Protection Force was stretched across Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina as the wars there went on. The Secretary-General had sent a series of reports and a letter in March 1994 recommending more personnel. The Council said it was determined to strengthen the force so it could fulfil its mandate, and to protect its security and freedom of movement.

Acting under Chapter VII for UNPROFOR in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Council welcomes the Secretary-General's reports. It authorizes an increase of up to 6,550 additional troops, 150 military observers, and 275 civilian police monitors. This comes on top of the reinforcement already approved in Resolution 908 (1994) a month earlier. The Council decides to remain actively seized of the matter.
unamuno-niebla-1914:
Miguel de Unamuno published Niebla in 1914, a Spanish novel he called a nivola, his own term for the form. Augusto Perez is a rich and idle man who falls in love almost by chance. His life drifts until doubts about his own reality grow. He travels to Salamanca to confront Unamuno himself, as his author.

Augusto argues that he, not the writer, should decide whether he lives or dies. The scene turns the usual rules of fiction upside down. Fog, or niebla, is the book's image for uncertainty about life and self. The novel is a landmark of early metafiction, long before the term was common.
underhill-practical-mysticism-1914:
Evelyn Underhill was already known for her large scholarly study Mysticism when she published Practical Mysticism in 1914. The short book brings the mystic life down to earth for ordinary readers with jobs and families. It serves as the popular companion to her heavier work.

Underhill argues that contemplation, the quiet attention to God, is not a rare gift but a normal power of the soul. She gives plain steps: still the mind, gather the heart, and look steadily beyond the self. The book appeared as war began, and she meant it as training for hard times.
us-amendment-14:
Ratified in 1868, the Fourteenth Amendment rewrote the rules of American citizenship after the Civil War. Congress proposed it during Reconstruction, when lawmakers sought to protect the rights of people freed from slavery. Its first section declares that anyone born or naturalized in the United States is a citizen.

The amendment bars states from taking life, liberty, or property without due process of law. It also promises every person equal protection of the laws and reshapes how states count in Congress. Courts have used these broad words in fights over civil rights for more than a century. Few texts shape American law so often.
veblen-instinct-workmanship-1914:
Thorstein Veblen traced industry to a basic human drive in The Instinct of Workmanship, from 1914. The instinct, as he names it, is the urge to make things well and fit for use. Against it stands the predatory instinct, the urge to seize, rule, and show off. Their long contest forms his anthropology of industry.

Veblen follows workmanship from early crafts through the machine age. Habits of making shape thought itself, in his account, across whole societies. The book digs the deepest foundation under his institutional economics. It explains why he distrusted business control of production. Readers meet his thought at its root. The dry irony is ever present.
vinogradoff-common-sense-in-law-1914:
Paul Vinogradoff published Common-Sense in Law in 1914, his most approachable book. Vinogradoff was a Russian historian who had become a professor of jurisprudence at Oxford, an exile at home in English ways. He wrote the book for general readers, to show that law is not a lawyer's mystery.

He explains law as the plain person's reason worked into a system: customs tested, rules refined, and common sense given forms that courts can use. Chapters treat the growth of law, the role of judges, and the meaning of rights in everyday disputes. His learning is deep but worn lightly, so the reader forgets the depths below. The book teaches England the wisdom of its own courts from the pen of an adopted son. It remains a model of how to write about law without jargon.
wallas-great-society-1914:
Wallas named the modern world The Great Society in his 1914 study of its strains. Rail, press, and industry had bound millions into one vast system. Human nature, formed in small groups, fit that scale badly. His book gives a psychological analysis of the mismatch.

He studies how thought, feeling, and habit cope with bigness in every sphere. War, boredom, and shallow public opinion appear as symptoms of the strain. Wallas seeks ways to humanize the great society rather than flee it. The work extends the argument of his Human Nature in Politics. It spoke to reformers facing a mass age. Its questions remain open today.
weeks-among-the-primitive-bakongo-1914:
John H. Weeks spent thirty years among the Bakongo of the lower Congo, and Among the Primitive Bakongo of 1914 distills that life. Weeks, a Baptist missionary, writes of nkisi, the sacred objects the period called fetishes, and of secret societies and village religion. His long residence gave him scenes no short visit could buy.

The book moves between belief and daily practice: charms, oaths, markets, and mourning in the villages he knew. Weeks's judgments carry his mission's stamp, yet his store of fact is rich. The work stands as a first-hand record of Kongo religious life before deep change.
yeats-responsibilities-1914:
Responsibilities, published in 1914, marks Yeats's turn from dreamy early verse to a harder public voice. The title is a claim: the poet now answers to Ireland, to family honor, and to history.

The collection opens with a bitter motto about the family's money and contains 'September 1913', his attack on a Dublin grown mean and material. 'To a Friend whose Work has come to Nothing' defends Lady Gregory against her critics. Gone is the twilight of the early books; in its place stands argument, grief, and pride. Yeats himself dated his mature style from this volume.
yoga-sutras-woods-1914: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali in James Haughton Woods's 1914 translation, subtitled The Book of the Spiritual Man. Its 196 aphorisms map the path of meditation. This edition preserves that yoga classic. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol14:
In Volume XIV, from Liverpool in 1872, the Journal of Discourses passes another year of Utah preaching into print. Brigham Young speaks alongside his counsellors, the Twelve, and other elders, all caught by shorthand reporters. The sermons had been heard in tabernacle and settlement alike before crossing the sea to the press.

The set's long perspective is its gift: teachings can be followed as they echo and shift across decades. Here the record shows a mature church instructing a second generation. Volume XIV keeps the doctrinal thread unbroken in the longest sermon series of its kind.
